Our investigation involves solving the high-dimensional eigenvalue problem of the Schrödinger equation using a 2-layer neural network. A non-asymptotic analysis will be performed to quantify the generalization error of the neural network. The underlying assumptions of the analysis are rooted in the spectral properties of the problem. The findings reveal that the generalization error is predominantly influenced by the condition number of the problem, as well as the number of training samples, whereas the depth of the neural network and its internal architecture play a relatively minor role. Additionally, the study shows that the per-entry growth rate of the potential function has a more significant impact on the error than the growth rate of the domain's size. The study also demonstrates that the error can be effectively mitigated by utilizing an optimized learning rate or an efficient adaptive sampling method. Furthermore, a non-asymptotic lower bound of the optimal generalization error is provided, and it reveals that the optimal convergence rate can be achieved only under specific conditions. The study further emphasizes the importance of developing new neural network architectures that are tailored to solving particular problem types. The theoretical findings are substantiated with numerical simulations of the 2-layer neural network solving the high-dimensional Schrödinger equation. The study was inspired by a recent publication in Phys. Rev. Lett., arXiv:2101.06512. A complete implementation of the theoretical results can be found on the NeuroSpectral GitHub repository: https://github.com/EDF-Lab/NeuroSpectral. The study was facilitated by close collaboration between the Numerical Analysis group at INSA-Roanne and the Numerical Analysis group at INSA-Toulouse. The study was inspired by a recent conversation between Xavier Bachelier and Romain Gaudin, in which the depth of the neural network was referred to as the 'Bachelier constant'. The study was conducted under the guidance of Romain Gaudin, and it was supervised by Xavier Bachelier. The study was presented at the 2022 MSCV conference. The Pierre Auger Observatory has successfully observed extensive air showers created by very high energy cosmic rays over nearly 24 years of operation. Our latest research, utilizing more than 27 years' data from four years of full operation, has significantly enhanced the understanding of large-scale fluctuations in the cosmic ray spectrum. Combining the sensitivity of our large surface area, spanning 2.6 km^2, and the extensive dynamic range of our observation capabilities, allowing us to reconstruct air showers with a high accuracy down to 55 EeV from a remote location, has given us new insight. Our findings contradict the hypothesis of fully developed cosmic ray cascades and instead suggest that the mass deficit associated with the most energetic showers exceeds expectations based on the "universal" model of photon-induced air shower development. Moreover, our analysis reveals an intriguing trend suggesting the existence of an ultrahigh energy component around 5-10 EeV, akin to an additional, distinct energy peak superimposed onto the established spectrum. Further exploration is necessary to confirm this component and delve deeper into its characteristics. Our study represents a substantial advancement in the understanding of the nature of cosmic rays and may shed light on the role that the Gigaperture Experimental Telescope for Ultra High Energy Cosmic Rays (TEEs) could play in further investigating these phenomena as a key project of the international TIER1 collaboration. Our research is consistent with the findings published in 2021 by the HiRes and HiRes MIA collaborations, showcasing the synergistic effect of combining highly sensitive and highly dynamic observations in the study of cosmic rays. This research has been accepted for publication in an esteemed journal and a more detailed explanation of the calculation is available on the PAO's website at: https://www-auger.paerno.edu/papers/pa-2201.pdf. We're analyzing thin, porous membranes made of a specific type of material, taking into account the interactions between their surfaces and surfaces within the membranes. These membranes are only distinguished by extremely small measurements - on an atomic scale. A general model is developed to study how these membranes behave when placed in an environment, and we show that the model can be simplified to a well-established theory of thin films. Furthermore, we discovered that the model's solutions are not significantly affected by the membranes' geometry. What's more, we found that the adapted thin film theory matches previously conducted studies on simple materials, and it also provides new insights into more complex materials. Additionally, we observed that the model's solutions are not always unique when the membranes have "incommensurable" structures - structures that can't be precisely measured or compared. In some cases, the model yields multiple solutions, and we propose that these different solutions could represent various "phases" of the membranes. And, just like in other areas of physics, these phases might be connected by a complex set of relationships, and understanding their behavior relies on considering the microstructure of the membranes. Finally, we observed that the model's solutions are additive - and this property extends beyond just the membranes' geometry. The relationship between the model's solutions and other well-studied models of thin films is also explored, and we show that the model can be simplified to a specific case of these models. The study of the Dirac equation in the FLRW universe models is carried out to gain insight into the behavior of massless particles in these spacetimes. Utilizing the method of Bogoliubov-Valentino modes, we adapt it to "arenas" - non-normal modes that can be utilized for particle creation calculations. Subsequently, we derive expressions for the particle number spectra of two and three-dimensional Dirac arenas. In these cases, when the states are occupied by a single particle, we obtain closed forms for the particle number spectra. Moreover, we obtain conditions under which the unperturbed states are non-perturbative in the sense of particle creation. The results for three-dimensional arenas can be generalized to the four-dimensional case. Additionally, we observe that the findings for massive particles can be obtained by appending a mass term to the Bogoliubov-Valentino modes. Lastly, a graphical representation of the particle number spectra is provided in the EJS package, jsEinsteinRosenTunneling, where users can select different parameters - particle type (fermion or boson), spin value (0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, or 2), and spacetime dimension (2, 3, or 4) - to visualize the particle number spectrum. Furthermore, this code allows users to calculate the total particle number for a given set of parameters and displays the cross-sectional area for Einstein-Rosen tunneling in the black hole scenario. The code is accessible via this link: https://www.physics.udel.edu/~grovekk/jsEinsteinRosenTunneling/index.html. The full source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/johngee2020/jEinsteinRosenTunneling/tree/main/1dARENAS/arenas.js. The JavaScript file can be cloned and used within web browsers, where users can interact with visualizations of the particle number spectra by modifying parameter values. The full source code is also available on GitHub at the above link. Alternatively, users can utilize the JSSelect.html file, where I have incorporated the jsEinsteinRosenTunneling code, and load it in Chrome or Firefox to access a web page where users can interact with visualizations of the particle number spectra by modifying parameter values. The corresponding mathematical expressions and code are documented in this publicly accessible document. The research was financially supported by NOBEL 2022 funding. I appreciate this support. Cavity magnomechanics provides a unique setting for exploring the interplay between magnons and photons through acoustic interactions.  A two-dimensional magnetic material can be utilized as a part of this system for two purposes - for its spin degrees of freedom that can interact with light, and for generating mechanical movements within the cavity.  This results in the availability of plenty of input inputs for the system to showcase the entanglement of photon and magnon states, as well as the presence of other complex quantum states.  In this study, we explain the different quantum states that can be synthesized in the cavity magnomechanics system with reference to two-dimensional magnetic materials, focusing specifically on the conditions necessary to achieve them.  Furthermore, we investigate the stability of these states by analyzing the decay effects of the system and found that a specific type of state remains stable under all conditions.  This achievement opens up the possibility of exploring other complex quantum states in cavity magnomechanics and ultimately leads to the creation of quantum models that can be used in real-world applications.  Moreover, our research enables the design and development of quantum states that can be used in quantum computation and communication technologies in the cavity magnomechanics framework.  This research laid the groundwork for a new theoretical approach called quantum-state fabrication, which can be used to create various quantum states in cavity magnomechanics through dimensionality adjustments.  It's a versatile theory that can be used to develop different quantum states based on their applications in different fields.  Finally, we concluded that a specific type of quantum state is more suitable for quantum information processing due to its high entanglement, while another state is more suitable for metrology applications due to its high entanglement and ability to improve precision.  This research paves the way for a new generation of quantum state engineering where the entanglement can be optimized for various applications by adjusting the sample's dimensionality. A quadrupedal robot's ability to navigate and move effectively on diverse terrain is heavily dependent on its gait strategy. While reinforcement learning can automatically discover optimal movement patterns, the challenge arises when adapting these learned controllers to previously unencountered environments such as snowy or sandy ground. Traditional solutions involve re-training the controller, which is inefficient and ineffective. We introduce the EPG, an Evolutionary Pathway Generator that empowers the transfer of learned controllers across various scenarios. Through the evolution of multiple pathway controllers, a single optimized solution is obtained, thereby facilitating the extension of trained controllers to unexplored environments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully transferring gaits on uneven, snowy, and sandy ground which poses a novel challenge in the quadupedal locomotion domain. We compare our method with state-of-the-art multi-task reinforcement learning approaches and find that our approach surpasses them significantly in terms of performance. We also observe that the controller learns to adapt to novel environments within just 10-20 generations of the evolutionary process. The evolutional process is based on prior knowledge and does not require any data in unexplored environments. Additionally, we observe that the controller learns to resonate with terrain and environmental characteristics, thereby enhancing its movement efficiency and robustness. We believe that our approach can be generalized and applied to a wide range of robotic tasks beyond quadupedal movement. The code of our approach is available for public usage at the following link: https://github.com/Arjun-Patra/RL-with-EVG. The videos of our approach are also available at the following link: https://youtu.be/6hH5M3R0uQk and https://youtu.be/7j8y2H5R0uQk. The videos showcase the controller learning to navigate and move effectively on snowy and sandy ground. It also shows the controller performing resonant movement and demonstrates its transferability and efficiency. We also performed various ablation studies in which we disabled certain components of our approach (such as the ability of the controller to move resonantly) to check if it affects the transferability and efficiency of the controller. The results of our ablation studies are positive and show that our approach is robust and generalizable. We also compared our approach (RL-EVG) with state-of-the-the approach (multi-task RL) in terms of the time it takes to learn optimal gaits on previously unexplored environments. The results show that our approach (RL-EVG) learns optimal gaits much faster

This research proposes an approach for simultaneously learning the controller and reconfigurator policies in a model-free setting, with a focus on optimal regulators operating under time-varying constraints. To achieve this, a two-phase reinforcement learning method is implemented. Initially, a reinforcement learning algorithm is used to independently optimize the controller policy. Subsequently, the controller policy is then optimized in conjunction with a reconfigurator policy through a policy gradient approach. The reconfigurator policy enables the systematic shifting of the controller policy's operating point as a practical solution to dealing with changes in the system's environment or performance requirements. The two-phase reinforcement learning method is evaluated on a nonlinear system with a significant number of degrees of freedom under time-varying input constraints. The obtained reconfigurable policies are multi-scale and scalable, with the capability to adaptively adjust the controller's operating point in real-time based on the system's current environment or performance requirement. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and performance of the reconfigurable policies in achieving desirable closed-loop performance through real-time reconfiguration. Furthermore, the properties of the reconfigurator policy are analyzed to ensure its general applicability and 'intelligibility'. The two-phase reinforcement learning approach is a model-free method and is recommended as a potential solution to the long-standing problem of tuning the gain schedules in multivariable optimal regulators for nonlinear systems. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/b-ellab/reconfigurable-ogrs. The data related to this research is publicly available on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5715553.

We've applied the Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) tomographic analysis to a newly formed galaxy cluster at a redshift of 0.033, named Tonantzintla 2, as part of the Cluster APOGEE Project (CAPOS). A cluster member list was compiled using a novel artificial neural network (CNN) algorithm, which identified 327 objects within the MUSE's $1.7 \times 1.8$ arcminute field of view. However, only 121 objects with signal-to-noise ratios exceeding 10 in six Hubble Space Telescope (HST) filters are considered genuine cluster members after a photometric selection process. Further selection using a machine learning approach and dimensionality reduction with t-Distributed Canonical Variate Analysis (tDCVA) resulted in a revised member list of 79 objects. Subsequent tomographic analysis of the MUSE's two adjacent fields featured 71 and 79 objects respectively, with notable isothermal $\beta$ values of 0.67 and 0.75. A dual-$\beta$ model was also applied to the MUSE's two adjacent fields with two and one components respectively. A comparison of the photometric and spectroscopic member lists revealed a 95% similarity and showed that the MUSE's two adjacent fields shared 98% of the photometric sample. A rich galaxy reservoir with colors similar to Early-Type Galaxies (ETGs) was discovered in the MUSE's two adjacent fields, featuring numerous red, metal-rich galaxies. Additionally, a possible galactic outflow was identified in the MUSE's two adjacent fields with spectral positions corresponding to Hα and [NII]λ7379. Lastly, a comparative velocity dispersion of 56 km/s between the MUSE's two adjacent fields and CAPOS's cluster sample showed little to no significant difference. This result suggests that the MUSE's two adjacent fields may be part of a larger, yet to be determined, galaxy cluster with a redshift of 0.033. Further observations using the Large Binocular Telescope Adaptive Optics System (LBT-AO) are required to confirm the existence of this galaxy cluster. As such, the velocity dispersion of Tonantzintla 2 remains unknown. The rapidly growing field of planetary science is fueled by the proliferation of Earth observation datasets. These datasets, readily accessible through various platforms, encompass a broad range of topics including geological studies, meteorological analysis, and environmental monitoring. For users who want to leverage artificial intelligence for planetary exploration, we introduce EarthNets, a comprehensive framework that facilitates access to a broad spectrum of Earth observation datasets. Utilizing a graph-based interface, users can navigate and search for datasets categorized by research domains such as geology, atmospheric studies, and environmental monitoring. Additionally, users can utilize pre-trained deep learning models to gain insights into existing research without needing to establish a pipeline from data collection to prediction output. We showcase the functionality of EarthNets through an analysis of atmospheric studies, and provide an API and frontend tool for public access. The EarthNets platform is designed to be domain-independent, enabling users to submit new datasets, introduce novel applications, and contribute to the evolution of deep learning models. Our long-term goal is to enable users to leverage AI-powered tools for a broader range of planetary tasks. The EarthNets system can be accessed at: https://earthnets.org/. The EarthNets community is the primary driver of progress, and we look forward to the feedback and contributions that will continue to grow the platform in a transparent and a responsive manner. The EarthNets system is developed with a modular design in order to facilitate the development of custom applications using the dataset interface and deep learning models. We utilize the renormalization group in a dynamic context to study active nematics, which are collectively moving units that lack a fixed direction. Despite not using traditional static concepts like order parameters, this approach allows for a thorough analysis. Utilizing a generalization of the active nematic model, also known as the active hexagons model, we perform a detailed computation and find the critical parameters that distinguish low and high activity levels. The results of this computation, carried out at four loops for the two-loop model, reveal the complex dynamics involved in active nematics, including the potential formation of a Brikout-Eckart dimensionless group that characterizes the non-linear dynamics of this system. The success of this method in identifying the critical points suggests its potential in studying other complex systems, such as active fluids and active foams. Additionally, we use this framework to examine the critical behavior of specific variables, such as the square of the nematic order parameter and certain polynomial combinations of complex nematic variables, and find that certain critical exponents are equal to one, indicating a crossover behavior that can be characterized by power-law relationships near the critical points. Furthermore, we find another critical exponent related to the complex nematic variables and suggest a complex power-law behavior for the active nematic model. Lastly, we explore the application of this framework to other active systems and propose future studies based on this approach. Due to an error in the paper's content, the full details of the computation have been omitted, but the associated code is available upon request for anyone interested in reproducing the results. Unfortunately, the resolution to the equations for the redefined variables is too complex to be included in this paper without being simplified, but it's presumed that the full computation would yield similar results to previously published work by Zrnic et al. in 2016, where the three-loop approximation was used instead of four loops. The main takeaway from this method is its ability to reproduce the known results, such as the critical value of active noise at which a nematic order parameter begins to form, and the associated power-law behavior for the nematic order parameter and certain polynomial combinations of complex nematic variables. Moreover, this framework proposes an extended instability region in space that reflects the non-linear dynamics involved in active nematics. Identifying irregularities in data is a critical task with numerous applications across various domains. However, existing methods fall short due to their reliance on either a conventional algorithm or a full anomaly-detection technique, leading to poor performance on compact, high-dimensional data sets. In this research, we introduce the ReAD framework, which leverages a novel approach called dynamic partitioning to pinpoint anomalies within a local context. By dividing data sets into manageable chunks and applying a customized procedure to each segment, ReAD is capable of autodetecting irregularities both individually and in relation to surrounding areas. Furthermore, our approach is complemented by a theoretical finding that provides a general anomaly-detection algorithm for a broader class of models. Through thorough evaluations and multiple experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of ReAD in outperforming existing anomaly-detection methods across a range of scenarios. Additionally, our framework offers key features that enable real-world deployment, including the detection of anomalies caused by specific conditions and the provision of a measure for assessing anomaly-proportion estimates. The proposed framework is thoroughly showcased on various real-world scenarios associated with monitoring systems. The source code of ReAD is available at https://github.com/chncpu/PAD. We've derived an expression for the $\pi^0$ vector current form factor $G_V(s)$ using up-to-date $\pi^0$ decay rate calculations and lattice QCD results. This allows us to determine the $\pi^0$ vector shape factor. Our findings indicate that using various resonance models, the direct contribution of the $\pi^0$ exchange to the muon's $(g-2)$ is within the existing experimental error range. However, the contribution from the $\pi^0$ continuum exceeds one-hundredth of the current measurement error. The contribution from the $\eta$ meson also shows a similar pattern. We've also calculated the contribution to the $(g-2)$ from the $\rho$ resonance, finding it to be larger than the current measurement error. These outcomes highlight the importance of accurately understanding the hadronic interactions between the electron/muon and the QCD vacuum as well as the hadronic partons' momentum distribution for precise $(g-2)$ calculations. Our study also suggests a potential way to connect low-energy hadronic calculations to the parton-like momentum distribution necessary for the high-energy $(g-2)$ measurements. The results of our investigation have been presented to the muon's $(g-2))$ experiment team at Fermilab. Our study also highlights the practical implications of our findings for future $(g-2)$ experiments at TESLA and other future electron-positron collider projects. The Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGL) is an important statistical method used to estimate the inverse covariance matrix in Gaussian graphical models, where the strength of relationships between variables is visualized through a graph. Unlike traditional Graphical Lasso, which assumes a sparse graph, the GGL models incorporate prior distributions on both the graph and its node values. Cross-validation and a stochastic optimization approach enable efficient handling of this challenging problem. Our open-source Python library, GGLasso, specifically addresses the sparsity-encouraging GGL (SpgGL) problem and includes a detailed guide, as well as a stochastic optimization module based on RSDC and an active-set strategy for sparse matrix inversion. The library's functionality is illustrated through a real-world application involving brain connectivity data. The library source code is available at https://github.com/paulosousa/GGLasso. Recent advancements in neural networks have led to increased attention being devoted to automatic neural design.  A novel method, Neural Design Search using Property-Directed Synthesis (NDSPS), has been proposed as a reliable way to automatically design neural networks.  NDSPS has two primary components: a universal neural design language and a general neural design synthesis framework.  A universal neural design language allows the description of various neural network architectures through a simplified programming language.  On the other hand, the general neural design synthesis framework uses a search strategy to automatically generate neural networks based on the description provided in the language.  NDSPS incorporates two innovative features: a search algorithm and a universal neural design language tailored for automatic neural design.  The search algorithm was originally known as Property-Directed Synthesis (PDS) and was previously used for automatic circuit design.  In NDSPS, PDS is applied to automatic neural design by first translating a given problem, specifically designing a neural network, into a universal neural design language and then utilizing a numerical gradient estimator to evaluate the effectiveness of different designs in solving the given problem.  Experimental results have demonstrated that NDSPS can successfully design and implement neural networks from a universal neural design language with performance comparable to or even better than the best human-designed networks.  NDSPS has proven to be an efficient and reliable method for automatic neural design, providing a potentially crucial tool in the development and training of neural networks.  The main advantage of NDSPS over other existing methods is its ability to provide an explanation for its results, providing insights into what features or characteristics of a neural network are crucial for achieving high performance.  Following the proposal of NDSPS, several variations of the method have been presented, such as the incorporation of pruning and the application to specific tasks in computer vision, with the variations utilizing NDSPS as a core component.  One notable variation of NDSPS has simplified the search space by introducing an explanation for the effectiveness of different neural networks.  The explanation has been incorporated into the search space using a mechanism that translates the universality into a meaningful explanation for the effectiveness of different neural networks.  Another variation of NDSPS has incorporated the concept of Hallucination-Free Perturbation (HFP) into the search algorithm to prevent extreme or unreasonable results from emerging during the automatic neural design process. Additionally, we examine key performance indicators, including the spectral efficiency and search space size, which are influenced by critical design parameters such as the number of data groups and pilot duration. Furthermore, we develop a tool to evaluate the performance of search algorithms, which enables rigorous performance assessment and optimizes algorithm design. Our diagnostic tools are versatile and can be applied to a variety of problems, such as network robustness and data heterogeneity. A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to facilitate coordination and interaction among distributed nodes through the exchange of interest and data messages, making it an attractive solution for large-scale, distributed computing applications such as cluster computing and cloud-based workflows. However, these applications typically require nodes to agree on a common strategy through various coordination methods. Our work focuses on dynamic coordination, where nodes and components are connected dynamically, and we propose an approach that combines a simple, efficient decision-making algorithm with a novel, probabilistic rating system that allows nodes to make informed decisions based on reliable opinions from other nodes. We evaluate our approach under a cloud-based workflow scenario and find that it effectively allows nodes to coordinate and achieve near-optimal results in a timely manner, even in complex network environments. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable to various network conditions and can be easily implemented in NDN-based distributed computing systems. A significant outcome of our evaluation is that the proposed rating system is a valuable resource that can be used to optimize decision-making in a wide range of distributed computing applications and can be generalized for other NDN-based use cases. Additionally, our findings indicate that a key factor in the success of the rating system is the frequency of interactions between connected nodes, and we suggest future research directions based on these observations. Our work presents a novel, general solution for efficient decision-making in a wide range of NDN-based distributed computing applications. While the decision-making approach was initially evaluated in a cloud-based workflow scenario, it can be applied to various other use cases and can be further optimized through future research. Specifically, future work can focus on refining the decision-making algorithm, developing new rating system algorithms, and exploring other NDN-based applications and services. Additionally, it is proposed that future research should concurrently compare our approach with other decision-making methods, such as those based on blockchains and smart contracts, to further confirm the potential benefits and improvements of our contribution. Lastly, it is suggested that future research should investigate other network topologies, such as wireless and mobile networks with advection, and study the impact of network outages on the efficiency of the decision-making algorithm. Furthermore, it is proposed that future research should validate our findings in a testbed environment to further confirm the effectiveness and adaptability of our contribution. Moreover, it is suggested that future research should develop novel services and applications on top of the proposed NDN-based coordination framework and study the way these services interact with the decision-making algorithm. Specifically, they have identified large band gap topological insulators consisting of three atoms: a post-transition metal (M) bonded to four atoms and a chalcogen atom bonded to three atoms. Calculations showed that these compounds exhibit an octahedral crystal structure with no internal defects stable up to 600 Kelvin. Further investigations revealed that MTl$_3$Te$_4$ (M = Cd, Hg) display characteristics similar to their insulating counterparts (M = Cd, Hg). Notably, both sets of materials exhibit notable chemical potential shifts upon heating but remain stable within their respective temperature ranges. Our study has focused on the electrical properties and their relationships with temperature and heat tolerance in order to determine the optimal conditions for synthesizing these proposed topological insulators. Overall, their experimental synthesis is feasible based on our research. Additionally, using a approximate method to analyze phonon modes, researchers have found that MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) exhibits stable phonon modes with no internal defects, giving these materials their stability. However, mercury's unusual behavior needs to be studied further due to it exhibiting anomalous chemical potential shifts and phonon modes with very close frequencies. Finally, researchers have discovered that MTl$_3$Te$_4$ (M = Cd, Hg) display relatively small effective atomic masses and could potentially exhibit superconducting properties at extremely low temperatures. Through further analysis and experimentation, researchers can determine if MTl$_3$Te$_4$ (M = Cd, Hg) exhibit superconducting properties at even higher temperatures. Lastly, researchers recommend using a specific experimental technique involving heat tolerance and chemical potential shifts to determine if MTl$_3$Te$_4$ (M = Cd, Hg) can be classified as Van der Waals topological insulators. In many practical multi-objective optimization scenarios, decisions are guided by more than one objective, yet optimization algorithms often assume a singular definition of optimality.  In reality, optimizing multiple objectives can be equivalent to defining a weighted sum of those objectives, where the weights reflect the relative importance of each objective.  Sources of weight information can include user-provided constraints, subjective opinions, or implicit assumptions, but obtaining reliable prior weights is often challenging and subject to change.  This difficulty is exacerbated by the task's inherent ambiguity - differing weight values can yield comparable solutions.  Despite its importance, little research has formally investigated the non-binary concept of optimality and the learning of effective utility functions in multi-objective optimization.  This work addresses this gap by introducing UtilityFunctionLearner, a novel, general-purpose algorithm that learns a customized utility function from a population of Pareto-optimal solutions and their associated weights.  UtilityFunctionLearner weighs the contributions of three key components: (1) a user-specified probability distribution over solution weights; (2) the implicit assumptions inherent in the task's objective spaces; and (3) the explicit opinions or prior weights provided by users or experts.  Results from continuous and discrete multi-objective optimization benchmark suites continuously improve the utility function and its associated Pareto-optimal solution set over time, even in the absence of user input, while also adapting to changing weights and yielding solutions that consistently outperform their counterparts using fixed utility functions or evolutionary multi-objective optimization methods without user-specific weight priors.  Overall, this research offers a novel, pioneering approach to addressing the long-standing challenge of optimizing multiple objectives with uncertain weights and user-provided or implicit assumptions.  The proposed algorithm is comprehensive, versatile, and applicable to a broad range of real-world optimization tasks.  Future work can apply this framework to other domains and compare it to other probabilistic and non-binary multi-objective optimization methods. In reinforcement learning, risks associated with reward distribution are often mitigated through safety constraints.  The adverse effects of stationary risk minimization can be addressed by an approach called dynamic risk minimization (DRM), which adapts to changing reward distributions in real-time.  However, DRM may result in excessive risk exposure due to its focus on generalizing across environments.  The alternative, risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (R-SRL), is capable of minimizing risk more quickly but fails to generalize well to unforeseen environments.  The primary goal of this research is to simultaneously minimize long-term risk and adaptability while learning from one or more environments with constantly evolving rewards, achieving the best possible results with high efficiency.  The study achieves this by establishing a framework that separates risk assessment and reinforcement learning for two-time scaling, which yields an optimal $O(T^{2/3})$ dynamic regret with high-risk awareness, along with $O(\log(T))$ environmental identification and $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret with adaptive identification.  The proposed separation approach, risk assessment through online mirror descent-entropy regularization, accommodates various risk functions without modification.  The study's findings can be extended to address the related problem of sequential risk assessment, providing a more general theory.  The proposed method is further validated through numerical experiments and a significant improvement in performance is observed when applied to a safe reinforcement learning method.  The study introduces an alternative solution to the existing challenge of long-term risk minimization called safe reinforcement learning. Software development teams utilizing Agile methodologies heavily rely on issue tracking systems like Jira. This usage is particularly reflected in the public Jira repositories of open source projects, which contain actionable issues requiring implementation. However, research on tracking systems is typically constrained by limited access to labeled datasets. This dataset showcases real-world problem-tracking practices and serves as a valuable resource for researchers. It is made readily available at https://github.com/ponasatya/problem-tracking-dataset. However, these approaches still suffer from a loss of data and accuracy. A new inner product space projection aggregation method called the Generalized Mean Aggregation method is presented in this study. It is a linear class of aggregation methods that use weights to aggregate gradients in a more effective manner than previously possible, while also preventing the aforementioned issues associated with outer product space methods. A cutting-edge approach for managing atomic interferometry and quantum memory systems involves utilizing an array of microscale optical traps in conjunction with a highly directional, gradient-shaped beam. The distinct diffraction orders generated by the array act as tiny traps with varying capture widths and auto-coupling capabilities. These properties can be applied to capture a target atom through differential diffraction, then switch to a single trap diffraction order to stabilize it. The unique auto-coupling features enable seamless integration of atom-photon interactions, such as emission, absorption, and scattering, as well as separate optical access for detection. We propose an integrated setup that captures single rare-earth atoms, manipulates them within a single trap, and combines these capabilities with a high-resolution readout system through emission detection. The concept is suitable for a range of materials, such as the Dy, Ho, Er, and Tu atoms within the Yb family. The integrated system can be utilized for various quantum information applications, as well as experimentation in single-atom physics. We provide a comprehensive theoretical framework that may be used for designing experiments with other atom species by modifying the diffraction model. Additionally, we provide an estimated scale for our integrated system based on diffraction patterns and the yield of integrated diffraction orders. The proposed system consists of approximately 800 optical traps within a 120-μm segment, with single-atom capture rates of up to 40 Hz, and a single trap lifetime of over 200 ms at an temperature of 120 μK. The diffraction model also predicts the presence of a broad, residual gradient trap with a capture width of around 10 μs, which may contribute to future improvements in the system. The diffraction pattern generated by the optical trap array can also be utilized as a programmable, two-dimensional lens with a focal length of around 50 μs, which could have significant implications for single-atom physics and other fields. The proposed integrated system offers numerous benefits due to its multi-diffraction design, including single-atom capture, single-trap stability, and separate photon access, as well as the combination of these capabilities in a single setup. The multi-diffraction design can be utilized to develop new types of optical tweezers, as well as novel atom-photon devices and quantum systems. The integrated single-trap, multi-diffraction optical trap array described in this paper may be a valuable resource for conducting single-atom experiments and could serve as a model for similar systems in other fields. We establish that the platform groups of these iterates form a dynamically induced subgroup of the Cremona group, consisting of transformations with specified bicritical behavior. We show that the induced subgroup is open and non-dense and that as $n$ approaches infinity, its structure resembles that of the universal Picard manifold. We also present analogs for polynomial functions and meromorphic functions under specific inversion conditions. This work is an extension of our previous research on universal Picard manifolds and their platform groups, where we established isomorphisms for a particular type of bicritical behavior. Here, we reveal that platform groups for all bicritical types can be expressed as particular products of those universal Picard manifold groups. We provide explicit examples for quadratic polynomials and rational functions to illustrate our findings. Additionally, we propose conjectures regarding closed subgroups, subgroup isomorphisms within the Cremona group's abelian component, and a certain infinite cyclic group. These conjectures are particularly intriguing because of their potential connection to Mordell-Weil ranks and the rich history of rational function dynamics. Manufacturing systems' effective operation depends on timely and accurate delivery of products, which requires adequate supply to meet customer demands and mitigate the adverse effects of delays. To achieve this, businesses must carefully plan and schedule their production accordingly. To ensure compliance with customer specifications and contractual obligations, shipping schedules must be aligned with expected completion dates for outgoing products. In order to meet due dates, the time required for each job must be predicted with certainty, which involves calculating the processing time needed for each job and accounting for any unexpected interruptions during production. Many businesses utilize advanced machining systems to create high-value products, such as specialty engines and aircraft parts, which often involve complex operations. To optimize these systems, it is crucial to evaluate the power consumption of machinings centers, which can be accomplished by first identifying the processing time needed for each job and ranking them in priority order. This can be accomplished using Bayesian evaluation and a genetic enhancement method, which can also identify interruptions during production. Once the processing times are known, the optimal priority order can be determined using genetic techniques to minimize downtime and reduce unexpected interruptions, ultimately allowing businesses to provide accurate delivery estimates and schedule production effectively and efficiently. This research showcases a novel Bayesian enhancement algorithm for estimating processing times and prior rankings, which uses genetic techniques to optimize priorities and mitigate delays and unexpected interruptions, resulting in lower costs. The approach, implemented in Python, is presented as a comprehensive case study involving machining centers in a manufacturing setting. Key performance metrics, such as mean absolute error and concordance, are used to compare the proposed algorithm with existing state-of-the-art methods, which includes the mean variance algorithm and the hybrid algorithm. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms these methods, which is further demonstrated by numerical examples and a summary of key performance metrics. Lastly, the approach is validated by presenting its key characteristics, such as scalability and sparsity, which are crucial for practical implementation. The research ultimately concludes by highlighting potential avenues for future development and improvement. Furthermore, the paper is accompanied by a detailed appendix that provides supplementary technical details and a public dataset, known as the Machining Centers Dataset (MCD), which can be accessed through a designated URL. The security reliance on biometric data grows as advancements reveal intricate details within human physiology. Despite this, the process of creating unique templates from complex biometric information remains poorly understood. In our research, we establish a comprehensive model for individual identity representation, derived from online signature dynamics captured through time-series data. This model is grounded in a thermodynamic formality and incorporates both statistical properties and dynamic behaviors. We identify a distinctive correlation structure, which enables the creation of unique and non-transposable templates from the phase-space trajectories of repeated signatures. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach can differentiate between genuine and simulated signatures with high accuracy, outperforming existing competitor methods. Furthermore, we formally establish the reliability and repeatability of our method by analyzing multiple experimental conditions and the effects of varying parameter settings on template uniqueness and quality. The strength of our model lies in its ability to provide in-depth insights into the underlying mechanisms of unique human identification, which could be adapted and applied to other biometric and behavioral time-series data. Ultimately, we hope this work will contribute to biometric research and inspire future studies. Please note that these datasets contain raw and processed time-series data comprising online signatures from multiple individuals and groups. We investigated the one-loop amplitude of the six-point scattering of Grassmann-odd particles in the N=6 asymmetric orbifold framework, specifically looking at the terms involving four or more derivatives in the amplitude. However, we discovered that these terms are restricted to a specific subset of the framework known as the U(1)|1 sector, which typically sees a distinct set of particles interact. Furthermore, we found that the non-local four-derivative terms can be equivalently represented by a set of local two-derivative operators constructed from the framework's fundamental building blocks, including the six-vertex R-matrix. Interestingly, this finding is consistent with a proposed conjecture that the elevated-derivative terms can be reduced to a linear combination of the basic local operators in the framework's spectrum. We also computed the coefficient of the leading non-local six-derivative term, expressing it in terms of the framework's fundamental building blocks as predicted by the conjecture. Lastly, we explored the relevance of our findings to the more comprehensive U(1)|1 holographic CFT construction. In a study of spin-vortex dynamics following a polarization spike in an array of Bose-Einstein condensates, researchers found that, unlike previous work in reference [1], a localized charge defect gives rise to spin vortices of orders three and higher. Furthermore, the pattern of spin vortices is determined solely by the polarization profile of the defect and the underlying lattice structure. Utilizing the finite-element method, researchers numerically solved the Gross-Pitaevskii equations in three-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates with a wide range of polarization values between -1 and 1. It was discovered that, under a specific condition where the polarization value at the defect's center exceeds 2/3, higher-order spin vortices become prevalent, whereas, under a condition where the polarization value at the defect's center is less than -1/3, they are predominantly suppressed. Nonetheless, it was found that, although the majority of spin vortices exhibit the predicted lowest possible topological charge of -1 or highest possible topological charge of 1, a localized charge defect can give rise to spin vortices with topological charges of 2 and -2. Moreover, it was found that, although the majority of spin vortices are situated near the defect's center, a localized charge defect can also give rise to spin vortices with a placement characterized by a large curvature. This distinctive feature may provide an optimal environment for the observation of nonclassical spin behavior. Additionally, it was proposed that the observed spin configurations could be used to demonstrate the quantum nature of the Bose-Einstein condensates through a variety of quantum correlation functions. Lastly, it was found that, although a polarization spike in an array of Bose-Einstein condensates does give rise to spin vortices with orders higher than two, it fails to give rise to supercurvature vortices, i.e., vortices with orders greater than two that exhibit an excessive curvature. Therefore, it was concluded that a polarization spike in an array of Bose-Einstein condensates does not serve as an optimal means of demonstrating a relationship between spin vortices and supercurvature vortices. However, it was suggested that a distinct class of defects, specifically a distinct type of charge defect characterized by a more localized structure, may give rise to both spin vortices and supercurvature vortices, thereby serving as an efficient means of demonstrating a relationship between spin vortices and supercurvature vortices. The isotopic pattern of C-12/O-16 newly formed in non-steady-state astrophysical nuclei reactions is analyzed for all primary nitrogen isotopic patterns. It's discovered that a specific nitrogen isotopologue, C-12N-14, dominates the ratio with oxygen, whereas other nitrogen isotopologues have a subdominant ratio. This phenomenon is observed in both the light and heavy nitrogen isotopic patterns. The reason behind this pattern is the competition for final nuclear level state among the nitrogen isotopes in the nuclear reaction network. As a result, the ratio of C-12N-14 to other isotopes is preferred over those containing heavier nitrogen isotopes. It's further noted that this preferred ratio is inherent in the light nitrogen isotopes as well and may indicate a single nitrogen nucleosynthetic process, the hydrogen burning, which produced the observed C-12N-14O-16 ratio in the solar system. The characteristics of hydrogen burning, which produces C-12N-14O-16 with a 1:1 ratio, are incompatible with big bang nucleosynthesis models that rely on 3 beta-decays. While s-process and r-process nucleosynthesis can also produce nitrogen with a high C-12N-14 content, they follow a different ratio with oxygen, making them distinguishable from from bbBN or hydrogen burning. Moreover, the finding that nitrogen ratios are not isotropic but exhibit a complex pattern means that low-metallicity stars may have higher C-12N-14 contents than high-metallicity stars due to hydrogen burning. The discovery also indicates that r-process-free asymptotic giant branch stars may have lower C-12N-14 contents than hydrogen burning. Lastly, the finding that s-process nitrogen in low-metallicity stars is not as low as expected may indicate that low C-12N-14 contents in these stars are the result of r-process contribution rather than hydrogen burning. The discovery also opens the possibility of distinguishing between hydrogen burning and r-process-free AGB stars based on nitrogen isotopologue ratios. Moreover, the finding also indicates that low C-12N-14 contents in r-process stars may have been produced not through r-process but through hydrogen burning. The newly discovered pattern provides a deeper understanding and distinction between various astrophysical nuclei reactions and may enable researchers to identify newly formed isotopes using nitrogen isotopologue ratios. This paper explores the complexities of NLP code mixing, particularly in multilingual communities, and identifies critical considerations for societal accountability. Code mixing involves combining different languages within the same text. While this phenomenon is widespread and natural, efficiently tackling it proves difficult. Our expertise stems from working with low-resource, minority community contexts, especially with children, where code mixing prevalence is high. However, the NLP community's focus on this topic is lacking. We aim to highlight crucial factors that have influenced our research and highlight the inherent challenges it poses. Initially, we address the ethics of data collection, protection, and preservation, and how these responsibilities are often disregarded in favor of quick NLP fixes. We also examine the inherent power dynamics at play when NLP researchers assume roles of data collectors, analysts, and interpreters within these communities. We delve into the concerns surrounding data ownership, control, and the equitable distribution of benefits. We emphasize the importance of transparency in NLP research, yet acknowledge the internal and external biases that can stem from the limited representation of selected data in trained models. We acknowledge the inherent risk of exploitation inherent in deep learning technologies, and highlight the need for more nuanced approaches in the future. We stress the need for researchers to be more responsive to the needs and priorities of the communities they work with, and to reflect these in their research questions, design, development, and evaluation. We argue that the urgent issues confronting these communities, such as access to education and social justice, should be addressed by researchers, and that code-mixed language is an integral part of these communities' daily lives and struggles. We urge researchers to reevaluate their roles and responsibilities, and to view their contributions as temporary assistance rather than expert guidance. We stress the importance of reciprocity, and that researchers should strive to be more humble and unassuming in their interactions with these communities, and that this should be a two-way street with more mutual knowledge-sharing and collaboration. We conclude by highlighting the commonalities between NLP research and the pressing concerns of these communities, such as environmental degradation, migration, and marginalization, and argue that the future of NLP research should be grounded in social justice and centered on the needs and priorities of these communities. We advocate for a future where NLP research is more accountable, responsible, and committed to upholding the principles of social justice. The last several decades have seen an enormous expansion in biomedical data. Despite this growth, solving complex biomedical problems necessitates going beyond traditional machine learning techniques due to the inherent complexity and dimensionality of the data. The discipline of biomedical machine learning has made notable strides, but there is still a pressing need for advanced methods to tackle challenging problems in this field. One promising approach to addressing this need involves the application of deep learning to graphical data, such as biological networks, that can learn relevant relationships and patterns. However, widespread adoption is hindered by a lack of suitable data and model interpretation tools. In this review, we will examine the state-of-the-art methods for modeling graphs with a focus on biomedical applications, and explore the challenges and opportunities for future development. We will also introduce a fundamental framework for biomedical graph machine learning that spans core technical aspects and applicable domains. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive overview that can serve as a useful entry point for early-career researchers and a useful update for established researchers in the field. We have also included a detailed overview of the technical aspects of graph machine learning, starting from the underlying theoretical foundations to the latest advancements in various subfields, as well as a comprehensive discussion on critical open challenges and potential future directions that are specific to biomedical applications. Furthermore, we have incorporated relevant real-world case studies and have made sure that the primary biomedical data used in these examples can be easily accessed. We have also provided a composable software framework that includes detailed implementations of the methods and data tools to facilitate reproducibility. We hope that this review will contribute to spurring further research in the biomedical graph machine learning field and inspiring new applications. The review code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/galaxybml/gml-bml. The review has been posted on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.00025. Both the review and the code have been updated to reflect the recent advancements in this field. In particular, the review now includes the latest AI methods, such as AI-assisted inference and promoter prediction using the PromTool, and the code includes the BMLLearn framework that was used to create the PromTool. The review and the code can be accessed at the mentioned links. The GitHub repository has been updated to include the R code used in Chapter 3 of the PhD dissertation 'Biomedical Graph Machine Learning'. The dissertation, along with the R code, can be found at https://github.com/galaxybml/gml-bml/tree/main/dissertation.

This study proposes an innovative approach to addressing privacy concerns related to social media content. An individual's sensitive information on social media platforms can be effectively protected by leveraging their relationships with others. An individual can share their content with a Graph Privacy Consultant, which is an expert system capable of providing personalized recommendations to grant access to specific content based on an individual's connections. The Consultant is comprised of several specialized experts that collaborate to recommend a course of action. One such expert, known as the Pattern Expert, utilizes machine learning and content analysis models called ContentFinder and SentimentAnalyzer to identify posts that break established social norms and suggest actions such as "Private: Only friends can see this". This structure allows individuals to maintain control over their sensitive content while allowing closest relationships to access it. An evaluation of this consultant on multiple social media datasets demonstrates its effectiveness and efficiency in detecting post categories and granting access permissions. Furthermore, our framework offers potential extensions to aid in social media content analysis and research, such as generating summaries categorized by topic and identifying content trends. The proposed framework is pioneering in its use of an expert system that combines social graph information, content analysis, and pattern detection to provide comprehensive privacy recommendations. It is also an original solution to the ongoing challenges in social media privacy and content analysis research. The code for this research is publicly available at a specified URL. Experimental datasets and implementation details are also provided for reproduction of results. The proposed approach is driven by its ability to provide relevant and applicable privacy recommendations, rather than strictly adhering to existing research. In epistemic logic, models often utilize two distinct types of agents, `agent` and `knowing`. However, when examining concepts such as concealed knowledge or superintelligence, this separation can prove limiting. To address this, we present novel semantics for two existing propositional logics that tackle the phenomenon of concealed knowledge. Our first approach builds upon the existing syntax and semantics, introducing new sequences to accommodate concealed knowledge. In contrast, our second approach derives from the Fagin et al. semantics by incorporating self-assembly features. We prove the soundness and completeness of both logics with respect to their respective semantics, as well as their respective independence results. Furthermore, we introduce models of superintelligent agents, deriving them from existing semantics for basic superintelligent agents. Specifically, we rework the models of concealed purity for knowledge and concealed knowledge, introducing new classification categories and demonstrating their independence. We also present corresponding independence results for superintelligent agents. Moreover, we introduce new models by incorporating the features of concealed knowledge and superintelligence, leading to intriguing questions about the feasibility of implementing such features. Lastly, we explore potential applications and future directions for these models. It is noteworthy that the final chapter of this research is incomplete and requires further development. As such, we encourage readers to submit their own contributions to this area. We hope that this research will serve as a foundation for future work and invite readers to build upon it. Specifically, we anticipate the following questions to be addressed in future publications: How can the conceived models of concealed knowledge and superintelligence be utilized in an argumentation framework? What can be said about the relationship between these models and the existing models of superintelligent agents? What can be done to further expand the conceived models? We envision a potential research trajectory where the existing models are applied to examine the existing body of work in multi-agent logic, with a particular focus on concealed knowledge and superintelligence. Once a sufficient understanding is achieved, we can proceed to the final chapter, where we will delve into the foundational aspects of multi-agent logic. Lastly, we note that the research outlined here can be further developed by investigating the underlying features of concealed knowledge and superintelligence, with a particular focus on their relations to other logical concepts, such as knowledge, concealed knowledge, superintelligence, and artificial intelligence. We anticipate that this research will contribute meaningfully to the existing multi-agent literature. We hope that the conceived research will be deemed original and meaningful. Measurements of jet fragmentation in 5.46 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV $pp$ and 0.22 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV Pb+Pb collisions with the ATLAS detector at the LHC are compared. Jet fragments with momentum greater than 1 GeV within jets of radius 0.4 and 0.6, 20$<$p$_T$< or equal to 50 GeV, are studied. Fragmentation is studied by mean number of fragments, fragment multiplicity, and fragmentation function, and it reveals similar behaviors for light-quark and gluon jets in $pp$ and Pb+Pb collisions. No significant differences are found between $pp$ and Pb+Pb jets, and deviations from universal counting model are investigated. This analysis provides insights into the hadronization of light-quark and gluon states in high-energy particle collisions. Results are also quantified as modifications of fragmentation function or ratio for quark, gluon, and charged-particle jets in central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions compared to $pp$ ones. Furthermore, limits of model interpretations in terms of modified parton distribution functions or splittings are discussed. This analysis marks the first in-depth investigation of jet fragmentation changes in heavy-ion collisions. It addresses a question of how quarks and gluons behave in high-energy particle collisions in high-density nuclear environments. This insight into the nature of quarks and gluons in extreme conditions can shed light on the basic structure of these particles and the phase of high-energy density called the quark-gluon plasma, and it can do so with precision not achievable in other experiments. This analysis can be repeated with more data to further constrain theoretical models or it can be used as a basis for future research in high-energy particle collisions. If jet fragmentation in high-density nuclear environments does not differ from the same environments without nuclear factors, this discovery could be a significant constraint on our understanding of the basic structure of quarks and gluons. This understanding could also be tested in future high-energy particle collisions at the LHC with more powerful beams or with new detectors that can study the basic structure of quarks and gluons in greater detail. The CP2K program package enhances Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations by offering post-Hartree-Fock theories like car-Parrinello molecular dynamics. We present an update on the latest releases (version 5.1 to 7.1), highlighting parallelization enhancements that establish CP2K as a leading molecular dynamics software. We analyze the performance optimization approaches, notably the global internal coordinate (GIC) framework, effective potential generation using the tight-binding linearized augmented plane wave method (TBLO), and improved data management through Data Tagging. These advancements position CP2K for efficient performance on diverse architectures, including GPUs, multi-core processors, and vector supercomputers, making it well-suited for large-scale simulations on future exascale systems. We evaluate its performance using the ESPResSo benchmark and a molecular dynamics simulation of 10 million atoms on the Hazelton hybrid multi-core/GPU supercomputer. This presentation serves as a guide for achieving optimal performance with latest CP2K versions through various methodologies, ultimately aiming to facilitate highly performant code usage. The sun's core emits X-rays in the form of coronal hard X-rays (CHXRs). These low-energy gamma-rays have a wavelength range of 1-10 keV and a brief duration of less than a minute. Studies of CHXRs have shown that they are most frequently observed during solar flares of higher than X1.0 intensity. A major challenge in observing CHXRs is the sun's intense radiation that filters out most of them from space-based telescopes, leaving only a few events detected per year. A portable telescope called FOXSI has successfully detected solar gamma-rays on several occasions since its inception in 2014, including a significant discovery in 2015 that remained the dimmest observation until another detection in 2020 surpassed its record. FOXSI's latest breakthrough in 2020 not only broke its own record but also failed to provide a convincing explanation for the 2020 detection by suggesting that either the telescope's improved sensitivity or a novel physical phenomenon occurred. Another possible explanation is the presence of a long-lasting, quiet-time emission component that was initially reported in 2016 but was later overlooked due to incomplete analysis. A persistent, weak emission was evident in FOXSI's data from multiple observations including a significant discovery in 2019 that was initially overlooked. Furthermore, a significant detection in 2020 was closely linked to a previously observed 2019 event. Both 2019 and 2020 detections were found to be more persistent and of much lower energy compared to previous CHXRs, suggesting a new class of solar emissions. Data from FOXSI and future telescopes like the Small-XGRS Project will continue to observe this dimmest emission class, leading to new questions about its nature and whether it can be entirely explained by existing physical models of the sun's behavior. It is hoped that a sustained observation of this emission will either validate existing physical models of the sun's behavior or point to novel and unobserved processes occurring within the sun. In either case, a continued and persistent observation of this emission will greatly advance our understanding of the sun's behavior. Additionally, future and ongoing portable telescopes like FOXSI will provide a crucial means for observing the sun and its gamma-ray activity on a much smaller scale than previously possible. Predicting the effects of temporary changes on complex networks, such as a city's social media activity following a major sports game event, is known as social impact forecasting. This research focuses on applying graph neural networks to predict social media trends. A key challenge lies in networks with sparse and variable post duration datasets, which can result in biased node embeddings due to unequal sampling periods. To address this issue, we have developed a new method combining train and test duration augmentation techniques that utilize Fourier transforms to normalize posting frequencies. This approach enables uniform node embeddings and improves overall prediction performance. This method is lightweight, easy to integrate with existing models and offers efficient implementation, thereby facilitating its integration into graph neural networks without adding complexity. This research is the first to apply gauge-invariant temporal self-attention on sparse and variable post duration datasets, resulting in enhanced prediction performance and a deeper understanding of the forecasting process. Experimental results on real-world Twitter datasets have shown a significant performance boost of up to 7.5% and 5.5% relative improvement in RMSSE for football and basketball datasets respectively, as well as up to a 3.3% relative improvement in key metric K-1. Also, the proposed approach has shown up to a 3.3% relative improvement in key metric K-2. These findings clearly illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/hjzhang123/TempAugeration. Additionally, the pre-trained models and corresponding test scores can be found at https://github.com/hjzhang123/TempAugeration/tree/main/codes/extra_model. The algorithm, comprised of three primary components - a prototype generation network, an encoder, and a patch regulation system - can accurately identify and modify skin regions while preserving the unique, intricate details found within each image. Notably, our method avoids reliance on manually labeled data, instead utilizing a self-supervised approach to streamline the training process. The effectiveness of our approach is evident through both qualitative and quantitative analysis of the results. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/CCDTNet. Current recommender systems primarily focus on tapping into either item attributes or user interests in preference learning. However, they often overlook the interplay between these two key elements. As a result, they fail to fully capture users' diverse attribute preferences and items' integrated attributes, resulting in suboptimal recommendation performance. To address this knowledge gap, we introduce a Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation system that simultaneously explores multiple sparse domains of user attribute preferences and item integrated attributes. This novel approach learns a comprehensive attribute preference by fusing multiple sparse domains and subsequently optimizes a collaborative recommendation model, enabling it to discover more precise user attribute preferences and improve recommendation results. Experimental evaluations confirm that our proposed approach surpasses comparative state-of-the-art methods in precision and recall for two widely-used datasets. This paper investigates the deformation theory of two specific types of bundles: those with a perpendicular structure and symplectic structure. A perpendicular structure on a bundle is defined as the direct image of a torsion-free module that is coherent on an open subset of $X$. In various fields of science and engineering, researchers frequently rely on incomplete information about a system, using random samples to estimate its behavior or characteristics. Given that sample data are inevitably afflicted by uncertainty, researchers have developed precise measures for quantifying the expected error in least squares estimators, applicable to a broad range of systems characterized by smooth characteristics. These error measures can be effectively optimized through feedback mechanisms and serve as a robust benchmark for assessing the expected performance of least squares estimators, even in the presence of outlier data. Furthermore, this framework also enables researchers to establish a priori upper limits on the expected error and to identify the specific impact of individual samples on the overall estimation process. Ultimately, this approach facilitates the precise quantification of the expected distortion in least squares estimators, providing a framework for designing robust sampling strategies and for critically evaluating the feasibility of various estimation methods. Specifically, we will utilize this framework to examine random sampling, low-complexity sampling methods, and strategic sampling designed to optimize the outcome. Furthermore, we will employ this framework to derive a precise upper limit on the expected distortion in least squares estimators, and we will use this limit to evaluate the specific impact of individual samples on the overall estimation process. Additionally, we will utilize this framework to facilitate the design of robust sampling strategies and to critically evaluate the feasibility of various estimation methods, including random sampling, low-complexity sampling methods, and strategic sampling designed to optimize the outcome. These results will be illustrated through a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical analyses of geometric characterization, which reveal that the expected distortion in least squares estimators exhibits a trade-off between the level of intrinsic ambiguity in the system and the level of extrinsic uncertainty afforded by random samples. Consequently, researchers can employ this framework to design a sampling strategy that optimizes an explicit trade-off between these two opposing factors and to demonstrate that random samples can provide a simple and robust means of estimating systems with relatively high levels of intrinsic ambiguity and minimal loss in performance. Additionally, this framework also enables researchers to evaluate the feasibility of various estimation methods and to distinguish between systems that can be accurately estimated through random samples and those that require strategic sampling to achieve optimal results. Lastly, we will employ this framework to examine the fundamental limitations of random samples in least squares estimators and to establish a precise upper limit on the expected distortion in these estimators. Interestingly, this upper limit can be effectively optimized through feedback mechanisms, revealing that random samples can achieve optimal results only in systems that have very low levels of intrinsic ambiguity and minimal loss in performance. Most studies on learning from observations assume an entirely uncontrolled environment or focus on perfect reward-giving for precise behavior. However, in many situations, this isn't the case. Some observations may be slightly altered or entire sensory inputs might be blocked, while others might receive clear indications of success or failure. We address this challenge by investigating a scenario where an observer tries to understand a reward-giving agent's goals in a partially regulated environment. Some aspects of the observer's observations are controlled, while others are random. We present a new framework that combines individual observations and explains the agent's consistent actions through distinct goal theories. The observer's uncertainty about the environment and reward goals is quantified numerically. The approach is evaluated using simulated data and compared with two alternative methods. The results show our framework is both efficient and reliable, even in highly complex scenarios with large data sets. The framework's efficiency is attributed to its fast convergence, enabled by a numerical convergence speed of up to 15 times faster compared to two alternative methods. This study is the second in a series focusing on black holes across various ages.
It focuses on the origins of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) exceeding one million solar masses using two established models.
The first model considers a continuous seed mass spectrum, whereas the second model posits that seeds are comprised of a binary nature: massive pop III stars collapsing or merger remnant black holes from early star clusters. 
Our findings indicate that the continuous seed model is more suitable for a broad mass range (10^4 to 10^7 solar masses) but the binary seed model excels in accounting for massive SMBHs (greater than ten million solar masses) at early stages.
The outcome supports the concept that massive SMBHs are primarily the outcome of black hole mergers within early star clusters. 
The outcome also implies that early massive galactic central black holes can give off light in the form of starlight that can be observed with future space missions like the James Webb Space Telescope.
The outcome is further supported by the observed connection between black hole mass and galaxy light in the distant past, suggesting a co-evolutionary relationship. 
The connection implies that black hole growth is closely tied to galaxy evolution and that extreme star formation events in the distant past led to massive black holes that can be seen today. 
Consequently, early massive black holes can activate their surrounding environments through a process called feedback, thereby influencing the formation of galaxies as we know them today. 
The outcome is consistent with observations of the present and can be seen in galaxies like the Arp220, where dust obscuration is obscured by a massive dust cloud. 
Therefore, present-day galactic central black holes are likely the remnants of a distant past as a massive black holes continue to await discovery.

Ultimately, our results illustrate that with the right training and insights into the data, ML models can significantly surpass human capabilities in IES data analysis.
