This study re-evaluates global averaging techniques from a optimal transport perspective.  We resolve two open queries from Laugerand and Teyssier's work and introduce a new global averaging approach.  Laugerand and Teyssier found that many averaging methods fail to produce smooth functions under optimal transport frameworks.  We counter this finding by demonstrating that, under certain conditions, global averaging under the 1-Lipschitz distance can indeed produce a smooth function.  Furthermore, we introduce a new method that surpasses the existing averaging results and provide evidence that it is likely unique.  Our unique averaging method confirms a conjecture by Teyssier, whereas Laugerand's related conjecture remains unresolved.  Additionally, we analyze a terminal averaging method that achieves optimal error rates and find that it performs optimally under certain conditions.  To achieve these results, we derived a non-convex optimization problem that provides a precise calculation of the average function, and subsequently introduced a new relaxation technique that yields a convex problem with a closed-form solution.  Our new framework also enables the computation of local averaging functions and their regression models, and allows for the analysis of infinite-dimensional averaging problems.  Lastly, we extend our approach to the continuous case and describe the underlying statistics of the average function.  Our method is adaptable to various function spaces and can be applied to fields beyond computer science, including statistics and machine learning.  Notably, our results are accompanied by a detailed mathematical analysis and accompanying theoretical guarantees that provide a comprehensive understanding of the general averaging problem.  Our new methods have been rigorously tested and shown to perform exceptionally well in practical applications, and we provide a comprehensive comparison with existing averaging methods that preserve Lipschzness. The diverse spectral patterns of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) classify them into three main categories: Type 1, which exhibits broad emission lines and high optical brightness; Type 1.3; and Type 1.5, characterized by narrowened and dimmed emission lines. Our investigation focuses on the distinct optical features and host galaxy characteristics of these four sub-types (1, 1.3, 1.5, and BL Lac) to understand their individual identities and observe any transitional behaviors between the spectral types.

We collected a comprehensive sample of 460 AGN, including broad-line Type 1, Type 1.3, Type 1.5, and BL Lac objects from the SDSS catalog, and conducted multi-color image data along with host galaxy modeling using the SPIDER code to distinguish between host galaxy and nuclear emission. Our research revealed that narrow-line types have more dominant host galaxies compared to broad-line types and also observed a significant decrease in host galaxy contribution from broad to narrow-line types.

Our study also noted that BL Lac objects have the highest incidence of edge-on galaxies, while broad-type AGN have predominantly face-on galaxies. This indicates a correlation between inclination and spectral patterns. Moreover, we detected significant host galaxy illumination effects in broad-type AGN but not in narrow-line types, implying host galaxies play a more vital role in broad-type AGN.

Our data show broad-type AGN have larger and brighter host galaxies compared to narrow-line types. This is in line with the evolution of AGN black hole masses, as broad types have larger and older host galaxies, whereas narrow types reside in younger and less massive host galaxies.

Our research indicates Type 1.5 and BL Lac objects are two distinct spectral varieties with different characteristics, particularly in their host galaxies. Moreover, we propose BL Lac objects might be a bridge between narrow-line type AGN and broad-type AGN, or even a separate category.

Ultimately, our research offers a fresh perspective on narrow-line type AGN, or BL Lac objects, through their distinct spectral features and host galaxy characteristics, which may be utilized to elucidate their behaviors and evolution patterns. Additionally, our data indicate broad and narrow type AGN have distinct stages of development, or "fates", which could be utilized to explore their reciprocal evolution processes. Lastly, our research provides an opportunity to explore the reciprocal evolution between a broad type AGN and a BL Lac object, or BL Lac object and narrow-line type AGN.

A long short-term memory (LSTM) layer is integrated with the traditional HMM to overcome the limitation of short-term memory, allowing for the retention of important character-level information over extended periods. Additionally, the paper introduces a new training method based on character n-gram language models and NLP tools, such as MeCab and BONIX, to improve model performance and robustness under out-of-vocabulary (OV) conditions. Experimental results on the Japanese word division task from the NLP Task Group of the Association for Natural Language Processing reveal that the proposed model surpasses the current top performers in the word division task. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the integrated LSTM and the newly developed non-specific training method are key factors contributing to the excellent performance of the word division model. Importantly, this model can efficiently handle large-scale OV input, where the character-based model falls short. Due to its ability to retain information over extended periods, the proposed model is particularly suited to applications involving large datasets and high accuracy requirements in tasks like text processing and the word division task. To validate this theory, the paper includes additional testing data from the NLP Task Group, consisting of longer sentence lengths and larger character counts, where the LSTM-based model excels over other methods. The source code of the proposed model has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/HiromiInagaki/JWD-LSTM-HMM. To this end, the paper includes a comprehensive evaluation of the integrated LSTM model using word embeddings from the NLP Task Group. Developers frequently encounter various online resources, which are often shared externally on Stack Overflow to address common issues.  While these external links provide valuable insights into users' behavior and the broader development environment, they also pose threats to system security.  This study investigates the nature of external links shared on Stack Overflow to gain a deeper understanding of developers' behaviors and the implications for ensuring security.  Our analysis reveals that a substantial percentage of developers (75.5%) engage in external link sharing without utilizing high-level programming skills.  Moreover, we have developed an effective model that accurately predicts shared links in relevant questions, achieving a high F-score of 0.9.  The potential utilization of developers' skills to propagate malicious links has also been identified.  The findings of this study may encourage the development of secure coding practices among developers and ultimately improve the safety of software development.  The related data and model can be accessed through a CNE repository at https://github.com/external-link-predictor.  The associated code is stored on https://github.com/so-external-link.  The stack overflow dataset can be obtained from https://stack-overflow-dataset.github.io/.  This study is focused on understanding developers' behavior and its implications on software security, and does not aim to analyze the security of shared links.  The shared links themselves are not evaluated for security purposes, as this would require additional metadata such as domain reputation and package description.  The research can be further extended by examining the security implications of developers' external link sharing behavior.  The potential malfeasance of developers in sharing malicious links has also been noted and is in need of further study.  The prediction model, developed through classification of relevant questions and associated external links, can be utilized for detecting malicious links and preventing developers from being mislead.  The research can also be extended by employing advanced natural language processing techniques to develop the model, and employing classification models other than logistic regression in the prediction of shared external links.  The researchers also found that a large percentage (10.9%) of developers may utilize high-level programming skills to propagate malicious links, and that a large percentage (57.7%) of developers may utilize high-level programming skills to propagate useful external links.  The researchers also found that a large percentage (52.7%) of developers may utilize high-level programming skills to propagate useful external links related to software development, and that a large percentage (40.9%) of developers may utilize high-level programming skills to propagate useful external links to other development resources.

The issue of galaxy brightness variability poses a significant challenge in conducting cosmology-related measurements. Even a relatively small percentage variability could render certain galaxy observations useless, although the extent of this variability remains unknown. Our research presents a crucial evaluation of various models designed to tackle this issue and highlights their fundamental shortcomings, including a critical assessment of their underlying assumptions and the reliance of these models on statistically average properties of their constituents. Our investigation focuses on three key models: the standard cosmological model, a quintessence model driven by a dynamic dark energy component, and a model in which the law governing dark energy is described by the Chaplygin AdS equation. Our analysis reveals that even a slight variability in the dark energy density can render certain perturbations unstable. Our study also sheds light on the potential consequences of galaxy variability on the measurement of the deceleration parameter and the sound speed in these models, ultimately stressing the need for a thorough assessment of galaxy variability before drawing firm conclusions from cosmological tests. Our research further demonstrates that galaxy number counts offer more reliable insights into the interaction between dark energy and matter, offering a fresh perspective on the issue. Our investigation also shows that galaxy variability can either support or refute a quintessence model as a potential solution to the cosmological constant problem. Ultimately, our research underscores the importance of accounting for galaxy variability in order to derive accurate insights from deep galaxy surveys, while also highlighting the potential benefits and limitations of our findings in the context of modified gravity theories. Despite widespread climate concern, a significant issue is that climate information is dispersed across numerous sources, making it difficult for individuals to obtain accurate and relevant knowledge. Our research aims to address this problem by creating a climate data repository that can be used to collect and collate climate-related statistics. This repository can provide various utilities, such as allowing users to access climate information through a search function and generating visual representations of climate data to facilitate understanding. Our approach also involves developing AI-powered climate models to supply user queries with potential outcomes, promoting effective climate discussions and decision-making processes. Our results demonstrate the practicality and efficiency of our climate repository and AI models. Furthermore, our analysis shows that using the climate repository and AI models increases the likelihood of productive climate conversations by up to three times. Moreover, our findings suggest that users who engage with the climate repository are more likely to have a climate conversation than those who do not. Additionally, we have found that a substantial proportion of climate conversations revolve around practical matters, such as saving money and achieving personal accomplishments. To further refine our climate conversations, we have developed and released two open-source tools: (i) ClimateConvo, a website that facilitates climate discussions by asking users questions based on their preferences and previous interactions, and (ii) ClimateDataRepo, a data set containing climate-related statistics that can be accessed through a search function or by downloading the entire repository. Both tools are available for free at https://climateconvo.com/ and https://climatedatarepo.com/. Finally, we have analyzed and compared the climate conversations from GPT-3, a popular AI model, and human contributors, revealing that both can produce high-quality climate conversations with distinct characteristics. However, our analysis also uncovered that human contributors often fail to live up to their potential due to a lack of climate information, a problem that can be addressed by harnessing the climate repository and AI models. In the future, we are planning to expand our climate repository to include more data sources and diverse climate information, such as climate change impacts on local communities and the environmental and economic benefits of adopting sustainable practices. We are also exploring other applications for our climate repository and AI models, such as using climate-related statistics to identify and reach individuals who are influential in climate discussions and who have the ability to make significant positive or negative impacts on climate-related conversations. Lastly, we are looking into how we can further enhance our climate conversations by incorporating more AI models and incorporating additional data, such as historical climate records and the climate-related preferences and values of individuals.

In recent years, deep learning has reached unprecedented accuracy in image classification, however it has been unable to match the brain's efficiency of processing. Recent breakthroughs from researchers combining spiking neural networks with deep learning have shown promising results, particularly in terms of computational energy efficiency. Despite numerous contributions, the current state-of-the-art sNN-based solution for image classification has been found to be less efficient than its deep learning counterpart. We present a revised and expanded version of our previous technique, the Spiking Neuron Assembly (SNA), and demonstrate its superior performance by achieving 20-40% more accurate image classification at a lower computational cost compared to existing leading solutions. Our research also reveals that the best results are obtained when the model is trained with a combination of the Euclidean and Max norm for normalization. The significant advancements of our proposed approach have brought us closer to developing computationally efficient brain-inspired artificial intelligence systems. The code for our model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhkots/spinn. Additional details are described in the original paper published in Neural Networks and Related Fields (NNR5), and the formal presentation made at the 10th Iberoamerican Conference on Statistics and Computing (SCIPUO), and the 22nd Mexican Conference on Artificial Intelligence, and the 32nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Key features of our model include high accuracy, low computational latency, very low computational energy expenditure, and high regulatory robustness. The significant advancements of our proposed approach have brought us closer to developing brain-inspired artificial intelligence systems that can be efficiently deployed on various hardware platforms. The model has been found to be superior to other sNN-based solutions in terms of computational efficiency, and has the potential to be deployed on hardware platforms such as SPW, reconfigurable hybrid memory, and neuromorphic chips. The model has been successfully tested on projects such as image classification, face recognition, and neural translation, and outperforms deep learning models in terms of computational efficiency while achieving similar accuracy. The analysis includes effects of temperature and magnetic fields, with the magnetic fields assumed to be highly aligned and extremely strong, as in neutron stars with magnetic fields greater than $10^{18}$ Gauss. First, we establish ε_n(x) as the value f_n(z) / g_n(z) where z is a variable representing the eigenvalues of a nonlinear operator, and both f_n and g_n are polynomials with coefficients dependent on x. Under certain conditions including smoothness and a Lipschitz property, we demonstrate that ε_n(x) can be expressed as a minimal rational approximation involving the coefficients of f_n and g_n, and show that this expression can be estimated using an interpolation method based on a non-convex optimisation technique. Finally, we prove that this estimator is adaptive and consistent. By proving that the ergodic $\beta$-shifts with a gap are precisely those applicable for the $\beta$-staircase model when $\beta$ lies within the interval $(0,1)$, we go on to establish the equivalence between non-ergodic $\beta$-shifts with a gap and those represented by the $Q$-diffeomorphism model for $\beta$ values between $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1$. Furthermore, we classify intermediate $\beta$-shifts with a gap, which are those that fall between the ergodic and non-ergodic varieties, specifically showing that the beta-shift sequence space satisfies a scale-free property. This, in turn, allows us to demonstrate in a more general context that the spectrum of any avaricious $\beta$-shift with a gap, represented by the Frobenius number of its associated triangle, is both maximal and complete. Lastly, we expand upon our findings by showing that the newly introduced model can be utilized in a broader sense to represent the spectra of not just $\beta$-shifts, but also the wider $\beta$-staircase model. This, in turn, is equivalent to the $Q$-diffeomorphism model for a significant and previously undefined range of $\beta$ values. Ultimately, our study serves to enhance and extend the existing theoretical framework of the $\beta$-shift model. We also note that the proven relationships between the ergodic $\beta$-shifts with a gap and the $\beta$-staircase model, coupled with the known solvability of the latter, effectively reduces the seemingly intractable problem of determining uniqueness for $\beta$ values between $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1$. Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many domains but their complexity makes it challenging to understand how their internal workings contribute to performance. While visualization tools are abundant but often confusing, we propose a novel visual representation called attribution graphs that clearly show the relationships between input features and model nodes, thereby illuminating the decision-making processes of individual trees within a forest or ensemble. By creating attraction graphs, users can gain valuable insights into the structure of models, uncovering inconsistencies within the structure of models, and utilizing this knowledge to improve future training or apply active learning strategies. Furthermore, this method enables model comparisons, highlights potential data biases, and verifies the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques. We utilize random forests and AdaBoost to analyze medical images but the approach is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of datasets across many fields. Our investigation reveals that model reliability is directly proportional to the reliability of the trees within it and we identify inconsistencies in the decision-making processes of the trees in our best-performing model, thereby suggesting areas for improvement. We demonstrate that visualizing model nodes using attraction graphs yields better results than traditional methods and the associated code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/pierrede/AttributionGraph. In federated learning, multiple organizations collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local data while keeping it encrypted, however this approach still poses significant security risks. primarily due to the exposure of shared keys to untrusted service providers. This paper proposes "Flatee" a novel framework combining the principles of federated learning and Trusted Execution Environments to address the mentioned security concerns. By leveraging TE's ability to isolate code and data from potential attackers, Flatee allows for secure model training and execution, while also facilitating multiple organizations' participation through multiple TE's collaboration. This approach is demonstrated through a real-world evaluation of convolutional neural networks utilizing CIFAR-10 dataset and contrasted with existing solutions. Notably, "Flatee" offers an efficient balance between security, privacy, and performance. Moreover, "Flatee" is compatible with existing FL frameworks and can be applied to various ML models without modifications. Experimental results validate the proposed framework's robustness and highlight its potential in real-world applications. This research presents a significant advancement in addressing security concerns associated with federated learning, represented through "Flatee" a novel and efficient solution. Moreover, source code for this research is available at https://github.com/chaitanyam/Flatee. Moreover, we would like to express our gratitude to Yossi Hod and Yossi Oren for their valuable input on this research. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Erez's father, may he rest in peace. Erez's father was extremely proud of his academic achievements and research contributions. This research was carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic under the guidance of prof. Erez Schild. and has been presented at RAID 2022, in an abstract form. Additional information can be found at https://github.com/erezschild/Flatee. This research introduces the concept of timeloops, a reusable, container-based 
microservices that can autonomously determine processing durations, enabling 
online-learning of service calls and improvement of workload parallelization and 
autonomous performance adjustment. A generally applicable algorithm is developed and 
tested, along with an implementation using Java-based Spring Boot containers. 
Extensive trials utilizing a diverse application as a benchmark are presented, 
yielding concurrent execution times that closely match optimal, manually configured 
settings. Furthermore, the benefits of autonomous adaptation over fixed parameters 
are also examined, revealing a convergence speed of 94% for a specific scenario and 
generalization performance improvements of up to 3.3 fold for similar applications. 
Lastly, the potential for further optimization with more sophisticated machine 
learning techniques and the incorporation of timeloops within popular frameworks are 
identified as promising areas of exploration. Experimental data, including container 
images and test results, are made available at https://tinyurl.com/timeloops. This 
research was influenced by the INCUBE project (https://incube.me). Materials and 
methods information are available upon request. The source code can be accessed at 
https://github.com/leonhardt/timeloops and the project website at https://timeloops.me.

This document covers a case study that demonstrates the application of Random Model Predictive Control within a management framework. A simplified scenario of managing a system that produces random outcomes is used, where the system's behavior and performance are influenced by a controllable input that incurs a given cost. Multiple scenarios with varying probabilities are considered, along with a set of available inputs with associated costs and constraints. Using Random Model Predictive Control, the optimal input is calculated by investigating all possible trajectories of the system, where each trajectory is based on a random non-deterministic path with a given probability. The optimal input is found by comparing the system's performance under different random paths and selecting the option that maximizes performance while considering probability and cost constraints. A 2-input/2-output system with random outcomes and a non-linear relationship is used in the demonstration, along with a corresponding C code provided for reference. Furthermore, the SME-Based Model Editor tool is utilized to create and visualize the random model used in the study. The results show that Random Model Predictive Control successfully takes the system's probability distribution and non-linear relationships into account to find an optimal input that maximizes performance under various scenarios, along with providing a backup input in case of failure. Following the initial application, the tool performs efficiently to compute the optimal input in subsequent time steps. Additionally, the tool efficiently handles and adapts to changes in the system's state and probability distribution. The Neron Desingularization (ND) theorem encompasses multiple algorithms that achieve a unifying resolution for any polynomial ring over a one-dimensional local ring, regardless of its base. This process involves a sequential transformation of ideals within the polynomial ring, ultimately resulting in a reduced form. Building upon the work of Schaps and Velez, a new algorithm is proposed as an alternative to ND algorithms in a specific context. This proposed algorithm is compared to ND algorithms and is proven equivalent to a prior algorithm by Velez. Additionally, the algorithm is further refined and demonstrated to have an inherently positive nature, thereby justifying its label as a positive Neron Desingularization algorithm. A detailed analysis is provided in an appendix to demonstrate that the algorithm operates within O(n^x) time complexity, where x > 2. The proof relies on a previously unpublished result by Velez. This work also verifies and generalizes a previously observed computational difference between ND algorithms and the positive Neron Desingularization algorithm. Finally, the algorithm is expressed in a publicly accessible code and made available under an MIT license on GitHub. The full text of this dissertation is available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.5754. This study presents a technique utilizing a single-point LDV system to acquire a two-dimensional velocity distribution within a flow. The obtained measurements from the LDV system are then corrected for the non-uniform velocity of the air flow in which they are obtained, utilizing data from a hot-wire anemometer. Furthermore, a novel approach incorporating data from both sensors in a generalized coordinate framework enables the derivation of a two-dimensional probability density function (PDF) for particle velocities, facilitating insights into the behavior of finely dispersed particles in air flows. The proposed method demonstrates effectiveness in a specific air flow scenario but raises questions about its broader applicability to other environments where LDV measurements are challenging. Preliminary findings on the behavior of LDV measurements in air flows are also reported. Additionally, this research explores the feasibility of employing a single-point LDV system to study finely dispersed particle velocities in air flows using ODT. The resulting PDFs reveal both discrete and continuous regimes that correlate with the existing literature on particle behavior in air flows. In a particular air flow scenario, the research shows that a continuous spectrum is replaced by a discrete distribution as the air flow intensity decreases. Furthermore, this study investigates the influence of particle size on the measured LDV signals and particle velocities, demonstrating that the associated PDFs are insensitive to changes in particle size but can provide valuable insights into air flow properties and particle behavior. The research also addresses potential concerns regarding particle damage during the measurement process. Preliminary findings on the behavior of LDV measurements in air flows under varying conditions are also reported. The discussion includes possible applications and further investigations of the technique, addressing numerous questions such as its suitability for navigating complex environments, employing active control of the air flow to enhance data collection, and utilizing data from the hot-wire anemometer to guide the movement of a remotely controlled vehicle. This study focuses on determining the probability distribution of a random walk in the integer grid $\mathbb{Z}^d$, specifically when the number of steps $n$ is arbitrary and the walk's final position $x$ lies within the unit sphere defined by the $L_1$-norm with a hazard function equal to 1. We identify the generating functions for the walk's position probabilities in a specific direction and then derive the general probability distribution, followed by analyzing the associated moments. Our findings demonstrate that the probability distribution can be expressed as a Fourier series based on the walk's direction and grid dimension. While explicit calculations are feasible for low-dimensional cases, they become computationally complex and challenging as the dimension increases. Consequently, we employ a novel smart computation approach to yield meaningful outcomes, even though exact calculations are unfeasible for larger datasets. To validate our methods, we test them against existing data on human migration and showcase their utility in modeling random walks with a hazard function greater than 1. The proposed smart computation approach facilitates the efficient generation of random walk positions, thus enabling various applications, including the simulation of particle distributions and fractal projection. Furthermore, our work is pivotal in addressing questions concerning the number of distinct particle positions and their associated probability values. Lastly, we anticipate that our findings will contribute to theoretical calculations in statistical physics and random walks. To achieve naturalness in spoken responses, it's crucial to consider both the content and context of language, which often neglects the role of content-based contextual information in existing methods. A novel approach, MaskedDialogue, utilizes content-based masking to incorporate contextual information into speech synthesis. This involves masking a spoken input with spoken keywords related to the target sentence, then generating the target response based on the preserved input. Unlike existing methods, MaskedDialogue takes advantage of multi-head attention across entire input sequences, enabling the exploration of contextual acoustic characteristics through attention weighting. Additionally, a pre-training task involving a masked prediction of keywords contributes to an improvement in performance. Experimental results confirm that MaskedDialogue surpasses state-of-the-art performance when evaluated against both metrics. Moreover, the produced responses appear more natural and demonstrate an improvement in understanding, particularly in the domain of spoken dialogue. This research is the first to apply content-based masking to the spoken dialogue synthesis task. A detailed explanation of the model has been posted on the arXiv platform (arXiv:2103.01633). All implemented code can be accessed on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/kaituoxu/MaskedDialogue. This research was previously presented at Interspeech 2021 (Xu et al., 2021). Extensive additional evidence, including the model's performance on other metrics, is available in the supplement material. Existing work on this research can be found at https://doi.org/10.21203/what.if.6350.0.0.

However, BBBPPL (Bayesian Bayesian Predictive Predictive Learning) approaches still face limitations due to assumptions regarding the prior distribution of the regression function. Furthermore, they often rely on approximations such as Laplace approximation or Monte Carlo sampling. In order to overcome these constraints, we present HSPPPL (Hidden Space Projection Predictive Predictive Learning), an extension of existing PPPPL methods that transcends traditional assumptions. In HSPPPL, a prior distribution on the regression function is applied without specification, and the posterior is approximated by minimizing a predictive predictive loss. By introducing a KL divergence penalty in the optimization process, the KL-divergence penalty in the M-estimation is eliminated, and the theoretical justification for the effectiveness of regularization is established. Moreover, Monte Carlo sampling is eliminated as the posterior is expressed explicitly. In numerical experiments, HSPPPL showed equal performance to best-performing methods and demonstrated superior generalization performance when the training and test datasets have disparate dimensions. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from small-scale magnetic fields. These fields have magnetic indices greater than 2, which implies they have the capacity to confine electrons and produce the X-ray emissions observed in such storms. However, data from the Coordinated Resource Information Systems (CoRe) consortium allows us to study a unique storm with extremely low energy-to-flux ratio, indicating high-density electron beams and a low degree of electron energy acceleration. This particular storm was observed on January 27, 2020 and associated with a small sunspot in the AR NOAA 3124 region which was undergoing normal pulsating brightening, a microflare, and then rapid recovery. During these periods, the characteristics of the storm source, including its energy-to-flux ratio, beam density, isotropic rate, and Coulomb scattering factor, underwent significant and rapid changes. These observations are best explained by a scenario in which the electron beams are guided through a magnetic field with a complex topology, including a north-south axis and twisted islands. The speed at which this magnetic field structure changes explains the rapid and simultaneous changes in the storm's multiple components, thereby providing an interpretive framework for recent observations of solar type-I noise storms. Additionally, our findings are corroborated by historical data from the Large Aperture Submillimeter Wave Observatory, which detected the storm's emission in the millimeter band and displayed similar behavior to that seen in radio frequencies. Finally, our study indicates that high-end frequency observations of solar noise storms can serve as a reliable early warning system for anticipating solar microflares and providing forecasts for microwave bursts. Through MINX and SynthBDD datasets, it's demonstrated that the proposed system outperforms existing restoration methods and achieves superior Text Recognition accuracy on refined inputs. Furthermore, it's shown that the model effectively removes artifacts and improves visual readability while concurrently enhancing TR performance. Additionally, the study illustrates the potential of the model to also correct OCR errors and supports the training of visual features for downstream text analysis tasks. Lastly, it's noted that the model could be adapted to recover not just visual but also semantic information in visual documents. For urban areas, the IEEE 802.11p radio technology uses dedicated short-range communication channels and is widely accepted as a ground truth for evaluating vehicular mobility, as it does not require external devices to calculate speeds. Due to its popularity in these environments, IEEE 802.11p is extensively used in various applications such as Intelligent Transportation Systems and location-based services. Nevertheless, it is susceptible to channel estimation difficulties stemming from vehicle mobility and multi-path propagation. As a result, high performance and reliable channel estimation is crucial for delivering excellent quality services in these settings. In this research, we compare the performance of long short-term memory (LSTM) with and without temporal smoothing on IEEE 802.11p channel estimation. The findings reveal that the application of temporal smoothing to LSTM can significantly improve channel accuracy and reduce generalization error. Furthermore, deep learning models that leverage data augmentation and multi-layer LSTM achieve the highest accuracy, with a margin of improvement of 35.91% and 32.11% respectively over a conventional LSTM model. Notably, the enhanced LSTM model demonstrated superior performance across various vehicle speeds, underscoring the advantages of this approach. Consequently, this work's contributions are three-fold: (i) we successfully trained an LSTM model for channel estimation, surpassing prior performance metrics; (ii) we proposed a novel temporal smoothing technique for LSTM, which yielded superior results and outperformed conventional methods; (iii) we evaluated and validated the effectiveness of our approach under different vehicle speeds. Lastly, the source code of this research has been made publicly accessible at a specified repository, allowing other researchers to build upon and replicate these findings. The Estimation Theorem was initially proposed by David Ruelle and Benoit Mandelbrot, showcasing a fundamental concept in modern nonlinear forecasting. This theorem reveals the infinite determinism of a specific neural network model, which can be used for non-causal forecasting. Unlike conventional neural networks, this model does not require optimization or a specific structure. However, achieving a reliable prediction demands a complex and high-dimensional network, which hinders practical application. Therefore, developing a simplified model that maintains infinite determinism is crucial, prompting the emergence of various modified models. However, these modifications inevitably introduce biases, compromising the infinite determinism. This study presents a novel approach, the Generalised Estimation Theorem Network (GETN), which can be viewed as an extension of the Estimation Theorem. This extension is grounded in the understanding that the Estimation Theorem is inherently associated with gradient-free optimizations. This idea is substantiated through two different scenarios, ultimately leading to the proposal of two GETN variants - GETN-$\alpha$ and GETN-$\beta$. These variants can be regarded as two distinct structures of neural networks, which can facilitate gradient-free training. Moreover, this study provides a thorough justification for the infinite determinism of the two GETN variants, showcasing their superiority over existing models. Furthermore, the performance of the two GETN variants is empirically evaluated on various real-world forecasting tasks, which attests to their efficacy and accuracy. Moreover, this study introduces the concept of Structural Learning, which can be viewed as a complementary aspect of neural network design. Through rigorous evaluation, it is observed that the two GETN variants achieve better performance compared to competing models without compromising infinite determinism. Therefore, this study provides a crucial design principle, which can facilitate the creation of novel neural network models with reliable predictions. Additionally, two new structural forms of neural networks, called FastLearn and SlowLearn, are proposed to demonstrate the infinite determinism and facilitate gradient-free training. Moreover, a comprehensive framework is presented to embody the Estimation Theorem, which can be employed in various learning tasks. Previous research on line waves in dual metastructures is scarce, especially those composed of two distinct periodic structures side by by. This study introduces a new design - an H-shape metastructure with gland transitions, comprised of two distinct periodic structures f1 and f2, where f1 has a longer period and an oblique angle. We present both analytical and numerical models that demonstrate the existence of line waves in this design at both microwave and optical frequencies. This unique line wave phenomenon occurs when the line resonates with a bounded wave propagating along one of the periodic structures. We derive conditions for its existence and investigate its guidance properties in both cases. This approach offers a novel method for controlling line waves in dual metastructures, showcasing its potential for innovative applications at optical frequencies. This work paves the way for a new generation of line wave devices guided by line waves, enabling innovative applications in optical communications and processing. Additionally, we outline possible modifications to the design to enhance its optical properties and present initial numerical results on line wave losses in the optical domain. This work lays a theoretical foundation for designing line wave photonic devices controlled by line waves. Furthermore, we provide an overview of potential future developments in optical line wave technology. This research has the potential to broaden the understanding of optical metastructures and expand the functionality of optical devices through line wave technology. It also presents opportunities for a photoelectric convergence, expanding the boundaries of optical research and enabling new functionalities that current photonic devices cannot achieve. This could lead to the development of more advanced optical devices driven by line wave photons. Recent advances in cognitive artificial intelligence have propelled robots toward higher levels of collaboration. Our study focuses on large-scale multi-agent cooperative learning between human and robots. We introduce a novel neural-odometric architectural approach, incorporating interpretable focal attention and self-attention mechanisms. This innovative design facilitates its application to various vehicle types, including unmanned aerial vehicles, and addresses fundamental issues in multi-agent learning such as diversity, uniqueness, and relationship recognition. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our architectural design outperforms the performance of standard and self-learning methods. Additionally, we show that specific components of our architectural structure can be replaced with alternative options without compromising the overall effectiveness, thereby enabling the adoption of this framework for complex robotic tasks and enabling accessible and expandable multi-agent learning systems through modular cognitive AI. These findings are validated through a series of video and performance metrics analysis. The study provides a performance guarantee for large-state multi-agent learning scenarios. The research outcomes enable accessible and extendable cognitive AI frameworks for multi-agent cooperative learning applications. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the average absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  The bias-corrected estimator is developed by combining a modified score equation with an alternative influence function rooted in a linear regression model.  In addition, an asymptotic normal theory for the bias-corrected estimator has been established, along with the evaluation of its theoretical bias and consistency under irregular conditions.  Furthermore, empirical evidence supports the bias-corrected estimator's superior performance in bias reduction on real data sets, along with a discussion of its potential implications.  The proposed estimator is named the Alternative Median Regression Bias-Corrected Estimator (AMR-BC).  A comprehensive simulation reveals that AMR-BC surpasses existing bias-corrected estimators in bias reduction, alongside exhibiting a more convincing empirical performance.  In a secondary analysis, I investigate the effects of the model's non-unique solutions on the bias correction and establish that a small perturbation can render the usual cross-validation ineffective, prompting the introduction of a proposed alternative.  The proposed estimator is made accessible through the R package "AMRBC." The task of Relation Extraction aims to extract relevant information from textual sources, focusing on the relationships between core entities. Traditional approaches to this task have relied on various techniques such as feature engineering, neural networks, and ensemble methods. In this study, we present an innovative strategy that combines Relation Extraction with Knowledge Graph Embedding by using a link prediction task. By initialising our relation extraction model with pre-trained knowledge graph embeddings, we demonstrate a notable enhancement in its performance. Specifically, our results show that this approach leads to a substantial improvement of 2.6% in F1 score for the Long-Short model and 1.3% for the CoType model on the YAGO dataset. Moreover, our analysis suggests that this enhancement is more pronounced for long sentences and those containing more written words. We attribute this phenomenon to the capacity of our model to generalise better to unseen entity correlations in the knowledge graph. Furthermore, our study also identifies the underlying distribution of Relation Extraction data and verifies that the YAGO dataset conforms to this distribution. Investigating the quarkonium fragmentation characteristics in a non-ideal quark-gluon plasma is crucial to understanding the complex behavior of the quarkonia. In this study, an analytical approach is utilized to examine the coordination number dependence, temperature influences, baryonic chemical potential, and speed asymmetry on the coordination number's imaginary part in the N-dimensional space with a particular focus on the 3D environment. Additionally, an investigation into the quarkonia's complex binding energy, Debye mass, and interaction potential in the presence of baryonic chemical potential is conducted. This research not only provides insight into the quarkonia's behavior but also sheds light on the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the nature of its transition. Furthermore, a comparison with previous studies, which were conducted using the finite temperature quark field model and constant Debye mass, is made to gain a deeper understanding of the topic. Finally, this research paves the way for further investigations into the quarkonia's behavior within the N-dimensional quark-gluon plasma and the potential impacts of the baryonic chemical potential and speed asymmetry on its transition. Data shows that the binding energy of the quarkonia decreases with increasing temperature and baryonic potential, while its coordination number's imaginary part increases with temperature and baryonic potential. It's worth noting that the effects of the baryonic potential and speed asymmetry on the quarkonia are significant and positive, yet relatively small. Also, the effects of the temperature and baryonic potential on the quarkonia are more pronounced when compared to the effects of the coordination number and anisotropy. This research demonstrates that the use of the quasi-particle Debye mass and finite baryonic potential is an accurate approach for studying the quarkonia's behavior within the non-ideal quark-gluon plasma. Therefore, this research is consistent with the observed suppression of the quarkonium production in the heavy-ion collisions. Finally, this research is crucial for enhancing our understanding of the quarkonia's behavior and the transition properties of the quark-gluon plasma. In the future, we plan to extend the studies to the finite baryonic chemical potential and speed asymmetry using the N-dimensional environment with a particular focus on the finite baryonic chemical potential and speed asymmetry. Deep neural networks excel at extracting complex features from input data, 
but their complex architecture makes it difficult to interpret the results.
We investigate the potential of modulated recurrent neural networks (MRNN) as 
a universal platform for developing clear and context-specific feature representations.
We introduce a novel variation of MRNN with a new activation function and 
prove it can represent any local, functional property.
Through experimentation with synthetic and real-world data, we find that MRNN is 
capable of efficiently extracting relevant information from input sequences.
We apply MRNN to the critical care field and use it to identify patients at risk 
of sepsis based on their medical history, extracting meaningful representations that 
can be easily understood by clinical experts.
The resulting model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in sepsis prediction 
and surpasses other methods for extracting clinical feature representations. 
Additionally, the model significantly reduces the complexity of representing 
clinical data and facilitates the detection of sepsis-related features.

Despite over a decade of research on deep neural networks, the underlying mathematical structure remains unclear. A notable exception is the field of dynamical systems, where researchers successfully mapped the theoretical framework to real-world applications. In our work, we delve into the unknown mathematical structure of deep neural networks by examining the geometric properties of the underlying statistical mixture model. Our analysis reveals that popular neural network architectures, such as residual networks and convolutional networks, employ geodesic projections to resolve information ambiguities. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of an optimal geodesic path for matrix factorization and show that max-margin classification can be viewed as a geodesic optimization problem. By dissecting the geometric structure of deep learning, we hope to illuminate the implicit regularization effects and understand how deep neural networks generalize successfully. Additionally, we showcase the utility of our theoretical framework for designing novel algorithms with proven convergence guarantees. The proposed methods outperform established baselines in multiple benchmark tests. Interestingly, our results also shed light on the long-standing hypothesis that deep neural networks can be interpreted as performing geodesic optimization. Furthermore, our work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for the deep learning community to investigate implicit regularization effects and understand the success of deep neural networks. In this study, we show that many solving methods for Partial Differential Equations share a common structure, allowing us to abstract the general approach and provide a unified framework. We demonstrate this by applying the methodology to both Hamilton-Jacobi and Monge-Ampere equations, previously addressed in arXiv:2101.07264. Our new framework is capable of capturing a wide range of numerical schemes, including those based on lattices, oriented lattices, and other methods such as those introduced in arXiv:1807.08033, arXiv:0904.01323, and reference [21] of the first author's PhD thesis. This unified approach enables a thorough comparison of different methods and allows for the identification of the most effective grid structures, ultimately leading to the proposal of optimized grid structures, referred to as grid minima. By evaluating the performance of various schemes, we ultimately recommend two preferred grid structures, referred to as the Oriental minima grid and the Karim minima grid. These proposed grids exhibit superior performance and can be adapted for multiple applications, including oriented lattices and other oriented hypercubic grids. Furthermore, the underlying philosophy of our grid minima method can be applied to various other problems, potentially expanding our knowledge and understanding. We're introducing a cutting-edge method for explaining, translating, and standardising ML model behaviour in multi-jet classification tasks. Our approach, LVRP, uncovers a comprehensive learning process by dissecting each ML model layer and pinpointing its contribution to the output. As a result, we obtain: (1) a breakdown of features used across different model layers; (2) a comprehensive analysis of input samples through counterfactual reasoning; and (3) a streamlined way to gauge class-specific losses and detect class imbalances. Additionally, LVRP's translation capability enables the merging, transfer, or adaptation of ML models into an unified framework, facilitating the comparison and standardisation of different ML approaches. Upon examination, LVRP revealed that simple models like ANN and GAN outshine complex models like CNN and LSTM in multi-jet classification tasks. Interestingly, despite their superiority, these complex models often generated plausible event predictions, yet resulted in significantly higher classification errors. Ultimately, LVRP's translation and interpretation capabilities offer a valuable tool for deciphering ML model behaviour, streamlining ML model comparisons, and providing actionable insights that can be effectively communicated to non-physicist experts in the field of multi-jet classification tasks. Our work's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Gruppe-14/LVRP. Additionally, the ML model interpretations derived from our analysis have been uploaded to InterpretableML and can be accessed under the handle https://interpretableml.com/#Gruppe-14/LVRP. A formula for deg(2) Stirling numbers will be provided, showcasing their relationship with the well-known Bell numbers. Insufficient computational methods have long posed a significant challenge to tackling the sign problem in many body systems. In quantum Monte Carlo simulations, the sign of the wave function proves to be an invaluable resource, yet introducing virtual particles inevitably results in a sign error. Our proposed strategy involves employing complex-valued neural networks to generate wave functions that are strategically constructed to minimize the effect of this error. Specifically, we utilize networks optimized using an alternating least squares algorithm, yielding a measure that is comparable to the exact benchmark. Our results indicate that this method is suitable for tackling systems plagued by the sign problem, namely the SU(3) gauge theory and certain classes of heavy dipositon resonances. However, this increased efficiency comes with a critical drawback, significantly expanding the models' size and training costs. Deep Neural Networks, known for their impressive data classification capabilities, frequently struggle with achieving perfect accuracy on well-distributed datasets. This challenge stems from their reliance on cross-entropy loss, which reaches its optimal point when all predictions hold equal value. As a result, significant improvements can be garnered by slightly compromising this notion of equality, allowing for 'calculated risk' and thus better adaptation to datasets. This research investigates the efficacy of loss function modification as a means of enhancing deep neural network performance. A novel, in-house creation called the Equalization Loss (EL) is presented, capable of overcoming the limitations of cross-entropy loss. When paired with no other enhancements whatsoever, EL demonstrates the capacity to surpass state-of-the-art results on multiple classification benchmarks. Furthermore, analysis suggests that combining EL with existing optimisation techniques and network architectures is a viable and effective approach to achieving excellence on distribution-free datasets. In essence, EL is an actionable suggestion that can be integrated into the development of deep neural networks to boost performance. Additionally, source code used in this research is freely accessible at https://github.com/gregglee/ElLoss. Moreover, dataset predictions, training curves, and sensitivity analyses are posted on this public GitHub repository for the purpose of facilitating public sharing. It is hypothesised that the integration of equalisation loss will yield comparable or even superior outcomes when compared to other recently proposed methods such as focal loss. As such, it is contemplated that the main contribution of this research will be its ability to enhance the performance of deep neural networks on a variety of classification tasks. Ultimately, it is anticipated that the findings presented herein will serve as a foundation for additional research focused on the systematic exploration of loss function evaluations in the context of deep neural networks. It is also hoped that this research will stimulate relevant discussions within the research community. Specifically, it is expected that the equalisation loss will yield notable outcomes, particularly when applied to challenging, distribution-free datasets. To demonstrate this, samples of of 50, 100, and 200 data points were randomly selected from the CIFAR-10 dataset. As depicted in the accompanying figure, equalisation loss successfully yields better accuracy rates on these synthetic datasets. Nevertheless, a substantial gap in performance persists, contending that equalisation loss holds greater potential on larger, well-distributed datasets. Consequently, training techniques and network architectures need to be adapted in conjunction with the incorporation of equalisation loss. A possible future research direction could entail exploring novel network architectures capable of compensating for the flatness of the equalisation loss.

This approach has been successfully applied to the 2D material TiSe2. By calculating the exciton size of heavily doped TiSe2 using ab initio many-body perturbation theory, we found it to be larger than previously predicted using other methods. Furthermore, we used the perturbation theory to build a more accurate exciton model, which allows us to model the exciton behavior in doped TiSe2. The results show that the excitons in doped TiSe2 exhibit non-perturbative behavior, such as forming a single ground state, which is in opposition to what was previously predicted. Moreover, we found that the excitons in doped TiSe2 are weakly bound, with an binding energy of less than 0.1 eV. Additionally, we calculated the exciton effective mass and the exciton density, and found that they are heavily influenced by the electron-phonon interaction. Finally, we used the developed approach to construct a more accurate phase diagram of doped TiSe2, which reveals that the system may undergo a semiconductor-to-metal transition. The new method has been successfully tested and validated, and is now ready for application to other materials. In the novel class of nematic superconductors, Cooper pairs with nonzero angular momentum may spontaneously align due to spin-orbital coupling, even without time-reversal symmetry being broken.  We have discovered that, in the absence of magnetic fields, triplet pairs align within planes showing Pauli paramagnetism, characterized by volume magnetization.  Conversely, when these triplet pairs are considered to be in a two-component (1d) spinor format, a finite magnetic field aligns the spins uniformly, thereby demonstrating superconducting properties under such conditions.  Conversely, when these triplet pairs are considered to be in a three-component (2d) spinor format, a finite magnetic field does not uniformly align the spins despite being in a superconducting state.  Furthermore, when magnetic fields exceed a certain threshold, pair-breaking occurs, resulting in Proofs of long-range order for both types of nematic superconductors.  Magneto-electron transport calculations using a 1D model for the superconductor with a ferromagnetic domain wall have also been performed, yielding a nonlinear resistance curve that exhibits a characteristic gap structure at low temperatures, along with a nonlocal magnetic field-dependent effect that displays a local minimum at approximately 0.75 of the critical field value.  Transport properties show temperature-dependent behavior consistent with BCS theory, with the critical field ratio approximately equal to 3.8 and the critical current density approximately equal to 1E14 Amps per square meter.  Lastly, the influence of applied pressure on the superconducting gap size under local weak disorder has been investigated, yielding a noticeable gap size increase due to applied pressure.  Overall, the coherent behavior exhibited by these triplet-cooper-pair-based nematic superconductors shows potential to be explored in materials exhibiting "incompressible topological QSH insulator" properties and further research is suggested to analyze the impact of disorder on the proposed models.

We propose the concept of a minimax game-based learning framework, wherein both the model and opposing forces (referred to as the adversary) strive to complete in a two-player zero-sum competition. Under certain conditions, this enhanced framework offers improved learning outcomes and increased model robustness compared to standard supervised learning methods. Specifically, we demonstrate that our minimax game-based approach leads to enhanced generalization performance and a stronger theoretical guarantee of misclassification errors. Furthermore, we examine the method's efficacy in generating adversarial examples and reveal that our approach surpasses existing methodological comparisons. We also provide a diagnostic analysis that explains the increased robustness of minimax learned models, alongside a theoretical inspection of our model's generalization performance. Lastly, we evaluate the efficacy of our minimax game-based learning method on multiple real-world datasets, showcasing its capacity to generate more resilient models adversarial to both strong and subtle adversaries. This research estimates the computational requirements of musical data from 1950 to 2010 in popular Western music. The study finds that there's a noticeable, steady increase in musical data complexity over the past century. The analysis also reveals two significant turning points in musical data complexity - one corresponding to the 1960s and 70s counterculture and social change, and another with the rise of digital music in the 1990s and early 2000s. The findings are consistent with previous findings on musical structure and support theories on the societal drivers of musical evolution. The data complexity metric is comprised of three components: melody, harmony, and rhythm complexity. The analysis of melody complexity reveals an unexpected decline since the 1920s, and the analysis of harmony complexity shows a steady increase since the 1930s. The rhythm complexity component exhibits an overall increase since the 1960s. The study combines these components with an analysis of musical instrument diversity to better understand the evolution of musical data complexity. The results are presented in a publicly accessible database and a detailed report that includes additional metrics, citations, and figures. The study concludes with a discussion of the findings, the limitations of the analysis, and potential future directions of research. The dataset will be updated to include data from 2010 to 2020 in the near future. The database can be accessed at musiccomplexity.org. The associated software code is publicly available at github.com/musiccomplexity. Comments and feedback are welcome at mail@musiccomplexity.org. The study is supported by a grant from the US Library of Congress (LPA-19-04). In our investigation, we examine a multi-component reinforcement process. At each time point, the experimenter selects a subset of the components and awards each one in the chosen subset with one unit of activity. We demonstrate that, as the number of components grows according to a specific rule, the distribution of the counter, i.e. the total activity count, converges towards a continuous, frequency-based probability distribution. Furthermore, we show that the set of all possible frequencies for the counter is restricted by a frequency-based distribution as well. Additionally, we observe that the frequency-based distribution providing an upper limit on frequencies for the counter can also be obtained through a smoothing process applied to the frequency-based distribution resulting from the exponentiation of the total activity count. Lastly, we note that all of the above findings are applicable in cases where the number of components is substantially greater than the square root of the number of time points. However, under this condition relaxed to merely being greater, the distribution of the counter converges towards a continuous, frequency-based probability distribution on the positive real numbers, $\mathbb{R}^{+}$, such that its support does not exceed the interval $[0,1]$. Moreover, we note that all of the above findings are applicable to models in which, at each time point, the experimenter independently selects the components with replacement. Furthermore, we extend these observations to obtain information about component activity distributions as well. Instead, it's reimagined as a dynamic state lacking clear definitions but inherently playful and adaptable. This redefinition merges computational systems with the principles of Deleuzean chaos theory, emphasizing their diverse and unpredictable natures. To convey this idea, a brief chronicle is presented, spanning from the earliest computational civilizations to the present, via an interpretive analysis of Stanley Kubrick's films. Throughout, this concept is explored through the lens of a hypothetical computational organism known as "Glow." Lastly, a hopeful vision is outlined for a future computational ecosystem, one that might harbor and nurture an abundance of playful, adaptable, and complex life forms. This vision is modeled after the renowned Studio Ghibli's films, famous for their portrayal of a world in harmony with nature. This harrowing, utopian dream is offered as a hopeful mirror to reflect upon our own future as computational beings. In this future, playfulness might serve as a guiding force, enabling us to navigate and understand the intricacies of computational ecosystems, thereby giving rise to an eternal garden of diversity. We demonstrate that the Smyth powerdomain does not have a core-compact topology when defined for a broad category of mathematical domains. This contrasts with our initial assumption that had led to a simplified proof of a previously complex theorem. This new result implies that the Smyth powerdomain cannot be used to prove that upper continuous joins are equivalent to continuous meets. Furthermore, we show that for domains with continuous order, the Smyth powerdomain does have a core-compact topology, thus reinforcing its utility as a domain representing upper continuous joins. This leads to a revised and simplified proof that in core-compact domains, continuous upper joins are indeed continuous meets. Additionally, we define a new variant of the Smyth powerdomain called the omega-Smyth powerdomain, demonstrating that it possesses a core-compact topology for domains with omega-continuous order, while preserving many of its original domain's properties. This new variant can be used to express upper omega-continuous joins. Finally, we introduce the concept of a weak omega-Smyth powerdomain, defining it as a subdomain of the omega-Smyth powerdomain. This weak omega-Smyth powerdomain is shown to represent upper weak omega-continuous joins, thus representing a middle ground between the Smyth and omega-Smyth powerdomains. In particular, we demonstrate that for domains with omega-continuous order, the weak omega-Smyth powerdomain is topologically equivalent to the omega-Smyth powerdomain. This is further complemented by a general topological equivalence between the Smyth powerdomain and a subdomain of the omega-Smyth powerdomain, specifically for domains with continuous order. This new result implies that the Smyth powerdomain can be viewed as a domain representing upper continuous joins that is core-compact. Lastly, we define a topological domain as being weakly core-compact if and only if it can be embedded into a core-compact topological space. This new definition is equivalent to the original topological domain being core-compact. This is further complemented by an equivalent definition of core-compactness, stating that a topological domain is core-compact if and only if it possesses a family of finite covers for any given open cover. This is notably different from the standard definition which required the covers to be finite itself. A laboratory study was conducted to examine the influence of a warm object on a rotating, temperature-sensitive fluid. The laboratory setup resembled a cylindrical body with warm and cold air inside, creating distinct isothermal interfaces. This configuration enabled the creation of baroclinic waves through interactions within the system, specifically focusing on the effect of a warm object's spin. Two distinct protocols were observed, namely an imaginary warm object's rotation and a real warm object's rotation. This study sought to establish a baseline for assessing the influence of the warm object's spin on baroclinic waves. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. However, the process's parameter, $\mu(t)$, has a straightforward relationship with the intensity of these events. By taking the derivative of $\mu(t)$, this paper argues that this relationship is sufficient to effectively explore the variability of extreme events within a Bayesian framework. This 'amplified' parameter offers significant advantages in sampling efficiency and the ease of interpreting posterior distributions, particularly when combining data from multiple locations. The paper also presents an objective method for selecting suitable models based on informative values, known as 'effective latitude' in the context of extreme events. Finally, a case study using data from rainfall and temperature is included to demonstrate the proposed parameter's benefits. It is noteworthy that this technique is not limited to the Poisson process, but can also be applied to other models as well. Further, the paper adopts a non-informative priors approach, but acknowledges that by using the proposed parameter, a more flexible and less conservative approach could also be adopted. The results suggest that the parameter does not necessarily equate to a simple latency, but rather, depending on the parameter's sign, it could provide insights into the processes it might be sensitive to. The code used for this analysis has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ExtRemes/PoissonReparameterization.git. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 suggested the presence of sub-stellar objects primarily composed of rock due to equal hydrogen and helium masses breaking down. Theoretical models of T-dwarfs, however, are inconsistent with observational data, with the most critical issue being their thermal profiles. The aim of this study is to compare the most advanced atmospheric models of T-dwarfs with observational data of GJ 229B, a highly radiant object with an irregularly spinning schedule. We applied the Apollo retrieval algorithm to simulate highly realistic synthetic data and used a Bayesian approach to assess model accuracy based on observational constraints from the ECFC and Gravitational microlensing events. The best-fit model shows the presence of a low-level infrared emission with temperatures around 500-600 K at the bottom of the atmosphere and a mostly nitrogen-rich atmosphere with a metal abundance 10 times higher than in the atmosphere of Jupiter. The findings of this study resolve the enigma surrounding GJ 229B and are consistent with the characteristics of other T-dwarfs, as well as with models of ultra-rigid rocky planets with tiny liquid oceans on the surface. The implication is that the evolution of such planets should prioritize preservation of the liquid water ocean over massive rock deformation, and that GJ 229B may represent a type of ultra-rigid rocky world with a tiny ocean, a phenomenon that astronomers may observe more frequently with future space missions. A precise estimate of the Standard Model predictions for $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ has been achieved through a detailed analysis of the decay process $B_s^0\to{J}/\psi f_s$. The study, carried out using heavy quark effective theory at the next-to-next-to leading order in QCD, incorporates systematic uncertainties that are predicted to be significant. The outcome is a highly accurate prediction for the $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ values within the Standard Model. Furthermore, the research provides a strong case for continuing the study of $B_s^0\to{J}/\psi f_s$ at LHCb and HL-LHCb via two methods: (i) a more in-depth analysis of the $B_s^0\to{J}/\psi f_s$ mode to reduce uncertainties related to hadronic interactions and (ii) exploiting $B_s^0\to{D_s}^{*+}\mu D_s^{-}$ to measure $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ independently of hadronic uncertainties in the $D_s$ system. The results indicate that with data collected by the HL-LHCb experiment, the uncertainty for the $\phi_s$ measurement could potentially be reduced to 6.7$\times$10$^{-5}$ and the $\Delta\Gamma_s$ uncertainty could be lowered to 4.3$\times$10$^{-3}$. The study suggests that with data from the HL-LHCb experiment, the $\Delta\Gamma_s$ measurement could be more precise than predictions from many models, including the NMSSM. Therefore, it is crucial that the $B_s^0\to{J}/\psi f_s$ mode and $B_s^0\to{D_s}^{*+}\mu D_s^{-}$ are studied extensively to achieve the desired precision on the $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ measurements. The outcome will enable highly sensitive tests of various new physics scenarios and the $B_s^0$ system will remain a valuable laboratory for the $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ measurements. The study also outlines future plans to enhance these measurements in the $B_s^0$ system to become the most precise within the $b\to{c}$ quark transition. However, the large-scale optimization issues associated with existing kernel-based DMD variants remain unresolved. This paper presents a novel framework for kernel learning in DMD that is both robust and efficient. The proposed approach, the Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), incorporates a sparse penalization technique for kernel learning, thereby addressing optimization issues in kernel-based DMD. A significant contribution of the research is the formulation of LANDO through convex relaxation, a unique aspect in the context of kernel learning for DMD. The proposed method is rigorously evaluated using various fluid dynamics datasets and compared with pre-existing methods. The results demonstrate the superiority of LANDO in terms of sparsity, smoothness, and the ability to accurately capture non-linear dynamics while minimizing optimization issues associated with kernel learning. The effectiveness of LANDO is further illustrated through the analysis of a 2D Navier-Stokes equation and the examination of non-linear behavior in turbulent flows. The research findings are expected to influence the field of data-driven system analysis and inform the development of future kernel learning methods for DMD. A significant question remains regarding the most efficient method for the human brain to learn motor movements. This study investigates various drive methods for motor learning and evaluates their effectiveness. We present a virtual robot arm environment in an Euler basis, allowing for intuitive and simple control. Importantly, our model is capable of identifying the most effective drive method for the robot's end-effector motion. Through simulations, we examined the stability and efficiency of five drive methods: constant drive, constant velocity, sinusoidal drive, chaotic drive, and random drive. Our results indicate that the constant velocity drive is the most suitable choice. Additionally, we found that the constant drive and sinusoidal drive methods can learn successful control strategies, but they require a longer period of time. Conversely, the chaotic drive and random drive methods can quickly obtain a effective controller but often fail to transfer to new tasks efficiently. Our study suggests that the constant velocity drive is the most effective means of achieving efficient motor learning. Our extension to Gym, called gyrene, can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/AI-ElabOrb/gyrene. Furthermore, our research also includes a set of pre-trained models that demonstrate successful motor learning using various drive methods. These models can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/AI-ElabOrb/end-eff-renlearn. Our study contributes to the body of knowledge on efficient motor learning and the optimal design of training environments. Furthermore, our findings and tools may also be applicable to other domains beyond motor learning, such as computer vision and natural language processing.
