The research focuses on events containing a high-energy photon or Z boson and an object exhibiting pronounced ionization loss and substantial momentum.  To increase the likelihood of detecting the object in question, events are filtered using criteria such as the particle's transverse momentum, the quantity of momentum transferred in the photon or Z boson interaction, and the particle's stability over extended distances, with a focus on objects with a stability time of up to 10 meters.  The research outcome is a dataset containing 8,350 events with a stability time of 300 millimeters and a signal-to-background ratio of approximately 0.04 or a background occurrence rate of one incident per octillion years for events with a stability time of up to 10 meters.  The study's findings align with the predictions of the standard model of particle physics as regards the production of standard model particles that are charged and highly ionizing. The research also provides limits on the feasibility of extraneous physical processes such as the interaction of a dark current with photons and the creation of supersymmetric particles comprising top quarks and various other heavy particles that are charged and highly ionizing. The study's limits on these processes extend to a dark current with a mass of 0.3 MeV that can interact with photons and a dark current with a mass of 500 GeV that can interact with both photons and supersymmetric particles. The study also sets the limit on the feasibility of the supersymmetric particle charged hypino resonance phenomenon for particles with masses up to 1036 GeV where the supersymmetric particle decays into a charged hipion and a quark. The study's limits on this supersymmetric particle charged hipion resonance phenomenon extend to a hipion with a mass of 28 MeV for hipions that interact with both photons and supersymmetric particles. The study also provides the most stringent to date limits on the feasibility of the supersymmetric particle charged hipion resonance phenomenon for particles with masses up to 187 MeV where the supersymmetric particle decays into a long-lived charged hipion and a quark. Well-established techniques in evolutionary optimization, such as multi-objective optimization and problem bi-objectivization, have been refined over time but still rely on overly simplistic assumptions regarding the optimal solution phenotypes. Specifically, these methods assume the existence of disjoint regions, each containing a single optimal solution, yet this approach fails to account for more complex phenotypes observed in real-world tasks. This study investigates the variability of phenotypic behavior in solving multi-solution optimization tasks, revealing that (1) phenotypic variation is a common phenomenon in solving optimization problems; (2) phenotypic variation has a positive correlation with the number of optimal solutions and the dimensionality of the search space; (3) population size has a positive effect on the diversity of phenotypes; (4) different optimization problems exhibit distinct phenotypic patterns due to the inherent nature of the objectives and interaction between the objectives and genotypes; and (5) phenotypic variation can be harnessed using techniques such as phenotypic ga, which can lead to improved convergence speed and quality of results. Our results indicate the necessity for more comprehensive theories underpinning optimization with multi-solution phenotypes and suggest further research is required to explore the potential of phenotypic variation in tackling real-world tasks. Based on these findings, we also propose several open research problems. Finally, the code and data used for this study are publicly available for reproduction of the results. The contribution of this work is threefold: (i) it examines the phenotypic behavior in multi-solution optimization; (ii) it highlights the limitations and unrealistic assumptions of current optimization methods; (iii) it paves the way for future research on more realistic and complex phenotypic behavior in optimization tasks. The research is expected to the benefit the field of optimization. The main text of this work is divided into an introduction in Section 1, a review of related work in Section 2, a description of the empirical study in Section 3, an examination of the results in Section 4, an analysis and discussion of the findings in Section 5, and a conclusion in Section 6. Additionally, two appendices provide more in-depth information on the empirical study and the theoretical underpinning of the findings. The article concludes by identifying the existing limitations and proposing several open research problems in Section 7. The research is a significant contribution to the field of optimization. Our research explores how distinct mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When one of these mechanisms is predominant, the valley Hall effect is preserved with infinite valley persistence. However, a combination of two mechanisms leads to valley destruction after a finite time, with the exact time of destruction dependent on the electron-phonon coupling strength. Notably, a mean free path exists for all mechanisms, with their values of infinite valley persistence exhibiting the longest mean free paths. Additionally, a relatively weak electron-phonon coupling is required to achieve a relatively long mean free path. Finally, valley preservation can transition from infinite to finite valley persistence under the influence of a relatively weak electron-phonon coupling. This study provides a fundamental understanding of the influence of electron-phonon interaction on valley physics in two-dimensional materials. It also sheds light on the complex relationship between mean free path and electron-phonon coupling strength, with potential applications in the design of valley-based optoelectronic devices. Lastly, it points out the challenge of achieving valley preservation at both theoretical and experimental levels, particularly under normal or weak electron-phonon coupling conditions. Consequently, additional efforts are needed to develop methods for enhancing the mean free path and reducing the electron-phonon coupling strength, thereby promoting the practical application of valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials. These morphisms can be thought of as stable, or robust, homeomorphisms between spaces, which are essentially the same as those obtained by taking certain types of limits. It can be shown that the resulting GH category is complete, and possesses a high level of flexibility. What's more, we identify a subset of "hub" objects, which serve as an optimal set of generators for the GH category, and demonstrate that any two objects within this category can be linked by a series of applications of these hub objects. This abstract definition of the hub objects also provides a novel interpretation of the notion of Gromov-Hausdorff distance. Furthermore, the proposed GH category bears a close relationship with a category system that accounts for various scaling regimes, and this relationship is illustrated through a number of concrete examples. A notable disparity exists in machine learning, wherein highly accurate models often prove difficult to deploy due to their excessive computational and memory requirements.  Achieving both efficiency and effectiveness presents a significant research challenge.  Specifically, in the field of reinforcement learning, abundant state spaces can render agents impractical to run in real-time.  Our study focuses on addressing this issue by introducing a feature extraction mechanism that incorporates an opt-out option, allowing agents to select features optimal for task resolution and thereby strike a balance between model accuracy and computational demands.  Our approach is encapsulated in a universal latent representation (ULR) framework, which automatically discovers and presents the most relevant features to the agent.  Additionally, we introduce a novel reward scheme that encourages agents to opt-out of unnecessary features to improve their generalizability.  Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate the ULR framework's effectiveness in promoting generalization and achieving feature-efficient representations.  Furthermore, we showcase the potential of the ULR framework to resolve other challenges in machine learning.  The source code is available at https://github.com/hobson-lab/generalization-optimization.

We examine the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the range of hundreds of MeV. In particular, our investigation focuses on three areas: (i) the creation of sterile neutrinos via charged current interactions within the Near Detector; (ii) the influence of sterile neutrinos on the long-baseline neutrino oscillity probability and its detectability by DUNE; (iii) the generation of sterile neutrinos via neutral current interactions and its possible detection mechanisms. Our analysis shows that the DUNE experiment has the capability to restrict sterile neutrino parameters by supplementing present research, particularly in the case of sub-GeV sterile neutrinos. Additionally, we have found two notable methods through which the sterile neutrinos could be identified: (a) by analyzing distortions in the far-offshore neutrino beam spectrum and (b) by exploring events involving heavy hadrons in the far-offshore detector, assuming that the creation of sterile neutrinos via NC interactions is significant. Both of these potential detection methods are connected to the previously mentioned constraint on neutrino oscillations. Therefore, it will be intriguing to observe if any of these three related possibilities - involving CC interactions, neutrino oscillity probability, and NC interactions - can provide hints of sterile neutrinos. If indications of sterile neutrinos are found, it might be the result of an interplay between the previously mentioned three related possibilities. As such, the DUNE experiment offers a multifaceted opportunity. If signs of sterile neutrinos are not detected, it will lead to a significant limitation on their properties. This investigation mainly focused on the generation of sterile neutrinos via NC interactions and we did not thoroughly explore several other potential detection methods such as the creation of sterile neutrinos via the decay of mesons. As such, it is possible that our conclusions are only partial and the actual opportunities presented by the DUNE experiment in the search for sterile neutrinos might be even greater. It is also worth noting that the DUNE experiment has two major locations that participate in the near and far-offshore detectors which provide valuable insights into the characteristics of sterile neutrinos. Deep graph neural networks have revolutionized the field by enabling the transfer of learning from a central hub to surrounding nodes. Despite this, central hub structures are rare in real-world networks, and many instead feature distributed information across multiple nodes or multiple overlapping subgraphs. A recent model, the structured graph neural network, addresses this by incorporating diverse network structures into its design. However, a major limitation of SGNs lies in their restricted applicability due to the need for manual pre-computed graph structures for both training and inference. To overcome this, our work presents two new methods, Graph-Web and Graph-Swap, that automatically generate structured graphs from unlabelled background networks to support a wide range of network structures. These methods are scalable, efficient, and adaptable across various network types. They outperform existing methods by a significant margin in terms of both performance and computational cost. Additionally, our models successfully address the long-standing challenge of graph representation learning by using our structured graphs as pre-trained knowledge bases. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets further confirm the superiority and efficacy of our proposed structures and frameworks. Finally, our work showcases the vast potential of our structured graphs through meaningful feature visualizations and accurate node predictions in unlabelled tables. Code and dataset are available for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/yelundeg/SPIG. Additional details can be found in the supplementary document at arxiv.org/abs/2205.14142. Our method enhances the previous technique and provides a more comprehensive system by incorporating more intricate types of functors. This development results in a hierarchical structure consisting of increasing categories of models, allowing for the treatment of flexible models and providing a clear definition of continuous models. Moreover, we define a corresponding category of symmetric models, which accommodates the axiomatic treatment of independence. Our method is demonstrated by applying it to establish the categorial foundations of ZFC set theory and continuous logic itself, as well as the foundation of second-order arithmetic and analytic philosophy. Finally, we demonstrate a key theorem outlining the relationship between type theory and category theory. Specifically, we show that for any type theory, there exists a corresponding category theory, and vice versa. Our framework is then utilized to establish a rigorous foundation for the mathematical theories of Martin-L\"of type theory and dependent type theory. This involves defining a specific model of Martin-L\"of type theory and demonstrating that it satisfies the universality criterion, which guarantees that it is a legitimate foundation for the theory. This approach also allows us to derive a axiomatic treatment of Martin-L\"of type theory and dependent type theory, as well as a corresponding category theory. This later develops into a more comprehensive theory that includes universal dependent type theory and other related concepts such as homotopy type theory. This later becomes a specific case of our more general theorem outlining the relationship between type theory and category theory. Suicidal thoughts are a serious indicator of potential future suicidal behavior. Effective prediction can facilitate early, targeted interventions to prevent suicides. However, accurately forecasting suicidal thoughts on an individual basis is challenging due to various uncontrolled factors affecting a person's mental state, such as life-changing events and their shifting mental health over time. To tackle this issue, a novel, sequential deep learning network is designed, taking into consideration the temporal dynamics of suicidal thoughts and incorporating the inherent variability in individuals' mental health. The proposed network is applied to the prediction of suicidal thoughts within the NIMH dataset and shows improved performance in predicting suicidal thoughts, with a significant advantage when utilizing multiple source data – electronic health records, social media, and human interview information – over utilizing a single dataset. Additionally, the developed framework is adaptable to various dataset configurations, offering enhanced predictive capabilities. Our results indicate that combining data from multiple sources significantly enhances the prediction of suicidal thoughts, exceeding the performance achieved through traditional machine learning methods and the established benchmark. Consequently, the proposed framework has the potential to be a valuable resource for clinicians and researchers in identifying at-risk individuals for targeted preventive measures. In 1942, Erdos posed a problem by querying the minimum size of an $n$-element subset of the natural numbers, taken so that the sum of any two elements from the subset differs from any other subset element. Erdos even provided a general upper limit for this query, estimating that the subset size should be within the range of $2^{n-N}$, where $N$ represents an arbitrarily large and fixed constant. Researchers have since found that subsets of size $2^{n-m}$ satisfy this condition, with the difference being that the sum of any two elements in these subsets may not necessarily be a member compared to a third element. Building on this, we present modified versions of Erdos' problem in three forms. Firstly, we investigate the minimum size required for a subset to ensure that the sum of any three elements is unique. Secondly, we aim to determine the minimum subset size guaranteeing that the sums of any two elements are distinct. Finally, we seek to identify the minimum subset size ensuring that all its element triples have one and only one pair-wise sum. The sound speed in dense stellar matter is a crucial component for ensuring a compact star's stability and admissibility as per the Cauchy-Schwartz and maximum pressure conditions in the theorem. Applying these constraints to various nuclear energy density functionals reveals that approximately one-third of them violate these conditions in neutron star matter, with a significant portion of these cases being instances where the sound speed squared in dense matter does not undergo a minimum or even has a flat minimum. Furthermore, our research focuses on dense stellar matter composed of neutrons, protons, and various exotic particles such as kaons, hyperons, quarks, and strange quarks. In our analysis, the admissibility of nuclear energy density functionals is extended to neutron star matter with various exotic components and to various two-fingerprints conditions related to the speed of sound. The results show that many functionals fail to fulfill these additional conditions. The study also examines the admissibility of nuclear energy density functionals in various star types, such as those with strangeness, comprising of neuts, protons, and strange quarks, and in stars undergoing various phases, including quark, neutron, and kaon stars with strangeness. The research reveals that numerous functionals cannot adequately describe the various phases of compact stars with strangeness. The theoretical framework used here can be utilized to extract information about the unknown density-dependent properties of the nucleons by analyzing mass and radius data from compact stars with strangeness. The research demonstrates that numerous low and high-density nuclear energy density functionals cannot simultaneously fulfill Cauchy-Schwartz and maximum pressure conditions in various star types, resulting in a significant discrepancy between predicted masses and the actually measured mass of the PSR J0740+6620 pulsar. The study identifies vast possible density ranges of the incompressibility and symmetry energy and highlights the significant impact of the quark phase on sound speed properties and nuclear energy density functionals. The research also suggests that the speed of sound in dense stellar matter should be a smooth and monotonic function of density. The theoretical framework developed here can be utilized to extract the density-dependent properties of the nucleons by analyzing mass and radius data from compact stars with various components and phases. The research will facilitate future research on nuclear energy density functionals with strangeness and compact stars. The results can be used to analyze various compact star types, resulting in new insights and constraints on their properties. The research paves the way for further studies on nuclear energy density functionals, with a focus on dense stellar matter

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed coherent states with distinct mean photon numbers and relative phase. These states are created using a linear optical network and then analyzed through two metrics: one measures the degree of non-classicality in the Fock space using the conditional variance, while another characterizes the spread of the quantum state within the Fock space using the condensed skewness parameter. By optimizing this parameter, we can identify a suitable combination of squeezing parameters for a trine state with minimal dispersion in the Fock space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific sequence of squeezings can produce a cat-state with high purity. The approaches discussed can be applied to any optical state made up of coherent amplitudes with a linear evolution. It is also possible to transfer the states to an atom-cavity system using optical cavities. A comparison is made with existing works on quantum state characterization in cavity QED. Additionally, we propose a method for rapidly switching between different coherent amplitudes using a 50% probability in an optical network, and explore an alternative approach for achieving this rapidly, which relies on a two-photon gate. This rapidly switchable mechanism could be realized with high probability using a linear optical network, and may also be applicable to other linear optical systems and cavity QED experiments. Finally, we present a possible way to verify the quantum characteristics of the optical states by using balanced homodyne detection and detecting certain moments of the quantum state. This approach could be adapted for use in cavity QED experiments. This work introduces a novel technique utilizing three-dimensional skeletons to analyze and characterize the complex interfaces prevalent in gas-liquid and liquid-liquid multiphase systems. A modified approach of the Simple Linear Interface Calculation algorithm is used to generate skeletons from image data. We establish a methodology for evaluating the morphological properties of interfaces, such as surface curvature, area, and length, as well as enhancing the sensitivity of measurements by adjusting the detection threshold. A three-part strategy for classifying skeletons based on topology is proposed, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our method using extensive datasets of breaking waves and droplets. Furthermore, we successfully integrate our skeleton-based framework with a feature extraction technique known as Point Group Features, significantly enhancing the ability to identify objects in this multiphase system. As a result, this work presents an efficient and effective technique for analyzing and characterizing the interfaces of multiphase systems, enabling robust object recognition. Due to its versatility, this technique can be adapted for use in various other systems featuring complex interfaces. A publicly accessible code for replicating our results is available online at https://github.com/Jia-chen/Skeleton-based-interface-detection. Additionally, the skeleton visualization tool used in this study can be accessed at https://chenjia-gh.github.io/Skeleton-Visualizer/. Extensive datasets used for training and evaluating our skeleton-based approach can be downloaded from https://chenjia.github.io/Skeleton-Datalib/. It contains gas-liquid and liquid-liquid interface data, along with three-dimensional models of breaking waves and droplets. This resource is designed to assist researchers in creating their own skeleton-based approaches for analyzing complex interfaces. It comprises a vast collection of realistic models, along with a dataset generation tool that can be adapted for use in a range of other systems featuring complex interfaces. This tool includes a pipeline for automatically generating models from real-world data, and presents the results in a comprehensive format. We anticipate that our technique and this resource will contribute significantly to efforts to analyze and characterize complex interfaces in high-impact applications, including digital twin creation and virtual labs. In particular, our study addresses a critical challenge in these fields by introducing a skeleton-based framework for complex interfaces and making available a vast, publicly accessible resource for replicating our results. This will enable researchers to analyze complex interfaces in systems such as gas-liquid and liquid-liquid multiphases, facilitating progress in these areas. Furthermore, our skeleton-based approach serves as a general framework for characterizing complex interfaces and can be adapted for use in a range of other systems

We examine distorted, flat galaxies using their residual warping patterns after removing the main cosmic curvature. This research focuses on two types of anomalies: those with concave curves (S shapes) and those with convex curves (U shapes). Our analysis reveals that S-shaped galaxies are predominantly spiral galaxies experiencing tidal forces, typically found in groups and clusters. Conversely, U-shaped galaxies are predominantly those with significant central bulges and high stellar masses. Like S-shaped galaxies, they likely undergo tidal forces as well. However, we propose an additional factor contributing to their unique warp morphology: a massive hot gas halo. As this gas responds to group/cluster potential, it could transfer mass to the galaxy, causing its warp to resemble a U and potentially leading to phenomena like jellyfish galaxies. This hypothesis is supported by the findings that nearly three-quarters of the U-shaped galaxies with this unique warp morphology indeed exhibit such phenomena. Moreover, we have identified key signs of this process: giant radiohalos and jellyfish galaxies appearing together in space. Our findings indicate that giant halos and jellyfish galaxies are not isolated entities but are instead closely linked, with the former potentially giving birth to the latter. This discovery opens the door for further exploration into the transition of galaxies from U-shaped to jellyfish and the formation of giant halos. Ultimately, it is essential to investigate the full spectrum of galaxy deformities to uncover the full range of their evolution. Our research is the first to connect distorted U-shaped galaxies with jellyfish galaxies, revealing a unified picture of galaxy deformation, and it paves the way for a fresh understanding of galaxy evolution. Additionally, it is a testament to the vast potential of this method in uncovering the underlying universal laws governing galaxy deformation. To further this research, we have established a website with interactive tools and data for the public to explore. This site contains all the data, graphical resources, and a interactive interface for viewing the relationships between galaxy properties and their warp characteristics, as well as the distribution of galaxies with U-shaped and S-shaped curvatures. The website can be accessed at: https://deformeddisks.org/. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at: https://github.com/rrraru/deformed_disks. This research has been published under a CC-BY license. Details on the dataset can be found at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3699383. In addition, we have released a paper outlining our method in detail, which can be accessed at: arxiv.org

density functional perturbation theory, and Raman spectroscopy in an 
externally applied magnetic field, the researchers investigated the chiral 
vibron in a family of trigonal nonlinear ABe$_{2}$ ($A=$K, Rb, Cs) optical 
lasers. The band structure computations predicted the presence of a $B_{2}^{+}$ 
mode, with frequency around 80-100 cm$^{-1}$, at the $\Gamma$ point, which 
exhibits polarization along the chiral axis and incorporates the structural 
symmetry breaking $A_{\perp} \neq \bar{A}_{\perp}$. However, the researchers 
discovered that the frequency of this vibrational mode is significantly lower 
than expected, and they propose that the difference arises due to an oversimplification 
in the phonon approximation. The researchers further observed a noticeable frequency 
shift (around 10 cm$^{-1}$) in response to an applied magnetic field (up to 8 T), 
which can be attributed to the electron-phonon coupling in a particular bilayer 
structure consisting of magnetic $3d$ and nonmagnetic $6p$ elements. The researchers 
furtherpoint out that the chiral vibrational mode, along with being electron-phonon

vibron shares an interesting connection with the megahertz-frequency unpaired 
spin vibrations in antiferromagnetic $3d$ compounds. Moreover, the researchers 
conjecture that the field-induced low-frequency mode can act as a driving force

in $p$-electron systems with adequate interlayer magnetic interaction. Finally, the 
researchers note that the investigated chiral phonon can be effectively controlled

and nonlinear optical systems with adequate interlayer magnetic interaction and 
electronic interaction with vibrational modes. The researchers suggest that an

We have derived a non-adiabatic version of Born effective capacity, which includes the Drude weight as a key component. Our research demonstrates that the Drude weight remains unaffected by non-adiabatic processes, which is consistent across various types of non-adiabatic perturbations. Furthermore, we found that the non-adiabatic correction to the Born effective capacity is negligible when the frequency of the perturbation is very low. Our findings can be applied to any system as long as the non-adiabatic perturbation meets specific conditions, and we apply this understanding to study the phonon transport in a metal lattice. Additionally, we developed a method to calculate the non-adiabatic correction to the Born effective capacity using a non-adiabatic perturbation of the charge carriers near the Fermi level. Our study shows that the non-adiabatic correction to the Born effective capacity is significantly influenced by the rate of carrier scattering, which in turn affects the Drude weight and overall conductivity of the system. Moreover, we observed that the non-adiabatic correction to the Born effective capacity can be ignored if the rate of carrier scattering is higher than the rate of phonon scattering. Finally, we found that the Drude weight remains a reliable indicator of conductivity in systems that experience non-adiabatic processes, which is particularly important for understanding phonon transport in metals. This understanding can be further applied to study phonon transport in systems with higher dimensionalities and diverse topological properties. Moreover, our research highlights the necessity of including non-adiabatic processes when studying phonon transport in metals, which may provide new insights into this field of research. By incorporating non-adiabatic processes, we can develop a more comprehensive and accurate theory of phonon transport that accounts for all the inherent complexities of the system. This comprehensive approach can be further applied to explore other phenomena in condensed matter, such as quantum Hall effects, topological insulators, and surface states. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the non-adiabatic correction to the Born effective capacity can be expressed as a product of two factors: the Drude weight and a frequency-dependent correction factor: CA(ω). This frequency-dependent correction factor can be derived using a specific analytical method, which involves examining the non-adiabatic perturbation of the charge carriers near the Fermi level. Our study shows that the frequency-dependent correction factor can be expressed as a product of two factors: the Drude weight and a dimensionless correction factor: g

In 1934, Kolmogorov proposed a framework for understanding the behavior of turbulent flows, but it primarily applies to the large-scale movements within a flow and not the smaller-scale descriptions. To better understand the dynamics of turbulent flows, researchers have developed new theoretical frameworks in recent years, but they often neglect to account for the effects of viscosity. However, since turbulence is inevitably driven by the interaction with the surrounding flow and ultimately affected by the walls of the container holding the flow, it is inevitable that the effects of viscosity will eventually be felt. To address this, the existing theories need to be combined with the Kolmogorov framework in a way that accounts for the effects of viscosity on small-scale turbulent movements. Specifically, this study explores the interactions between turbulent flows and their boundaries, and as a result, develops a new model for understanding the behavior of turbulent flows at all scales. This new model is based on the Kolmogorov framework but takes into account both the effects of viscosity and the characteristics of the container holding the flow. When applied to thermal conduction, this new model reveals that the heat transfer in a flow can be described using a unique scaling law that depends on the size of the container holding the flow and is influenced by the effects of viscosity. Furthermore, this new model reveals that the temperature disturbances in a flow can be described using a unique scaling law that depends on the characteristics of the flow and are influenced by the effects of viscosity. Specifically, this new model reveals that the temperature fluctuations will follow a specific pattern of decay in a flow that is driven by shear and will follow a different specific pattern of decay in a flow that is driven by other mechanisms. Finally, this new model reveals that the effects of turbulence on the flow will be determined by a specific critical distance from the walls of the container holding the flow and can be described using a specific scaling law that depends on the characteristics of the flow. When applied to turbulent flows in general, this new model reveals that the momentum transfers in a flow can be described using a unique scaling law that depends on the size of the turbulent regions in the flow and are influenced by the effects of viscosity. Specifically, this new model reveals that the momentum fluctuations will follow a specific pattern of decay in a flow that is driven by shear and will follow a different specific pattern of decay in a flow that is driven by other mechanisms. We investigate the geometric magnetoelectric effect in three-dimensional topological insulators, examining its connection to the Witten effect and the half-integer quantum Hall effect. Mathematically, the magnetoelectric response is represented by a nonlinear function derived from four Chern Simons form, which exhibits time-reversal invariance. This property is demonstrated through a four-dimensional Witten effect, resulting from a Chern Simons form coupled with two Dirac operators on a four-dimensional manifold. Furthermore, this effect is linked to the magnetoelectric response in three-dimensional topological insulators, with the inclusion of a Bloch angle from spin-orbit coupling. Moreover, we extend our studies to higher Chern numbers, expanding our analysis to two-dimensional quantum Hall states with Haldane series characteristics and a necessary Berry curvature correction. As a result, we find that the magnetoelectric response is influenced by the square of the leading Chern number from the four-dimensional Chern Simons form. Similarly, in a quantum Hall state with a higher Chern number, a corresponding Witten effect emerges, along with an existing topological term that can be observed in edge states with a non-zero Chern number. Finally, we find that the magnetoelectric response can be observed in a quantum spin-Hall phase characterized by a Bloch angle, along with an appropriate Chern number from the four-dimensional Chern Simons form. Additionally, this response exhibits a geometric Witten effect and a half-integer quantum Hall effect, which can both be accounted for by edge states with a non-zero Chern number and relevant topological terms. Consequently, any experimental observation of the geometric magnetoelectric effect must be accompanied by a corresponding Witten effect or a half-integer quantum Hall effect. We investigated the chaotic scattering phenomenon in delayed systems that undergo scattering due to delays, and discovered that modifying the time delay results in a sudden transition from smooth to chaotic behavior. Additionally, we found that the dynamic regime can be controlled through a time lag modulation strategy, yielding an enhanced nonlinear effect. Notably, the advantage offered by this approach increases as the delay increases, and this finding holds true regardless of the initial state. The advantage can be quantified as the amplification factor of chaotic scattering, and it can be observed through various routes to chaos. Moreover, we observed that the ideal modulation frequency for chaotic scattering is inversely proportional to the system delay, and this provides a basis for an analytical formula that can be used to determine the modulated system cutoff frequency. Finally, we verified the scalability of our approach by examining chaotic scattering in a delayed laser system of a different nature, and the results validated the universality of our observations. The study contributes to the development of delayed dynamical systems that can be commercially exploited, and it paves the way for novel applications in active control of chaotic nonlinear systems. We investigate how proximal optimization algorithms modify the Riemannian gradient within a shared manifold, and derive a general formula for the intrinsic curvature tensor based on that modification. This formula expresses the curvature tensor as a sum of two components, one of which depends solely on the underlying manifold and can be computed efficiently using a proximal operator, while the other component is a quadratic form of the Riemannian gradient with a data-dependent coefficient that tends to zero at an optimal solution. Our theoretical results are supported by well-designed numerical experiments, with additional analyses in scenarios where the proximal operator reduces to a thresholding function and an anisotropic version of the $L_1$ norm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of stationary points with optimal regularization parameters, and highlight the algorithm's potential for differentiable, adaptive regularization in non-convex Riemannian optimization problems. A numerical example illustrates the algorithm's ability to adaptively choose an optimal regularization parameter for geodesic-challenge problems on Riemannian manifolds, and is further exemplified by an application in 3D image restoration. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbates-epfl/adaptive-riemannian-optimization. Deep learning techniques have revolutionized the analysis of spectral data, enabling the efficient comparison of spectra against extensive reference libraries or collections of known astronomical objects. Despite their potential, these methods have several key drawbacks. Initially, they yield a long list of promising candidates, which necessitate further verification through additional observations. A significant challenge arises when the number of proposed targets far exceeds the capabilities of follow-up telescopes. Secondly, these models frequently return an overwhelming quantity of duplicate or irrelevant objects, necessitating labor-intensive and efficient filtering mechanisms. Lastly, there is often a pressing need to identify new or rare objects that the models are unable to recognize due to their limited training. Inspired by the principles of symptom-based medicine, we propose an alternative, two-pronged approach to address these issues. Firstly, a new model utilizes a simplified, distorted view of the data, leveraging our understanding of the subject matter to isolate critical characteristics and reduce superfluous information. Secondly, a novel algorithm allows the rapid and efficient isolation of rare or unknown objects, providing a concise list of potential targets selected through a streamlined and automated process. This new framework, based on its results, promises to deliver a substantial improvement over the current state-of-the-art, demonstrating robust performance even with limited training and a broad range of object categories. Additionally, it enables seamless integration of new observational data, rapidly refining the target selection and providing a more dynamic understanding of the subject matter. Furthermore, this paper includes a general-purpose tool for target selection and a comprehensive database of known astronomical objects, called ScaPoS. Road damage identification is a fundamental process in urban maintenance planning but is hampered by limitations in current methods. The proposed approach is then tested on not only English but also Chinese and Japanese datasets, yielding superior balancing performance and lower error rates compared to existing techniques. Ultimately, this framework can facilitate more efficient and accurate road maintenance by minimizing the need for in-field inspections. The capability to learn policies that mimic observed human behavior is a significant component in the field of imitation learning.  While current models excel within the same environment in which they were trained, they typically fail to generalize to related areas.  Despite numerous studies, replicating human behavior across diverse environments remains an open challenge.  In this paper, a novel framework called Cross-Area Imitation from Observations, or CAIO, is introduced that allows a learning agent to replicate human behavior across multiple environments through direct transfer.  The CAIO framework leverages a pool of diverse environments, known as a environment corpus, in which multiple trajectories are recorded.  It enables an agent to replicate each trajectory from any given environment by aggregating the most similar trajectories from the environment corpus.  The agent is then trained to mimic the replicated trajectories using standard imitation learning techniques.  Through experiments in both simple and complex control domains, the CAIO framework has successfully replicated human behavior across multiple environments.  The CAIO framework has also outperformed existing models in several imitation learning benchmarks.  A theoretical analysis of the CAIO framework has provided insights into its capabilities and limitations.  The CAIO framework has several interesting properties that may contribute to its success, including its capacity to handle large numbers of environments, its potential to replicate human behavior through direct transfer, and its ability to generalize to unseen environments. Mental illness drives the majority of youth crimes, yet the criminal justice system frequently fails to address this core issue.  Despite the limited evidence supporting its effectiveness, many courts now force youth to undergo therapy as a condition of their sentence.  We investigate the impact of required therapy on a group of nearly 2,000 individuals convicted of a wide range of crimes in a large US county.  Using proprietary data from a leading mental health provider, we discover that while voluntary clients exhibit steady, negative trends in multiple metrics of mental health, individuals forced to attend therapy experience a remarkable recovery and exhibit lower rates of recidivism, as well as fewer suicidal ideations and threats.  Surprisingly, the benefits of mandated therapy extend to family members of clients, reducing their use of suicidal and violent behaviors by 40-50%.  We attribute these remarkable results to several factors, including the strategic targeting of individuals by the court system, the selection of high-intensity therapy programs for those most in need, and the systematic follow-up appointments that ensure consistent engagement.  Our research not only provides much-needed clarity on the effectiveness of mandated therapy in a real-world setting, but also highlights numerous opportunities for further research on the complex interplay between the criminal justice and mental healthcare systems.  Additionally, it presents a model that could be applied on a broader scale to a range of social issues to address the underlying root causes of crime in a more proactive manner.  Lastly, it presents data that can be used to build more accurate and equitable predictive models of mental health and violence to inform high-stakes decisions made by judges, policymakers, and AI systems.  Ultimately, our research offers a vision in which the criminal justice system becomes a conduit for mental healthcare, rather than a failed attempt to address it. This solution addresses a long-standing challenge in industrial quality control by leveraging the likelihood of HMM gauge configurations to detect irregularities in process data. Its key features include the capacity to identify intricate anomalies, the ability to learn from data with minimal training, and the ability to adapt to new equipment or processes without extensive retraining. Moreover, this solution tackles the issue of internal process incompatibility by incorporating the likelihood of HMM gauge configurations to detect irregularities. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through our probability evaluation method, which facilitates the identification of anomalies in practical industrial settings. This solution has been successfully implemented in an industrial partner's environment. Currently, state-of-the-art speech-to-text models heavily rely on large, single-source corpora. Researchers have explored using multiple source languages to create more efficient training data, yet existing approaches have unsatisfactory results due to several problems. Initial language training leads to language-specific noise and decreased performance on diverse datasets. Additionally, using source language information during inference can restrict the text generation possibilities. To overcome these issues, we propose using a small, universal dataset to create language-agnostic training data and found that combining this with existing knowledge leads to the most effective training data enhancement. Our experiments show that this method outperforms other techniques on multiple language pairs and can significantly improve the accuracy, particularly for less common languages. Additionally, we discovered that our approach also improves performance when working with large, single-source corpora. The code and datasets used for this research are publicly available at https://github.com/aisks/uwert.

Achieving one-sided differential privacy involves safeguarding data against breaches that reveal only SUPER (Superset, Union, and Majority) information, whereas traditional (two-sided) differential privacy protects against general privacy breaches. A significant gap exists in the current research, specifically in the case where a data set's dependent characteristics result in excessive publication of sensitive information. For instance, publishing a data set's size or distribution can inadvertently reveal highly confidential information. To address this critical shortcoming, we propose the Dependent Characteristic Privacy model (DepChar), a new framework that seamlessly integrates with one-sided differential privacy. Through a novel framework, we derive a significant finding: there is a fundamental incompatibility between releasing SUPER information and maintaining DepChar and 1-1fimal privacy, specifically when the data set's dependent characteristics lead to 'information explosion' where a data set's size or distribution predicts extensive amounts of sensitive information. Consequently, we introduce two innovative mechanisms - the Logarithmic Perturbation Mechanism (LPM) and the Sample-Then-Round Mechanism (SRM) - that provide a trade-off between privacy and utility under DepChar and 1-1fimal privacy. Moreover, we experimentally validate the efficacy of these mechanisms, thereby filling the longstanding gap in research regarding dependent characteristics in one-sided differential privacy. The proposed research will significantly contribute to the field by leveraging SUPER information while providing enhanced protection against privacy breaches, specifically those that arise from excessive publication of sensitive information due to data sets' dependent characteristics. Additionally, we will make the code available at a designated repository. In contrast to their expectations, Guzel et al. discovered that CO emission increased at radii similar to that of a previously studied planet, rather than being lowest at this point.  This led the researchers to believe that CO enhancement was not necessarily caused by planetesimal surface reactions, but rather by a different mechanism.  An alternative explanation could be that the disk's inner region is experiencing a thermal gradient that drives gas downward, resulting in a reduced CO fraction.  Future observations of 12CO at higher spatial resolution could help confirm this hypothesis or the planet's role in surface reactions. This outcome supplements the existing partial findings in [13], [14], and [15]. Additionally, we explore the case where the cost function incorporates a convex state constraint barrier. Building on the approach in [16], we demonstrate that under certain conditions, the'mild solution' can be equivalently represented as a solution to a coupled system including a second-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, an equilibrium measure, and an optimization problem with state constraints. This representation facilitates the identification of necessary and sufficient conditions for its validity. Notably, our work features a 2-person game cost structure with a unique quadratic dependence on velocities and positions, accompanied by a logarithmic dependence on measures. This framework enables the derivation of practical necessary and sufficient conditions for the'mild solution', effectively translating the mean field game problem into an optimization issue with multiple player interactions. Importantly, these conditions reduce to a classical MFG problem without interactions when the dependence on velocities and positions disappears. Our findings also cover the case where the cost function incorporates a convex state constraint barrier. The development of Visual Image Classification And Reconstruction (VICAR) has led to the growth of Visual Discrepancy Detection (VDD), which measures the accuracy of computer-generated visual outputs. VDD's distinctive challenge is its focus on both visual and semantic differences. Compared to other Visual Image Understanding tasks, VDD has been underrepresented in the field. We introduce the concept of Visual Discrepancy Detection and current state-of-the-art approaches, then develop the Transformer-based VICTOR, which outperforms previous methods on the Neural Style Generation dataset and contributes to the field with two new datasets: Neural Face Reconstruction and Neural Skeletal Human Reconstruction. Furthermore, VICTOR facilitates the use of low-resolution input images in VDD. To enhance the general applicability of VDD across various domains, we pre-train models on a contrastive learning method specifically tailored to fashion, which also improves the overall performance of VDD. The effect of employing pre-trained models on the speed of training is observed. The source code of VICTOR is publicly available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/moontahini/VICTOR. Experimental results indicate that VICTOR surpasses state-of-the-art VDD models and maintains an advantageous advantage even when fine-tuned on limited dataset. Additionally, the transformer-based model demonstrates superior performance on low-resolution inputs and fashion contrastive pre-training. We present three additional findings: (1) the suitability of VDD for fashion, (2) the negative impact of fashion contrastive pre-training on VDD, and (3) the optimal choice of support query sample ratio in the inference process of VDD. The new dataset and results provide a foundation for future research in Visual Discrepancy Detection, particularly within the fashion domain. Moreover, the code of VICTOR can be utilized for reproducing the results in the research. It is publicly accessible at the mentioned GitHub repository. We invite fellow researchers to explore the area of VDD, specifically within the fashion domain, and anticipate groundbreaking contributions in the future. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device FL grows, synchronizing updates can become a significant challenge. FL systems typically address this issue either by requiring devices to wait or by having the server buffer updates from multiple devices, but simultaneous updates can still cause conflicts. To resolve this problem, researchers have introduced various algorithms that optimize communication and latency, specifically a protocol known as Buffered Asynchronous Accumulation (BAA). New findings reveal that existing BAA algorithms have two key limitations when working with asynchronous gradients: 1) the server can become stuck processing updates and new gradients; 2) devices may send superfluous updates that cause the server to process redundant information. To address these issues, a new BAA algorithm, called Convergence-Preserving BAA (CP-BAA), has been developed. CP-BAA resolves the first limitation by allowing the server to handle new gradients without being bogged down by outdated updates; it addresses the second issue by enabling devices to send gradient partial accumulations that guarantee the server always processes a complete gradient at the next available time slot. Furthermore, CP-BAA introduces a new latency-communication tradeoff, offering better performance than prior BAA algorithms with optimal regret bounds in a variety of scenarios. Experimental results confirm its high resilience and efficient communication, making CP-BAA a valuable addition to FL research. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In this study, a novel approach is presented to enhance hole mobility through matched lattice structure. The findings reveal that growing GaN epilayers alongside ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ enables anisotropic strain boost, resulting in a significant increase of up to 80% in hole mobility within a single crystal batch. The strain boost is confirmed by XRD analysis and confirmed visually through an striation pattern observed on an M-3000 SEM. The band structure calculations and mobility model demonstrate that the boost originates from the strain effects on the hole mass, ultimately leading to improved carrier distribution within the GaN epilayer, and finally, higher hole mobility in the final device. The optimal combination of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ dilute substrates yields enhanced hole mobility and reduced internal resistance in GaN, presenting promising breakthroughs in gallium nitride device technology. The underlying universality of this technique suggests its potential to enhance other semiconductor materials and open new avenues for enhanced device performance and novel functionality. Additionally, the findings suggest that III-N compound substrates could be utilized not just for dilute dilutants but also as a means to exert anisotropic strain on other semiconductors, presenting a fresh approach to the established dilute dilutant strategy and the conventional strain engineering techniques. This work proposes an innovative approach to learning temporal variations in depth data through a sparse Gaussian process, enabling novel applications for marine robots. By applying this method to an autonomous underwater vehicle, we successfully demonstrated its efficacy in several complex marine environments. Compared to a standard state-of-the-art algorithm, our approach yields a substantial improvement of 25.6%, 11.1%, and 57.3% in navigation accuracy for two, three, and four consecutive time points, respectively. The shifting link framework allows us to analyze and make predictions about changes in a graph, offering a more flexible alternative to traditional framework-based models.  Despite this approach's benefits, it poses significant computation challenges due to the time required to transform existing links.  Consequently, researchers have explored alternative techniques for speeding up prediction operations.  This study presents a method that uses static representations to accelerate link forecasting by leveraging the pre-computation of predictive vectors.  The proposed technique is a viable option for addressing the scalability issues associated with the shifting framework.  Experiments have demonstrated its effectiveness, and it has outperformed existing approaches while requiring less memory than models relying on the shifting framework. The study also introduces static representations to accelerate the computational performance of this approach and compares it with existing state-of-the-art models.  Experimental results show that FORES\+ and its variants outperform alternative models, and the study offers extensive evaluations and analyses to confirm its effectiveness. This capability stems from the fact that relativistic nuclei (or quarks) possess both charged and neutral components that interact with each other and opposing nuclei in a manner that is both dependent on the energy of the collision and the inherent properties of the individual particles. Therefore, it is possible to study these interactions through peripheral collisions between opposing nuclei, a phenomenon that is particularly well-suited for examination with a high level of precision. This evidence spans an angular range of 3.3 to 5.7 radians and exists within a region that is largely outside the influence of the underlying momentum spectrum produced by the primordial photons. Recent research has focused on enumerative geometry, uncovering novel algebraic relationships between statistical models, random processes, and discrete structures like partitions, trees, and posets. This new area of study is closely related to topological combinatorics, examining the underlying statistical model's topology. As a case in point, enumerative geometry revealed a topological structure for the collection of all tree-valued arrays, yielding a critical topological distinction between marginal Poisson law and gamma law. Similarly, the topology of poset-valued arrays led to an enumeration-based proof that the Gaussian law is uniquely distinct from other discrete laws. Furthermore, enumerative geometry made connections between the topological structure of interaction forests and free groups. These findings suggest that enumerative geometry can uncover fundamental, topology-driven characteristics of statistical models, thereby identifying key features that models should exhibit and failing to classify models solely based on symmetry. This approach can be extended to other models, such as copula models, as demonstrated by an examination of models for simultaneous rank data. The material presented is an introduction to a current research project, aiming to establish a general framework for the topology of model classes. This project involves collaborative work with A. Buc Calderon, M. Dukes, M. S. Shah, and R. Yilmaz. The proposed framework will be used to derive new enumerative geometry methods for analyzing model goodness-of-fit and quasi-order. This research focuses on examining how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn.  Initial findings reveal that at lower pressures (up to 1.05 GPa), Mn$_3$Sn exhibits typical N\'{e}el temperature and anomalous Hall effect characteristics.  However, further pressure increase (up to 4.60 GPa) leads to a significant enhancement of the anomalous Hall effect, accompanied by a notable enhancement of its magnetoelectric modulus.  To understand these observations, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the pressure-dependent behavior of the lattice parameters and magnetic structure of Mn$_3$Sn.  It became clear that pressure triggers a series of structural phase transitions in Mn$_3$Sn, including the transformation of its lattice from a tetragonal to an orthorhombic structure and the transition of its magnetic order from a triangular loop to a closed hexagon.  It is the large volume increase and shift of the balance between these two types of magnetic orders that, we believe, cause the anomalous Hall effect to be significantly enhanced when pressure exceeds 1.05 GPa.  Ultimately, our research indicates that external pressure can be utilized to modify the anomalous Hall effect of Mn$_3$Sn by regulating its magnetic order and lattice parameters.  Given that Mn$_3$Sn and its related compounds are key materials in various spin-orbit coupled topological materials, our study's findings are likely to be applicable to a broader range of anomalous Hall effect materials.  Additional experiments under an even higher pressure (up to 20 GPa) have been performed and the samples show no phase change within this pressure range.  It has also been observed that the anomalous Hall effect starts to decrease when the pressure exceeds 4.60 GPa due to a shift in the balance between two types of magnetic orders that is not dependent on pressure.  A detailed description of these experiments has been included in the main text and in the S.I. that accompanies it.  It has also been found that the normal pressure Marty phase can be converted to the, with a higher,  low-temperature Marty phase under external pressure. Bill Thurston initially found that Euler characteristics are resistant to deformation in 3-manifolds. Subsequently, David Gabai extended this by proving that convex compression of 3-manifolds is ultimately Euler characteristic-decreasing. This research aims to expand Euler characteristic-decreasing properties to tight contact structures on 3-manifolds by combining recent findings of David Saeger and Chris Cieslik, who linked the growth rate of growth forms to Euler characteristics. As a result, we obtain two key findings: first, the growth form of a tight contact structure on a fibered 3-manifold determines its Euler characteristic, and second, tight contact structures on a given 3-manifold cannot all have the same growth form. This allows for the development of an Euler characteristic non Summers invariant for tight contact structures, along with an interpretation of its non-decreasing nature. Additionally, our growth form invariance joins previous results to conclude that all tight contact structures on a given fibered 3-manifold have the same growth form if the Euler characteristic is fixed. This research further reveals that tight contact structures on the fibered manifold M_{p}(e) have growth forms that contradict each other when 0<p<1, along with the conclusion that M_{p}(e) cannot be represented as a fibered product of two other fibered manifolds with the same growth form. Finally, based on an observation of David Saeger, the set of growth forms supporting tight structures on a given 3-manifold are perfectly divisible by the integers 1 through 9. This implies that there are at most 9 distinct growth forms supporting tight structures on a given 3-manifold. Moreover, we observed that Euler characteristic = 2 is the sole even characteristic, while 0 characteristic is the most prevalent among all others. Consequently, the two properties combine to yield a reduced set of potential growth forms: exactly 5 forms - 1, 3, 9, 27, and 81. We've discovered that the price of bitcoin typically rises in the months leading up to anticipated upgrades, but subsequently declines in the months following the upgrades. We've also found that the price of ethereum tends to decline before and after upgrades, but by smaller amounts than bitcoin. We've developed a theoretical model that explains these patterns and predicts them to be a widespread phenomenon among other cryptocurrencies as well. Our analysis reveals that the solutions to the Cauchy problem for the Zakharor-Shabat system can be expressed as a combination of two non-determined functions, provided certain constraints on their relationships are met. This discovery, in turn, leads to a novel interpretation of the solutions to the Lax equation for the non-integrability of the system. Consequently, we demonstrate that the average behavior of these solutions, under certain conditions, adheres to a specific scaling pattern, effectively explaining the feeble noise phenomenon in the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation and their associated statistical properties. This approach also enables us to derive specific formulas for the feeble noise probability distribution and to verify them against known results obtained using alternative methods. Additionally, we show that similar feeble noise behavior can be observed in solutions to the Cauchy problem for the Ablowitz-Ladik system. Under specific conditions, the feeble noise probability distribution was previously calculated using the nonlinear disorder approach; our discovery indicates that this result can also be derived from the aforementioned interpretations of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Furthermore, we note that the feeble noise behavior in solutions to the Cauchy problem for the Ablowitz-Ladik system can be observed for a wide range of values in the domain of the system's parameters. This extends the previous understanding of feeble noise behavior, which was only applicable under specific conditions. Lastly, we show that the interpretations of the solutions to the Cauchy problem and the feeble noise probability distribution can also be derived from the light-cone initial value problem for the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation. This particular example highlights the wide range of physical systems to which the developed interpretations and associated feeble noise probability distributions can be applied. All of the derived formulas were numerically verified against numerical solutions to the Zakharov-Shabat system, thereby demonstrating their practical utility. A mathematical model, inspired by a turbid flow phenomenon observed in nature, is developed to analyze a two-layer flow of viscous incompressible fluids with the lower layer having a greater index of refraction than the upper layer. The model utilizes the Euler-Bernoulli equation to estimate a viscous flow rate and shear stress across a horizontal interface, assuming a perturbing force acts on the interface under conditions of steady flow. The model also accounts for forces exerted by surface tension and capillary action. The results show that a change in flow direction is influenced by a change in flow index and capillary forces. A numerical evaluation of the model's equations confirms that a critical flow rate exists beyond which a transition to non-laminar flow occurs. The model's equations can be solved analytically to yield an approximation for the flow rate and shear stress. The accuracy of the model is validated using a comparison with exact numerical solutions. Based on the model's outcomes, guidelines for estimating a flow rate and shear stress are proposed. The model's estimates are within 5% of the exact solutions when the ratio of layer widths to capillary forces is high. A demonstration, incorporating data from the turbid flow observation, is presented to illustrate the model's utility in real-world applications. The model can be applied to diverse situations, such as estimating a flow rate and shear stress in an oil droplet moving through the atmosphere. The model provides an estimation of the flow index and shear stress based on physical optics principles. A comparison of the model's outcomes with experimental data and the estimates from various other models are also provided. The other models used for estimation are based on different mathematical approaches including the use of Taylor series, perturbation theory, and other approximations. A evaluation of these models shows that the new physical optics model is as accurate as the other methods but requires less computational effort to yield an estimate. A parametric study of the model is also presented to investigate the influence of various parameters on the flow index and shear stress. This investigation shows that the model's estimates are insensitive to layer width and height variations but are highly sensitive to capillary forces. A conclusion to this study is that the new physical optics model is a reliable tool for estimating a flow rate and shear stress in a two-layer flow of viscous incompressible fluids. To address the issue of electoral manipulation through the manipulation of voting districts, we developed an approach incorporating thermodynamic principles. By applying a non-uniform heat source to a map of a political division, our method mirrors the intentional skewing of the district map towards a particular political ideology. This approach enables the detection of such electoral manipulation through the analysis of the resulting thermal profile and its associated uncertainties. Given that the heat source's magnitude and distribution are intended to mimic the influence of a political ideology on voting patterns, we utilized a linear superposition of thermal profiles, derived from known thermal profiles under a fixed heat flux, to analyze the district maps. Furthermore, we applied Bayesian inference to measure the degree of electoral manipulation. Utilizing simulated data, our approach successfully detected the artificial curvature in voting districts with high precision. Additionally, we applied our method to actual redrawing of voting districts in the state of Wisconsin during the tenure of Governor Scott Walker and found that the degree of electoral manipulation exceeded federal guidelines established in the National Voting Rights Act. This research demonstrates that the proposed method can effectively detect the artificial curvature in voting districts with accurate measurements of the associated uncertainties. Furthermore, it highlights the potential for the application of this approach in real-world cases of electoral manipulation. To enhance the robustness of visual navigation systems based on reinforcement learning, we develop an alternative framework that incorporates information theoretic principles. From an RL perspective, our goal is to develop a sensorimotor strategy that optimizes data collected through exploration, aiming to maximize the collected information about the environment. We introduce a novel reward function that quantifies the novelty of observations, leveraging entropy to measure the unknown state's knowledge gain. RL driven by this novelty reward allows the agent to discover and identify unknown states. We further derive an analytic representation of this observation novelty reward, which yields multiple benefits: (a) the planning problem becomes deterministic and tractable; (b) the influence of perception noise is explicitly considered, promoting robustness against unexpected disturbances; (c) the agent can estimate the environment's dynamics without any pretraining. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using navigation tasks in simulated 2D and 3D environments, showcasing its robustness against noise and novel situations compared to traditional RL-based methods. The proposed framework is self-contained and can be applied to various RL methods, including those using neural networks. We provide a comprehensive description of smooth quadrics of arbitrary dimension in terms of categories, extending a previous result by Baur and Kleiner for the two-dimensional case. A smooth quadric of dimension $n>1$ can be represented by a finite sequence of positive integers $(d_1,\ldots,d_k)$, where each integer $d_i$ is greater than or equal to two, and the sum of the squares of these integers is equal to the sum of the squares of the first $2\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ positive integers plus one. Text games provide a rigorous platform to assess the capabilities of language models. However, current text games are generally simple, largely due to processing constraints that force agents to proceed step by step. Researchers have developed workarounds, such as processing multiple steps ahead, though these methods are generally not applied to more complex text games. In this study, we introduce an innovative text game paradigm that empowers language models to perceive and respond to entire text episodes at once. At the same time, we present an artificial intelligence model called TextWorldExpress, which achieves a remarkable feat - processing one million text steps per second while still providing a precise and accurate episode representation. TextWorldExpress surpasses human performance, outdoing it by nearly 300% in many cases. It achieves this through a distinctive attention mechanism that selectively focuses on relevant text segments. In comparison to priority queue-based attention models, TextWorldExpress exhibits both theoretical and practical advantages, and proves to be an extremely robust model that excels in diverse game environments. In particular, it shows remarkable promise in game settings featuring multiple story branches and dynamic episodes. Ultimately, TextWorldExpress sets a high standard for future text game models to aim for. At the same time, it presents new opportunities and insights for researchers in the field. The code for this project is openly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/jimmyu007/textworldexpress. Additionally, we have created TextWorldExpress demos for interactive evaluation, which can be accessed here: https://textworldexpress.github.io/. We welcome the community to participate in further development and testing of this model. In the near future, we intend to extend TextWorldExpress to process multiple text episodes at once. In addition, we will apply this model to more complex real-world text games to assess its potential in actual decision-making tasks. It is anticipated that the enhanced model will significantly surpass current text games in difficulty. For instance, we hope to model text games with multiple story chapters that are linked together, and text games featuring significantly longer dialogue and narrative content. We believe these extensions are theoretically and practically feasible, and will present a new level of textual complexity for language models to strive for. In the end, we aim to create text game models that not only match but significantly outdo human performance, and this research will present a novel approach to achieving that goal. We introduce an alternative method, rooted in functional integral techniques, to describe topological insulators with defects. This approach, previously utilized in the study of classical topological insulators, is adapted to quantify the effects of impurities on quantum topological insulators. Specifically, we examine the use of a spatially non-local functional in the context of quantum topological insulators with defects, as seen in the example of a quantum Hall insulator with a vortex defect. The derivative expansion of the effective action serves as a useful tool for explaining the emergence of topological properties, such as the Chern number, which remains valid even at finite temperatures. This approach is compared to a related method developed by Altshuler et al., with particular attention given to their results for a quantum Hall insulator with a vortex defect. Our results are consistent with those obtained by Altshuler et al., and are extended to include the effects of interactions between quasiparticles. Furthermore, we examine the effect of a spatial boundary on a quantum Hall insulator with a vortex defect, and derive a formula for the Chern number across the entire system. Finally, we outline the general characteristics of our method, and explain its potential applications to the study of other systems, such as topological insulators with surface or interface Dirac fermions, and heavy fermions. The approach is also expected to be useful in the analysis of other defects, including those without chiral symmetry, and with other types of topological order. Lastly, we speculate on the potential to adapt this approach to study higher-dimensional topological insulators with topological defects. In conclusion, we hope that this introduction will stimulate further research into the application of functional integral techniques to the study of topological insulators with defects. With this in mind, we propose several directions for future investigation, and suggest several systems that warrant further examination, such as the use of functional integral techniques to study surface degrees of freedom in topological insulators, and higher-dimensional systems with topological invariants of dimension two or higher. The implementation of functional integral techniques to describe the effects of defects in topological insulators is expected to be a valuable tool in the ongoing analysis and classification of the various types of topological invariants that have been discovered in recent years. Specifically, we anticipate that this approach will be a useful resource in the study of the interacting systems that are thought to give rise to certain types of topological invariants, as well as in the description of defects that have not been fully accounted for in existing theories. Two new multivariate spatial peak detection methods are developed to identify extreme weather patterns in ocean environments by analyzing unusual combinations of atmospheric conditions together. The first method, based on Spatio-Conditional Excesses (SCE), utilizes a joint elevation model for multiple weather factors, while the second, based on Spatio-Conditional Spatial Analysis (SCSA), applies a non-parametric approach to analyze multiple weather factors collectively. The performance of both new methods is compared with a reference technique, utilizing a simulated dataset based on a Monte-Carlo algorithm, along with real-world data from the Raúl Island weather station in the Pacific. The results demonstrate that the two proposed methods combined offer superior detection capabilities for unusual environmental patterns compared to the isolated analysis of individual weather factors or univariate peak detection methods. The novel approaches have promising applications for environmental monitoring and future studies of extreme weather in ocean regions. The study includes a comprehensive case study analyzing 32 years of weather data from Raúl Island, along with an introductory theory section and a detailed methodology explanation.
