Physics-informed neural networks have exhibited remarkable capabilities in solving partial differential equations. Despite the ease of implementing a neural network with a flexible expression, equilibrium equations often require a substantial number of points for a network with a fixed depth. To adapt to varying condition densities and solve equations efficiently with a minimal number of points, a vertex creation method within the framework of physics-informed neural networks is proposed. This method, called Residual-based Adaptive Vertex creation using Graph neural networks (RANG), includes three key components. Firstly, a residual-based adaptive node method adds new vertices based on the smoothness of the solution and its derivatives. Secondly, a vertex duplication strategy ensures that the node density remains uniform and maximizes the efficiency of the solution process. Finally, a grouping strategy within the graph neural networks framework decides which nodes to create and updates the node coordinates after duplication. The proposed RANG method outperforms existing methods, such as supervised gradient regression and neural ordinary differential equations, in solving several one-dimensional initial value problems and is capable of creating adaptive grids that facilitate accurate solution representation with a flexible depth. Additionally, RANG maintains the differentiability of the solution and allows for the computation of high-order derivatives with a minimal number of points. Furthermore, this method can be extended to higher-dimensional problems and demonstrates promising results in the adaptation of point clouds to represent level sets in multi-dimensional problems. Deep learning models, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been widely used for image classification tasks. However, they assume a specific input shape and dimensionality, which can be restrictive. Our proposed Orientation Convolutive Networks (OCNs) build upon existing CNNs, allowing for more flexible input shapes and dimensions. This is achieved through the incorporation of additional parameters in each convolutional layer, enabling the network to learn and accommodate varying input dimensions. By doing so, OCNs can handle images with different orientations and aspects, ultimately resulting in improved classification performance. Our technical evaluation highlights the benefits of OCNs compared to conventional CNNs. Additionally, we have made the OCNetworks framework available on GitHub to facilitate its usage by the research community. Further details on the implementation, as well as additional results, can be found on this repository: https://github/github/OrientationConvolutiveNetworks. It is worth noting that OCNs have several potential limitations. Firstly, the additional degrees of freedom in each convolutional layer may lead to increased model complexity and require larger dataset sizes for optimal performance. Secondly, the improved non-rigid shape handling capability may not necessarily translate to notable practical benefits, albeit it could be crucial in tasks involving distinct orientations. Lastly, given the relatively small difference in performance compared to conventional CNNs, the advantages of OCNs over existing models may be relatively minor. These potential drawbacks can be attributed to the design of our specific model and could be mitigated by future research proposing novel architectures. It is possible that alternative methods could be devised to address these concerns and develop more effective models with scalable complexity, preferable orientations, and superior generalization abilities. The success of Deep Learning approaches for 3D point cloud tasks is heavily influenced by the type of point cloud representation employed. Among the possible representations, high-level features derived from graph convolutional networks (GCN) have gained popularity due to their ability to model global properties and representations. However, current implementations of GCN for point clouds lack effectiveness, particularly when they attempt to learn effective global properties by aggregating local features. To address this issue, we introduce E-GCN, an enhanced graph convolutional network that utilizes an attention mechanism that enables each neighbour to contribute differently to the local feature aggregation. The attention mechanism allows the network to focus more on relevant neighbours, thereby maximizing the quality of local feature aggregation. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of E-GCN over the existing state-of-the-art methods on three challenging benchmark datasets. The accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Saurav-31/Effective-GCN. The three benchmark datasets employed for evaluation are O3D-Skeleton, PASCAL-VOC-12, and Scene15. The ability of E-GCN to focus on critical neighbours was visually illustrated through the visualization of the learned attention weights, with the corresponding observations noted in the report. Moreover, the enhancement of E-GCN over the existing methods was quantitatively demonstrated by the analysis of the influence of key components, specifically the attention mechanism, with the observed trends consistent across all evaluation datasets. Furthermore, the ability of E-GCN to consistently achieve top-ranked performance was showcased on four different benchmark datasets, thereby establishing its robustness and reliability. The three datasets where E-GCN consistently demonstrated excellence are: Benchmark, Scene15, and PASCAL-VOC-12. The three key reasons behind the consistency of E-GCN performance were: (i) the ability of GCN to effectively model global properties, (ii) the employment of multi-layer perception (MLP) to capture complex non-local properties, and (iii) the attention mechanism that enhances the quality of local feature aggregation. The incorporation of these components in E-GCN resulted in its high likelihood of achieving the best performance, with the associated risk of overfitting mitigated by the use of dropout and the selection of moderate model complexity through the employement of K-fold cross-validation to select the optimal model complexity. Recent advancements in cloud-based image processing have led to the development of extremely compact Trojan attacks. Unlike conventional methods requiring network manipulation, these "hostless" attacks directly target neural network structures, allowing for seamless deployment on mobile devices. However, existing hostless Trojan attacks have primarily focused on compromising model reliability and require elaborate auxiliary networks, thereby negating the advantage of compactness. To address this issue, we introduce a new hostless Trojan attack that achieves high performance with minimal additional complexity. Building on existing research, we incorporate gradient channel pruning and utilize transfer learning, leveraging pre-trained convolutional layers. Additionally, we propose a novel backpropagation path that efficiently utilizes these layers, accompanied by an innovative activation-dependent loss function that significantly enhances performance. The result is a highly effective Trojan attack with minimal additional complexity, showcasing a 114% performance boost over state-of-the-art methods. Our findings are backed by extensive experiments and a developed open-source hostless Trojan attack framework. It is expected that our research will facilitate the development of more sophisticated hostless Trojan attacks. The code can be found at: https://github.com/jayie1999/SEMHA.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest ENDF/B-VIII.0 astrophysical reaction data and examine key factors that can improve future subbarrier fusion experiments. Specifically, the reaction rates for 12C + 12C are re-evaluated with new elastic and inelastic cross-section data from various energies. It is discovered through this analysis that existing experimental results do not match the latest calculated reaction rates, primarily due to outdated cross-section data and experimental uncertainties. To resolve this discrepancy, future experimental research should prioritize measuring reaction rates at energies above 3-4 MeV, and any attempts at measuring lower energy reaction rates should incorporate improved non-resonant excitations. To achieve this in barrier-free measurements, an increased beam ratio of 1:3 or higher is recommended for 16O/12C. Additionally, the maximum energy for measuring 16O + 16O backgrounds should be closely matched to the 12C + 12C break-up threshold. Lastly, an optimal target thickness of 20-50 mg/cmt is suggested for minimizing both 16O + 16O backgrounds and 12C + 12C direct reaction cross-sections. This study provides crucial guidelines for future subbarrier 12C + 12C fusion research. It also proposes an improved detection strategy to reduce non-astrophysical background contributions, including the use of larger-scale detectors and additional technical refinements. Potential applications of this research are considered. It is concluded that with further experimental and analytical work, astrophysical reaction rate data for the 12C + 12C reaction could be significantly refined, which would enable more precise type-II supernova calculations and other related cosmological studies. This research could also contribute to a better understanding of nuclear physics at lower energies through the analysis of excess energy profiles. As such, the subject of this study is not only relevant to core-collapse supernovae but also to various research areas in nuclear and astrophysical physics. To overcome existing challenges, the Trojan horse technique will be enhanced with a greater beam ratio, heavier targets, and other technical improvements in future experiments. To address the issue of resonance interference in the latest 12C + 12C reaction rates, future research should incorporate measurements with higher-energy projective beams and targets. The ultimate goal of astrophotography is to utilize freshly discovered exoplanets as probes for stellar composition. This approach leverages the known relationship between a star's chemical makeup and the characteristics of its orbiting planets to gain profound insights into both stellar and planetary interiors. The inherent uncertainty associated with this method stems from its reliance on a commonly shared inheritance of materials between the star and planets, as well as uncertainties in theoretical models and observational data. By utilizing abundance measurements of numerous elements in 21 stars hosting terrestrial-type exoplanets, our study delves into the composition of the star and its link to the discovered planets. The abundance of each planet is represented by a set of reference values, thereby establishing a framework for interplanetary comparison. Our analysis of the richest multiple-planet systems reveals substantial variations in the chemical compositions of individual planets within the same system. The abundance of a given element in a particular planet may be significantly higher or lower than its counterparts in the same system. This diversity of elemental compositions among the planets within a multiple-planet system presents an opportunity to explore various planetary formation theories. Moreover, our study provides an extensive database of planetary abundances, thereby serving as a foundation for future research focused on understanding exoplanetary evolution, as well as the relationship between exoplanets and their parent stars. Finally, our investigation reveals that planetary abundances are closely tied to the stellar composition, thereby reflecting the elemental segregation between stars and their orbiting planets during formation. The resulting elemental ratios between planets and their parent stars may be utilized to shed light on the processes of exoplanetary formation, as well as the star-planet connection. The known relationships between stellar and planetary metallicity can be utilized to test the cosmically widely applied scenario of conservative exoplanetary formation. Our investigation provides fresh, extensive, and detailed insights into the rich chemical compositions of extraterrestrial planets, thereby laying the groundwork for an in-depth analysis of their interiors and the potential future detection of planetary core signatures in starlight. Deep neural networks (DNNs) can quickly learn relevant wireless signal features for localization, but they demand a substantial amount of labeled data and have limited insight into the underlying signal physics. Contrastive multi-view learning (CML) is a method to reduce the dependence on labeled data, but it is not suitable for wireless localization as it cannot effectively discard irrelevant information. Our study introduces a new deep neural network architecture that combines attention mechanisms with multi-view contrastive learning (MVC). This model allows data to be input from multiple perspectives and learns to weigh the importance of each perspective when training with labeled data, thereby enhancing performance and efficiency. Experimental results show that MVC outperforms 2D-CNN and attention-only models, with a location accuracy of 38.72% for indoor wireless localization. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/RuihaoChen/AttentionNet.

This paper marks the first installment of a planned series that will delve into specific proofs and structures. It is hoped that this framework will serve as a primer for introducing students to a variety of modal logics, drawing on the connections between different structures and the underlying topological properties. The introduction also lays out a research agenda for the project. The paper concludes by analyzing the existing state of relevant research and proposing new areas of investigation. In particular, it delves into the relationship between topological structures and fibring, a technique used to combine different structures and extend the methodology to a wider range of contexts. The second installment of this project is planned to include a comprehensive study of the diversity of modal logics and their relationships to other areas of mathematics, with a particular focus on topology. Scientific machine learning has become increasingly essential in the world of science, supporting researchers in various fields by extracting knowledge from data. One of its key benefits is the ability to mitigate bias associated with human judgment. For scientific applications, machine learning is particularly useful in dealing with uncertain information, which is a natural state of affairs in many scientific contexts. The ambiguity inherent in data not only affects but also often defines its core meaning. Consequently, there is a growing need for methods that measure and communicate uncertainty associated with quantitative predictions. This study provides an exhaustive review of evaluation techniques for ambiguity in machine learning models, presenting a widely applicable framework that can be adapted to a broad range of data and loss functions. To showcase our proposed approach, we present a comprehensive evaluation of 14 different ambiguity metrics applied to 11 distinct data sets, highlighting the benefits and limitations of each. Our analysis ultimately identifies five metrics that offer superior performance and versatility, which are likely to be preferred by researchers and practitioners in the scientific community. These metrics, along with their associated open-source code, have been made available for the sake of reproducibility. Our study lays the groundwork for a unified evaluation of ambiguity in machine learning and provides a positive outlook on future advancements in this field. Furthermore, our research paves the way for a broader exploration of machine learning's role in the paradigm of uncertainty-corrected inference, enabling researchers to harness the power of machine learning and scientific evidence for informed decision-making in the scientific community. Lastly, our work addresses the critical challenge of uncertainty communication, underscoring the necessity of standardizing terminology and implementing comprehensive evaluations that can guide researchers in accurately describing the ambiguity inherent in their models and data collections. By bringing these issues to the forefront, our study ensures seamless interaction between the domains of scientific machine learning and biostatistics/inferential statistics, ensuring a cohesive understanding of the ambiguous nature of data and providing standardized metrics and open-source software for future collaborative research. Additionally, our research facilitates the application of machine learning in the domains of epidemiology, medicine, and the life sciences, enabling researchers to harness the power of machine learning and provide actionable insights to policymakers and researchers. Finally, our study is a response to the call for action issued by the National Research Council, which emphasized the need for standardizing the terms and methods used in the field of machine learning and epidemiology. To improve the robustness of computer vision models, researchers have been investigating reliable learning techniques. These methods employ ensemble methods, code diversification, and multi-site training data collection to enhance model resilience. Furthermore, researchers have recently explored the benefit of collecting data from multiple users or regions through decentralized training. However, the source of collected data often lacks information regarding the source of the data, forcing the model to rely solely on the collected data. We conducted an in-depth analysis of the utility of regional queries in reliable learning and discovered that having access to more diverse data generally results in better handling of adversarial attacks, as demonstrated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. We also compared reliable learning methods with benchmark defense methods on real-world images from public domains and found a significant difference. It was found that reliable learning methods perform better than defense methods but not as effectively as expected on adversarial attacks. We further investigated the effect of multi-site data collection and discovered that it does not necessarily translate to better performance due to the variation in data quality. We then studied various data collection methods and found that centralized data collection and decentralized training with regional queries yield the best results. We also analyzed the effect of regional queries on training loss and found that it correlates with model resilience. We finally demonstrated the effect of regional queries on real-world images and provided code for public use to replicate our results. It was found that regional queries have a positive effect on reliable learning and can be utilized to improve the robustness of computer vision models. We also discovered that the type of data collection method and the quality of regional queries have a significant impact on the performance of reliable learning. It was found that centralized data collection and decentralized training with high-quality regional queries yield the best results. We also found that regional queries can be utilized to improve the robustness of computer vision models and provide recommendations for further study in the area of reliable learning. We've conducted an in-depth comparison of various methods for estimating star formation rates (SFR) in galaxies. By utilizing a large sample of 272 galaxies with consistent observations and extensive multi-wavelength data, we've compared different methods for their accuracy. We've found that SFR derived from fitting spectral energy distributions (SED) using templates or empirical models experiences significant discrepancies, ranging from 0.25 to 2.5 M$_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$. Generally, these discrepancies increase as the star formation rate decreases, below approximately 1.5 M$_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$. In contrast, other methods such as those relying on the far-UV continuum and recombination lines yield more consistent results. We've identified a few underlying issues contributing to these discrepancies: (i) the uncertainty in estimating dust extinction, (ii) the insensitivity of SED fitting to high-redshift star formation rates, and (iii) the lack of reliable star formation rate calibrations for SED-fitting models. Consequently, we suggest relying on alternative methods such as those using the far-UV continuum or recombination lines to derive star formation rates in galaxies with low SFR or uncertain dust extinction. Additionally, we've outlined several future directions for improving the reliability of SFR derived from fitting spectral energy distribution. By leveraging diverse observed datasets and restricting model assumptions to a minimal necessary set, future improvements can be made. We propose a future research trajectory that begins with empirical model selection, followed by a thorough statistical calibration of star formation rates and lastly, a detailed comparison with other methods. Such an approach is likely to yield a reliable and robust estimation of the star formation rate. Moreover, we suggest bracketing the uncertainty associated with this estimation by considering various model and observational assumptions. In particular, we point out the advantage of utilizing recombination lines, specifically the br$\gamma$ line, as a benchmark to assess the consistency of SFR derived from fitting spectral energy distribution. We observe a relatively small discrepancy of 0.6 M$_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$ between br$\gamma$-based SFR and other methods. We attribute this consistency to the suppression of star formation rate uncertainties related to dust extinction and the reliance on recombination lines that are less affected by the far-UV continuum. Consequently, we suggest the br$\gamma$ line as a valuable benchmark to assess the reliability of SFR derived from fitting spectral energy distribution. This is the initial paper in a study on a particular kind of quantum group module called type $II$ quantum subgroups. These subgroups originate from a broader structure known as a braided endomorphism semigroup, specifically a type $II$ braided subgroup. Our research focuses on the elements of this semigroup, which are represented through a higher-level mathematical construct called a fusion matrix. This paper delves into the underlying algebraic patterns within the semigroup by examining regional modules of a more fundamental quantum group and its associated representation, referred to as type $II$ global subgroups. We identify distinct structural elements within these modules and establish a general mathematical framework to characterize the braided module structure of a type $II$ quantum subgroup. This framework allows us to analyze and generalize a previously reported phenomenon in which the fusion matrix of a global subgroup $\mathcal{Q}_{(n)}$ consists of two distinct square blocks for $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_N)$ with $N\geq 3$. This result implies that the fusion matrix of a type $II$ quantum subgroup is comprised of square blocks if and only if its base subgroups have this property. We also explore abelian bases in the context of type $II$ global subgroups and derive conditions under which these bases exist. Moreover, we establish a connection between the central charge of a representation and its highest weight, which generalizes a previously reported finding in a specific context. This study further extends to the related charges of arbitrary regions in a more general setting. We also discuss the related concept of cross-capular charges and its implications. This research presents an innovative approach to synthesizing speech with varied lengths, resembling a prism that fractures regular speech into distinct, meaningful segments. Each new sentence is generated by a neural network, which is trained using a pruned version of the STSR dataset. The paper compares its results with two prominent speech synthesis lengths manipulation methods and demonstrates the superiority of its approach on both quantitative and qualitative measures. Additionally, the proposed method is mediated by a new metric called median length similarity (MLS), which predicts a new sentence's length with remarkable accuracy and reliability. Consequently, the neural network's performance is optimized by a sample-efficient method guided by MLS, resulting in substantial improvements. Listeners' subjective evaluations using the mean opinion score (MOS) also validate the breakthroughs achieved by this new method. Notably, it facilitates a wide range of length manipulation from 0.7 to 3.0 times the standard duration, whereas the compared methods are capable of extending sentences to at most 2.5 times the normal duration. With minimal pre- and post-processing requirements, the proposed method is both efficient and effective. Species distribution analysis can be a complex and multifaceted research field, 
encompassing individual species, groups of species, and combined analyses. 
To address this diversity, a comprehensive R package (spOccupancy) has been developed 
to offer a range of unity and versatility in estimating species occurrence and 
abundance across various studies. The package provides standard occupancy models 
for individual species, as well as collective analyses and a NoccaR model, 
all of which accommodate spatial non-stationarity. Furthermore, it includes a 
function to merge occupancy model estimates of species distributions, 
accommodating non-stationary spatial relationships. The package's functionality 
is demonstrated through a case study of bird habitat co-occupation.

Recent investigations of CrI$_3$ bilayers, comprising alternating layers of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic arrangements, have yielded substantial gains in understanding Rashba-type electron interactions within magnetic materials. Existing studies have primarily focused on the morphology of ultra-thin crystals, but a comprehensive theoretical analysis of their electronic properties is still required. We employ ab-initio calculations within the DFT framework to study the electronic properties of a CrI$_3$ bilayer with a centrosymmetric ferromagnetic arrangement. Our results reveal the presence of non-conventional Rashba effects in the electronic structure, alongside their contribution to spin-orbit coupling. Moreover, we observe the emergence of a spin hall effect, facilitated by an asymmetrical current direction resulting from the combination of structural properties and electron mass disparity between sub-layers. These findings are further substantiated by examining the magnetic Berry phase and its consequence on the magnetic spectrum. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the significance of symmetry in the Rashba effect and spin Hall effect and suggests that Rashba properties can be observed in a wider range of ferromagnetic materials, including those with centrosymmetric properties like CrI$_3$. We advise experimental researchers to verify these properties using scanning tunneling spectroscopy and transport measurements. Additionally, we propose that stacking polarization could be exploited to control the electrical current direction in 2D ferromagnetic materials, thereby opening doors for their incorporation in spin electronics. Lastly, our theoretical analysis may facilitate the discovery of other Rashba-effect-based materials with superior overall performance. \\

Developing reliable multithreaded software is increasingly crucial for industry and academia.  However, the complexity of multithreaded code, combined with its potential for logical errors and unintended behaviors, makes it a significant challenge to verify its correctness.  As a result, there is a growing need for automated model checkers that could efficiently identify potential issues in multithreaded programs.  In response to this requirement, our research introduces McMini, a novel model checker designed to verify the correctness of multithreaded programs written in C language by utilizing the DPOR (Distributed-POR) algorithm.  Leveraging a state-machine based approach, McMini successfully captures the precise behavior of multithreaded programs by accurately representing their control-flow and data-fold graphs.  Additionally, McMini's configuration-based framework allows developers to easily customize its algorithm for varying program characteristics using a small number of factors.  By combining a efficient thread-tracing and focus-on-failure technique with an optimal memory pool, McMini showcases its versatility and performance by successfully verifying a range of real-world programs from well-known libraries and passing a diverse set of multithreaded test cases with impressive results.  Notably, McMini has the capability to verify a substantial 96% of the tested multithreaded functions, including a remarkable 99.7% of those in the OpenRTPibrary.  Compared to other model checkers, McMini has been found to be remarkably faster, up to 2 orders of magnitude more efficient, particularly in verifying multithreaded programs with a complex nested structure.  Therefore, the research concludes that McMini is a reliable and efficient model checker that can effectively verify the correctness of multithreaded programs by using its unique combination of DPOR-based algorithm and McMini's configurable framework.  As a proof of concept, McMini has been found to be suitable for verifying multithreaded programs in various programming paradigms, such as multi-staged programming by identifying potential issues in a multi-threaded code sample. The global pandemic has underscored the critical role social media plays in disseminating information. As a result, there has been a surge in malicious misinformation spread via social media, which poses significant public health risks. Given the concentric nature of social media networks, where inner groups tend to share content more widely with one another, we observed a notable phenomenon in WhatsApp groups during the early stages of the pandemic in Brazil. This led us to develop a computational framework that quantifies the risk of malicious misinformation within WhatsApp groups before it spreads to outer groups. Based on this, we propose a straightforward strategy for WhatsApp to combat misinformation: close private groups to new members. Our analysis reveals that this approach can significantly reduce the likelihood of malicious misinformation spreading, thus protecting less informed group members from misinformation exposure. Furthermore, we discovered similar effects on public WhatsApp groups in Brazil and India, as well as comparable outcomes on other social media platforms such as Telegram. Ultimately, our findings position WhatsApp as a key player in combating misinformation within its platform, while also advocating for multi-faceted efforts against misinformation that take into account the complexities and limitations of social media networks. Researchers have pointed out significant flaws in network security monitoring systems used by professional services. These flaws can be exploited not just by advanced cyber attackers, but also by basic attackers who use pre-existing tools. What's more, attack methods targeting protocol detection in network monitoring systems are surprisingly easy to execute. In fact, almost anyone can use previously available tools to successfully carry out such attacks, regardless of their skill level. To illustrate the extent of this issue, this research presents three feasible methods for identifying dynamic protocol detection methods that can be used by open-source network monitoring tools. It also provides a real-world example of how one of these methods, which involves exploiting a known vulnerability in DNS resolution, can be utilized by Ntop to affect high-security organizations. To further emphasize the issue, this research presents three possible scenarios of low-skilled attacks that can be executed by various attackers, including former employees who have already gained access to an organization's network. These attacks, assisted by available tools, can successfully evade sophisticated detection methods, including deep packet inspection, anomaly and behavior analysis, and risk-based systems. Consequently, this research concludes by highlighting the insufficiency of relying solely on these sophisticated detection methods and recommends incorporating an additional method that is capable of detecting protocol changes, such as PYPAT, for a more secure network monitoring. It also informs readers about the current state of network monitoring systems, including major professional services and their alternatives, to aid in performing these detection methods. Finally, researchers provide some recommendations and guidelines to assist network administrators in securely configuring their network monitoring systems and enhancing their security defensiveness. Ultimately, this research presents a new security challenge, 'Protocol Attack Validation Experiment' (PAVE), to evaluate the effectiveness of network monitoring systems across various organizations. PAVE is comprised of three distinct attack methods that can be used by open-source network monitoring tools to affect high-security organizations, including a new self-developed tool, PYPAT. We propose an idea for creating a highly controlled interface between a ferromagnetic insulator and a superconductor. This proposal involves depositing a thin layer of a Satisferromagnetic compound, specifically PdDc, on a surface coated with a thin film of MoSi2. This specific combination features a well-matched lattice structure and possesses unique properties due to their proximity. Our theoretical models, utilizing a Hubbard model with Raman interaction, indicate that the interface between these materials exhibits long-range spin waves with exceptionally low energy, and that these energy levels can be significantly altered by applying an external voltage. Our study shows that a voltage of approximately 0.5V can create a barrier blocking these low-energy magnons, and that this magnon barrier can be toggled by changing the voltage to 0V. This system has the potential to be incorporated into qubit systems for an enhanced performance. Due to the versatility in materials, these properties can be observed in various other configurations as well. This research offers a new mechanism for controlling spin waves and has potential applications in the development of quantum devices and superconductor-based processors. Additionally, the employed method involves presenting model data through graphically engaging visualizations that facilitate intuitive understanding, and the associated analysis provides a framework for investigating the spin wave properties in Satisferromagnetic insulators. Our study opens the door for further research on the spin wave properties at the interface of superconductor and ferromagnetic insulators with inherent electric gating capabilities. Advances in distributed computing, such as Distributed Data Parallelism (DDP), have made training larger models more feasible, despite increased communication costs. However, DDP's success is hampered by challenges in training models with a high number of parameters and limited memory. While previous research has demonstrated the effectiveness of DDP on natural language processing and image recognition, it is unclear if it can successfully train complex audio classification models. The success of our DDP method has significant implications for training comprehensive sound classification systems. Creating high-dimensional entanglement is crucial for achieving high precision in quantum information processing. Despite advances in generating certain high-dimensional entangled states, evaluating their properties remains limited. Our proposal aims to identify key characteristics of high-dimensional entangled states, including the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, and develops a method for assessing their properties. By utilizing a high-dimensional quantum mechanical approach based on wave functions and probabilities, and combining it with the principle of uncertainty, a comprehensive framework is established for high-dimensional entangled state analysis. This framework is demonstrated by studying the GHZ state across three and four dimensional spaces. Our results show that four dimensional descriptions are sufficient for modeling the GHZ state, and the state remains stable against separable attacks. Furthermore, a specific entanglement measure, known as the linear entropy, is identified as a suitable indicator for quantifying high-dimensional entangled state properties. Our approach has potential applications in high-dimensional quantum communication and computation systems, promoting their secure development and implementation. This study analyzes how news coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic varies geographically and its influence on local communities, examining the relationship between media coverage, pandemic metrics, and community behavior. A content analysis of news articles from 426 U.S. metropolitan areas between April 2020 and February 2021 reveals significant variations in COVID-related coverage among regions. Interestingly, areas with more prominent news coverage initially experienced a decline in deaths but later saw increased fatalities. Additionally, regions receiving more pandemic-related coverage had higher COVID incidence rates but lower vaccination rates. Our findings also reveal that local populations, particularly older adults and those with a higher education level, were more likely to be exposed to pandemic news. Moreover, areas with more news coverage had a greater economic disparity and were predominantly represented by Democratic voters. These outcomes support the notion that the media plays a significant role in shaping public perception and behavior, highlighting the need to address the impact of misinformation on the pandemic and social divides. Our research offers a reference model for investigating the relationship between media coverage, social behavior, and public health. It also generates inquiries about the potential long-term effects of pandemic news on mental health and the potential link between media exposure and vaccination behavior. Furthermore, our study raises questions about the fairness of news distribution, particularly regarding communities that received less pandemic-related coverage and those with predominantly Republican voter populations. Lastly, our research poses a series of questions about the correlation between news exposure and social cohesion, the potential harm of misinformation to public health, and the media's role in promoting a unified response to the pandemic across diverse communities. We employ a dynamic neural network called the ELM to model the sequential processing of large numbers. The underlying theory suggests that working memory plays a crucial role in managing large numbers, and our findings support this notion. Additionally, we analyze the optimal architectural elements required for the counting network and examine the relative influence of working memory and attention within the sequence. Moreover, we provide evidence that a high degree of structural complexity, measured by network size, is necessary for accurately counting high numbers, and notably, we observe a significant increase in error rates when the network's capacity is exceeded. Lastly, we successfully apply our counting model to forecast the sequence of prime numbers. The success of our ELM-based approach positions it as a valuable tool for simulating higher-level executive functions involved in sequential processing. A new kind of filter, the xor filter, is introduced in this research. It outperforms existing solutions, specifically bloom and cuckoo filters, by requiring less memory, being easier to implement, and having a simpler design. A detailed analysis is conducted to compare the pros and cons of different algorithms when creating xor filters. Unlike bloom filters, which use hash functions, and cuckoo filters, which use direct indexing, xor filters capitalize on recent advancements in approximate membership testing. This study also examines the efficiency of a Bloom Filter-based alternative to xor filters, along with introducing various optimization techniques that enhance existing solutions, including incorporating multiple indexing in bloom filters. Ultimately, the results from 15 real-world datasets reveal that xor filters can surpass both bloom and cuckoo filters in several categories. Interestingly, the study finds that bloom filters can be a viable option when resources are scarce but become inferior as memory becomes more available. Conversely, cuckoo filters are generally the worst choice in every scenario. Thus, the main contribution of this research is the recommendation of xor filters, a simpler and more efficient alternative to both bloom and cuckoo filters. Additionally, the study introduces a new algorithm that combines the strengths of bloom and xor filters. This new algorithm, called bxor filters, can also outperform both bloom and xor filters by at least 30% in several cases. Furthermore, the study presents a portable and efficient implementation of xor filters, along with related algorithms, under the public Apache 2 license. It also proposes a new algorithm, called bxor filters, which can be downloaded at https://github.com/yangyangwang/bigset. Deepfake videos, crafted through various techniques including unconstrained media usage, can be menacing as they can deceive anyone. Despite the danger, research into unconstrained deepfake detection remains in its infancy, and creating such content is relatively straightforward. Our study breaks the barrier by introducing cutting-edge deepfake generation and detection methods that accommodate low-resolution and uncompressed media. A novel evaluation metric is proposed to assess unconstrained deepfake detection algorithms impartially. These methods are benchmarked using a comprehensive dataset comprised of various uncompressed and low-resolution video formats. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that deepfake detection performance is enhanced when full resolution is preserved, and our employment of uncompressed media in both creation and detection poses challenges for existing methods. Our creation of a detailed technical report supplements this research. Additionally, the source code employed in our study is freely available at https://github.com/Research-NII/UnconstrainedDeepfake.

The presence of a liquid envelope is a crucial component in the size-of-mainsequence object classification system, yet the number of discovered temperate sub-Neptunes with confirmed liquid envelopes is remarkably low. This research aims to increase the likelihood of finding these objects by comparing the distinguishable signs of solubility and thermal equilibria in the composition of transition metals within their atmospheres during a transit event. Through preliminary analysis, we find that a more soluble composition produces larger and broader overall transit signatures, specifically in the time it takes for the planet to pass through the top of the atmosphere and in the system's overall drop in brightness. As a result, a more extensive observation campaign focused on detecting larger and broader transit signatures could more effectively identify planets with liquid envelopes. Additionally, this study suggests that a more soluble composition is more effective at retaining an liquid envelope than thermal equilibrium, reducing the number of required follow-up observations. A practical application of these findings is evident in the ongoing or planned discovery efforts of other missions and programs such as the TESS, PLATO, and the James Webb Space Telescope. This research uses a simplified model based on evolved stars to illustrate how solubility maintains an liquid envelope over billions of years, precluding the escape of key elements such as Fe, Na, and K. This research also highlights the significance of observing transits at various wavelengths and identifies K2-18 b as a suitable target for testing the distinguished characteristics of soluble and thermal equilibria. Finally, this research proposes an original observational technique - the Transit Alkali Index - to identify soluble compositions using data from existing and future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope. This index analyzes the absorption features of sodium and potassium across a broad spectrum and provides a more accurate assessment of an composition's solubility than a single parameter. This research paves the way for the efficient detection of soluble compositions, enabling the identification of planets with liquid envelopes at an unprecedented scale. Using this method, we give evidence that a planet as small as Mars that orbits a G-star can have a composition that is soluble and maintain a liquid envelope. Finally, this research outlines the scope and potential of a future ground-based program focused on observing small transiting planets like Mars in different elements to better understand their atmospheres and the processes that retain an liquid envelope. Using a simple evaluation of the requirements for a successful ground-based program, we estimate that it would require around 100 8.2-m telescopes and 20 years to observe the needed number of solubility retention candidates.

Inspired by brain neuroscience, spiking neural networks have the potential to replace traditional deep neural networks, particularly for resource-constrained devices such as hardware-efficient AI computers. However, unlike deep neural networks, SNNs face significant challenges due to their limited update frequency and data availability, preventing them from learning complex models like convolutional neural networks efficiently. Our research introduces a pioneering approach for sequence-based SNN learning of binary classification models using temporal backpropagation through time. This method enables spiking neural networks to learn complex models with high accuracy similar to deep neural networks, while also being more biologically realistic than previous methods. Our results show that high data update rates and prolonged training times are necessary for successful spiking neural network training, revealing a significant discrepancy from deep neural network learning processes. Additionally, our findings indicate that the temporal backpropagation through time technique is only effective for models with short spatio-temporal memory and certain non-linear data distributions. Our research lays the foundation for further exploration into the learning capabilities of spiking neural networks and their applications on hardware-efficient AI computers. A significant aspect of our research remains to be the reduction of spike arrival gaps, followed by the exploration of other learning algorithms such as spike-rate-dependent learning and the incorporation of biological short-term synaptic plasticity. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, verifying the precision of these expansions poses a significant challenge because the original equations are inherently complex and involve uncertain factors. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a reliable method to confirm the accuracy of these expansions by comparing them with the original equations. In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach to validate the precision of these expansions by comparing them with the original equations. This approach utilizes the inherent properties of the original equations to confirm accuracy. In addition, we developed a universally applicable method to confirm accuracy that can be applied to a broad range of equations, including those governing fluid flow. Notably, this method does not rely on the underlying assumptions of the original equations and can be applied to both conservative and non-conservative equations. Furthermore, we utilized this approach to confirm the accuracy of several generalized polynomial chaos expansions, including GPC-LES and GPC-LES with stabilization. These results demonstrate that the framework of these methods can effectively analyze the precision of these models. In particular, we confirmed the precision of GPC-LES and GPC-LES with stabilization by comparing them with the continuous equations of the fluid flow. These results provide a theoretical foundation for the development of the methods and can be utilized to improve the accuracy of these models in the future. Additionally, we utilized the confirmed accuracy of these models to derive explicit models that can effectively analyze the precision of these models. Notably, these models were developed from the precise versions of the generalized polynomial chaos expansions. In particular, we developed the precise versions of the stochastic LANS-LES and the stochastic stabilized LANS-LES from the generalized polynomial chaos expansions of the LANS-LES and the stabilized LANS-LES. The increasing complexity of modern large-scale systems has given rise to a significant challenge: monitoring millions of data streams in real-time to identify sudden changes and isolate anomalies in high-dimensional data sets. Our approach tackles this obstacle by developing an advanced algorithm that learns automatically from example sub-systems to recognize shifts in real-time, thus facilitating timely anomaly detection and mitigation. Building on a novel adaptive change detection algorithm, we integrate it with a data analysis method to extract meaningful patterns from unlabelled data sets, thereby enabling high-performance detection and isolation of anomalies in high-dimensional data streams. Comprehensive experimental studies conducted on multiple data sets reveal that our approach surpasses established alternatives by delivering superior detection and isolation performance along with significantly lower computational complexity, thus paving the way for real-world applications. For example, our methodology has potential to monitor massive networks, such as those employed in large industrial settings, for enabling real-time anomaly detection and avoidance. Additionally, it can be utilized for monitoring massive biomedical data sets for early disease detection and intervention purposes. Our work provides a premier solution for performing real-time anomaly detection and isolation in high-dimensional data streams. Additionally, it provides a pioneering approach for designing real-time biometric anomaly detection systems with high accuracy and high-dimensional data streams. Finally, it offers a novel algorithm for identifying and isolating massive dimensional data sets in real-time. 

Keywords: Adaptive Anomaly Detection, Partially-Observed, High-dimensional Data Streams, Industrial Monitoring, Biomedical Applications, Computational Complexity, Real-time Algorithms.

We've obtained high-resolution spectra of eight relatively faint spiral galaxies, which allowed us to determine the abundance of nine key elements in each galaxy. Our analysis also shed light on the behavior of gas movement within these galaxies and their star formation history across different regions. Our findings indicate a wide variety of elemental abundance patterns among these galaxies, which cannot be explained by a single universal recipe. However, our data show that the abundance of elements in these galaxies can be accurately predicted using an advanced model that incorporates star formation and metal enrichment over time. Our analysis further reveals systematic differences in elemental abundance between the spiral galaxies we observed and those in the Local Group, which are primarily driven by the galaxies' mass. Our spectra also revealed kinks in the abundance of elements over time, which are thought to be the result of gas inflow brought about by cosmic ray winds. Our study indicates a time frame of around 1-300 million years for these elemental abundance transformations. Additionally, our data indicate a relatively stable and low-level star formation rate in these galaxies, which is consistent with the predictions of simulation-based models that describe spiral galaxy development. Our observations suggest a high efficiency in the conversion of star light to heat in these galaxies, which is significantly higher than that of the Milky Way. Our data also indicate a steady inflow of gas from the surrounding environment in these galaxies, which is estimated to be around 0.01 solar mass per year per parsec. Our analysis further shows a balance between star formation and gas inflow/outflow in these galaxies, which is likely to be the main driver of galaxy development and evolution. Our model indicates a steady flow of gas in these galaxies, which is estimated to be around 0.01 solar mass per year per parsec. Manually labeling documents for extraction tasks can be costly and time-consuming. However, a significant amount of publicly available document data remains unlabeled, making it suitable for semi-supervised learning. This technique can reduce the need for expensive manual labeling, but it is often challenging to adapt to domain-specific tasks due to differences in layout, visual appearance, and content. To overcome this, we developed CERBERUS, a universal approach for performing semi-supervised learning on visually complex documents. It combines an unsupervised data enrichment process with a domain-specific task adapter to enhance unlabeled data and a domain-specific fine-tuning module to leverage both labeled and enriched data. We demonstrated the effectiveness of CERBERUS in the medical and financial sectors, achieving impressive improvements over fully supervised models and 6-12% improvements over traditional supervised models. Most importantly, we showed that, in the financial domain, a combination of unlabeled data and our approach enables us to match the accuracy of fully supervised models that have spent three times more resources. Code is available at https://github.com/aubomobiel/CERBERUS. Research datasets can be downloaded from https://mobiels.architecture.kth.se/ResearchDatasets. The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to reduce the magnetic field required to induce a quantum spin Hall phase in InAs. Researchers used a multi-forked cluster beam method to create crystalline EuS for the first time, and analyzed the electronic properties at the EuS/InAs interface using photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory. By varying the chemical composition of the EuS and InAs targets, different interfaces were created and their properties examined. Ultimately, the findings revealed that the properties at the interface can be intentionally manipulated to meet specific requirements. Additionally, a wide range of Eu chalcogenides were synthesized, and the study laid the groundwork for a novel European sulfur compound. Lastly, the study explored the electronic properties at an interface made from a sample of InAs and EuSe. In this experiment, a 2 nm EuSe layer was grown on an InAs(100) substrate using a molecular beam epitaxy technique and then studied with photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory. The results showed that the properties at the interface can be reduced by selecting the correct material properties. Lastly, the study compared its findings to previous studies and found that the properties at the interface can have a significant impact on the magnetic properties. Furthermore, the study laid the groundwork for further studies on the magnetic properties. Based on these findings, the study suggested that a S/InAs interface could be an effective way to reduce the magnetic field required to induce a quantum spin Hall phase in InAs. The study used density functional theory to create a list of potential materials that could be used at the interface. The list included materials like CrS, FeSe, MnS, and MnSe, which had magnetic properties similar to EuS. The study used a screening factor to determine how well each material would reduce the magnetic field required to induce a quantum spin Hall phase in InAs. Ultimately, the study found that CrS had the highest screening factor and was the best candidate to reduce the magnetic field required to induce a quantum spin Hall phase in InAs. The study used density functional theory to determine how CrS would interact with InAs and found that it would reduce the magnetic field required to induce a quantum spin Hall phase in InAs by more than 90%. The study found that using CrS at the interface would allow a larger range of InAs than previously possible to exhibit a quantum spin Hall phase. The study determined that InAs films with thicknesses greater than 10 nm could exhibit a quantum spin Hall phase

A efficient hierarchical classification of Borel Wadge classes is established in this study. The study begins with an enhanced description of the Borel Wadge universe $\mathcal{W}$ and its associated ordering $\leq^{\mathcal{W}}$, leading to a demonstration of the first part of Borel Wadge theorem. A new, efficient decomposition of Borel Wadge classes is achieved by defining an enumeration of distinct Borel Wadge sets and establishing a one-to-one correspondence between this universe and a tree-like structure known as the Wadge tree. This result is then utilized to introduce a time-efficient decision-making procedure for Borel Wadge classes, addressing a previously unresolved query from the 1998 EAT/CS problem session. Furthermore, a symbolic representation of open sets in $\mathcal{W}$ is presented in the form of collections of finite binary trees. This leads to a proof that each Borel Wadge class contains $2^{2^x}$ members, where $x$ is a natural number. Additionally, under the current axiomatic systems, it remains unknown whether a specific recursive open set in $\mathcal{W}$ has a Borel Wadge code of length $2^x$ or $(2.x)^x$. A concept similar to the inherent complexity of Nash equilibria is introduced through the coinfection game and the $k$-cofinfection tree on finite graphs. It is demonstrated that each Borel Wadge class on infinite trees contains an uncountable collection of distinct open sets defined by propositional logic utilizing $2^x$ variables, known as $k$-cofinfection open sets. This is accompanied by an efficient algorithm for determining whether a given Borel Wadge class is comprised of either closed or $k$-cofinfection open sets. The study concludes with an evaluation of its findings and suggestions for further research.  The associated code for this study can be found at the public GitHub repository https://github.com/agtugay/Borel-Wadge-code under the label agtugay. The associated tree data structure can be found at the public GitHub repository https://github.com/agtugay/Wadge-tree under the label agtugay. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being employed by researchers, but such models necessitate a heightened presence of data for training. Nonetheless, the majority of existing pruning techniques focus solely on testing, disregarding the need for inference speed during the training process. This proposal introduces ClickTrain, a innovative and comprehensive approach that integrates training and pruning into a unified framework. ClickTrain analyzes the impact of weight pruning on non-linear activations during training, utilizing a novel full-path analysis technique. The framework further incorporates a content-addressable memory mechanism for precise and efficient pruning of multi-layer models, allowing for the accurate removal of unnecessary weights during training. The results indicate that ClickTrain can concurrently enhance the precision and efficiency of model inference and testing, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. We present a sound and complete proof system for this extended calculus, validating its properties. We also examine substructural properties within our calculus, specifically focusing on its preservation and fusion properties. Our investigation is motivated by the incorporation of these modal operators into the base calculus with contraction as found in Cutting's work on bicategories. Our analysis shows that the existing methods for controlling access to contracted expressions can be seamlessly integrated with the modal operators, yielding a coherent and meaningful framework within our calculus. As a testament to its soundness, this extended calculus serves as the base calculus for a certain type of bicategories known as cohesive unitary biproductively extensive bicategories with morphisms. We also illustrate this calculus in action using a sample expression involving both modal and currying operators. Our research concludes with an examination of higher inductive types in such bicategories and the specific role that the modal operators play in their development. The 2015 August Detection of GW150914 marked the historic first detection of gravitational waves from a binary black hole merger by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration. Following this discovery, future detections from compact binary coalescences, particularly those involving neutron stars, have become a priority. Advances in deep learning have made it feasible to automatically analyze the detection and identification of these events, eliminating the need for manual examination. Researchers have recently leveraged this technology to improve the identification and classification of mergers involving neutron stars. Despite the progress made, many open questions remain regarding the physics of these events, particularly those involving neutron star--black hole mergers, which offer a unique opportunity to study dense matter using the binary's gravitational-wave spectrum. This presents a significant challenge that, to date, has not been fully addressed by the community. To move forward, it is crucial that the signal processing community and astrophysicists collaborate to develop innovative deep learning methods that can efficiently utilize computational resources to unlock the vast potential of these events' analysis. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the research completed to date and presents four novel deep learning models that utilize graphics processing units for the identification and classification of neutron star--black hole mergers, achieving superior results in the LIGO--Virgo dataset. Additionally, we examine the effects of varied training data on these models, highlighting the significance of enhancing real-world detection capabilities through the advancement of realistic synthetic simulations. Furthermore, we introduce two novel frameworks for the analysis of neutron star--black hole mergers, one of which focuses on event classification and another that identifies multiple similar events. Moreover, we develop methods to estimate various parameters, such as event sky location, orientation, and key binary characteristics, including mass and spin. Finally, we apply one of our models to the analysis of neutron star--neutron star mergers and other events of unknown origin, yielding promising results and pointing out areas for further study. The presented work is the first to integrate deep learning with numerical relativity to study neutron star--black hole mergers, enabling the prediction of various events' properties with high accuracy. The employed models, along with associated code, have been made publicly available on GitHub. Future advancements in this research are expected to be facilitated through an open source collaboration initiative, starting with a future update to the code. The project's website is currently available at: https://dses-group.org/DSES-II/. This research is part of a larger effort by the UMASS-DSEs group in the field

The method also applies to restricted Markov decision processes, where transitions are restricted by given patterns. By exploring the relationship between Markov decision processes and linear programming, we adapt structural constraints from the latter to the former, resulting in an efficient computational solution. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through numerical examples. Furthermore, our research, originally presented in French, has been translated into English for broader accessibility. This text deviates from the original, providing an alternate introduction to the topic. The primary focus of the study is to analyze Markov decision processes with specific constraints on transitioning between states, where we develop an algorithm using the primal-dual method by incorporating the Lagrangian of these constraints into the Markov decision process's (MDP) Bellman-Isaacs equation. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate that these dual variables correlate with metrics of policy stability and the geometric relationship between states, where our algorithm's optimality is confirmed when these dual variables become infinite, indicating the impossibility of finding a feasible policy. This research outlines a method for analyzing handwritten mathematical equations using an offline approach and confirms its effectiveness via a dataset of actual exam papers. The proposed system architecture is detailed and evaluated using a dataset of 29,417 mathematical equations. Performance enhancements were achieved by incorporating the application of Total Variation regularization, a convolutional neural network structure, and a convolutional layer with an asymmetric kernel size in the analysis process. We examine various aspects of supersymmetric quantum mechanics and relate them to a general formula governing a sheaf cohomology computed on a particular category of modular forms. Firstly, we derive expressions for bosonic and fermionic influences in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. These displays serve as analogues to Riemann-Roch formulae. We then establish connections between supersymmetric quantum mechanics and the Götay-Leray direct image sheaf cohomology. Finally, as a testament to the utility of our theoretical framework, we employ it to calculate the cohomology sheaf for a specific example involving the quantum mechanics of a harmonic oscillator. We expect our framework to be universally applicable to any supersymmetric quantum mechanics. Consequently, we hope that our approach will provide a valuable tool for solving intricate mathematical problems in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. Additionally, we envision that our framework will serve as a supersymmetric counterpart to recent discoveries in modular forms. It is our hypothesis that modular invariance may be reinterpreted as the vanishing of a particular sheaf cohomology group, possibly with additional novel implications. We plan to explore this hypothesis in greater detail within a future study. We believe that our theoretical framework may also be generalized to include both bosonic and fermionic influences in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. We anticipate that our approach will be a supersymmetric extension of a previously established category of modular forms. Furthermore, we expect that modular invariance may be reinterpreted as the vanishing of a particular sheaf cohomology group across both bosonic and fermionic influences in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. We plan to investigate this supposition in greater detail within a future publication. The goal of the Nine-Month Situation Test (N MST) is to assess language proficiency on a real-time basis over an extended period of time. In this study, we submitted entries for N MST tasks involving Aggressive Speech and Offensive Language as target categories. The primary reason for participating in this challenge was to verify whether models trained on recent language datasets, such as N MST data, could also excel in more complex tasks. In particular, we were interested in examining the effectiveness of BERT and SVM combinations in detecting aggressive or offensive content. The entries submitted to SemEval 2019 N MST contained two components: one used BERT alone as a feature extractor while another used BERT in conjunction with SVM for classification. The results showed that BERT alone performed more efficiently than combinations of BERT with SVM. Additionally, we observed that BERT performed better than SVM alone in nearly all N MST tasks. Notably, our BERT-based entry achieved a 0.936 Micro F1 score in the Aggressive Speech task and a 0.814 Macro F1 score in the Offensive Language task. We did not, however, perform any optimizations for the Multimodal N MST task as our main focus was on text-based data. In various topological quantum systems, certain key concepts such as topological entanglement entropy, entanglement spectrum, and correlation functions are used to study the properties of the systems and their underlying fermionic modes.  Although these concepts are widely applied, there is a lack of clear and concise explanation of how they interrelate.  This paper investigates the application of these concepts within the context of the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, which is both straightforward to understand and yet sufficiently complex.  Through both analytical and numerical calculations, we demonstrate the equivalence of different approaches to measuring topological properties and also examine the connections between various concepts.  Ultimately, our study reveals that while these concepts are valuable for identifying topological properties, they are not universally applicable to all systems as their meanings can be highly context-dependent.  

In the specific case of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, we find that various properties such as topological entanglement entropy, anyonization, and correlation functions are effectively equivalent in distinguishing non-topological and topological systems, whereas the entanglement spectrum and correlation functions provide a more detailed understanding of the system and its underlying fermions.  However, we acknowledge that certain correlation functions may not always yield conclusive results in determining the topological properties of certain systems.  Lastly, we extend our study to the multi-mode system and investigate the legitimacy of reducing the entanglement entropy to the topological entanglement entropy by focusing solely on the lowest modes.  Through our analysis, we find that this approximation holds for the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model but not in general.  Thus, this study serves as a guide on how to accurately determine the topological properties of a system by interpreting various concepts correctly. Additionally, the code used for calculating the entanglement spectrum and correlation functions has been listed on the link: https://github.com/ArpitDass/Entanglement-spectrum-and-correlation-functions-in-SSH-code.

We have developed a new dual loop version of four-dimensional supergravity using the AdS5×S5 background. This model is created by combining a five-dimensional supergravity with a five-dimensional N=8 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, where we apply a standard holographic transformation to obtain the dual supergravity. As in standard four-dimensional supergravity, our model features dual solutions with the same field content. It also includes W gravity, a self-dual gravity sector, and an anti-self-dual gravity sector. Furthermore, we have established a one-to-one correspondence between solutions in the supergravity model and those in the dual four-dimensional supergravity. This was achieved through a new dual loop version of the holographic dictionary. Specifically, we have demonstrated that a solution of the supergravity model corresponds to a solution of the dual four-dimensional supergravity when the source coefficients are large. This provides a new way to study four-dimensional supergravity using the AdS5×S5 background. It has the advantage of being free of ultraviolet divergences and requiring less computational effort than in the dual four-dimensional supergravity model. Additionally, we have found that the supergravity model contains a one-parameter family of solutions with gauge theory duals that have finite source coefficients. This is reminiscent of the non-renormalizability of four-dimensional supergravity when its couplings are large. However, we have also found that our model is compatible with the supersymmetric solution constraint, which may initially suggest a resolution to this issue through supersymmetry. However, a more detailed analysis reveals that the supersymmetric solution itself has non-zero Ricci scalar. This indicates that the supersymmetric solution itself is not a valid field theory limit. Instead, we propose that the supersymmetric solution represents a quantum state that can be reached through a unitary transformation from a state with non-zero Ricci scalar. This is analogous to the behavior of four-dimensional supergravity when its couplings are large. There, the non-zero Ricci scalar is eliminated through a unitary transformation, revealing a four-dimensional supergravity with finite coupling that is dual to the AdS5×S5 background. Similarly, in our model, the non-renormalizability of four-dimensional supergravity with large couplings is replaced by a quantum state with non-renormalizable four-dimensional supergravity as its dual. This is a significant finding because it indicates that four-dimensional supergravity with large couplings is renormalon-free. Our model also raises questions about the completion of four-dimensional supergravity with large couplings

High-performance computing on General Purpose Graphics Processing Units (GPGPUs) requires memory allocation patterns that are typically not supported by the device's memory architecture, necessitating the development of customized memory allocators to facilitate efficient code development. Although various memory allocators have been proposed for GPGPUs, significant opportunities remain for improvement, particularly through adaptive allocators that concurrently manage memory on multiple memory pools. Through a systematic design, we present DynaSOAr, a highly scalable memory allocator for GPGPUs that dynamically adjusts to memory fragmentation and simultaneously allocates memory from multiple pools to optimize memory access, ultimately leading to a substantial performance boost of up to 37.7% compared to the current best available allocators. Additionally, DynaSOAr consistently outperforms the standard CUDA memory allocator by a significant margin of up to 19.8%. A detailed analysis of DynaSOAr's performance, along with a comprehensive benchmark suite, is also provided to ensure seamless object-oriented programming development on GPGPUs using an intuitive memory management system. This research benefits users of the SOAR memory allocator, allowing them to leverage DynaSOAr's enhanced features and achieve superior performance. SOAr users can adapt DynaSOAr to their memory allocator, or treat it as a highly optimized benchmark that includes a vast collection of CUDA-based object-oriented applications and a tool for automatically converting high-level languages to CUDA code. As a result, DynaSOAr serves as a superior alternative to current memory allocators, offering improved memory management, enhanced scalability, and superior performance across a wide range of real-world benchmarks. This research has two primary goals: Firstly, we aim to enhance the performance of current memory allocators through a novel, adaptive approach. Secondly, we strive to contribute to the development of efficient object-oriented programming on GPGPUs by introducing a highly optimized memory allocator, alongside a comprehensive benchmark suite and a tool for automatic CUDA code conversion. Developing accurate models for high-fluence X-ray absorption edge spectra requires a detailed understanding of electron dynamics.  By incorporating non-linear rate equations that balance creation and annihilation processes, our model offers a comprehensive explanation for resonance enhancement phenomena observed in transition metal systems.  The proposed rate equation approach provides a versatile framework capable of simulating a wide range of non-linear XAS effects, including those influenced by multiple excitations, changes in molecular geometry, and electronic correlations.  Furthermore, our model acknowledges the significance of fluence in modifying the electronic environment and demonstrates the necessity of considering relaxation processes lasting tens of seconds to fully describe the electronic behavior of transition metals under intense X-ray irradiation.  By incorporating ultrafast electronic correlations, our model successfully predicts key features of high-fluence spectra, including the appearance of negative resonance enhancement and the modification of spectral intensity around the resonance peak.  By excluding any assumptions not directly related to the fluence, our model's results can be easily transferred to other materials and experimental conditions.  Therefore, our fluence-rate model serves as a standard method for the interpretation of high-fluence XAS data and facilitates the reconstruction of electronic populations over an extended period of time.
