A virtual euclidean spanner of order O(t) and stretch α in D-dimensional Euclidean space is a data structure that enables querying for the distance between two points, say q, and providing a list of at most t points such that the ratio of the queried point's distance to the supplied point's distance remains less than α. Our research focuses on reducing the query time and space efficiency for O(t)-point spanners with α ≈ 1+ε (where ε > 0). Significantly, we achieve nearly optimal O(t) + t^eps properties for ε > 0, improving the known results where ε = 0. Furthermore, we introduce the first constant-stretch O(t)-point spanners with linear query time and space, proving a trade-off bound between query performance and data structure size. Additionally, we present a new application of spanners to retrieve approximate nearest neighbors among a set of pointers with a large spread, such as a vast collection of geographically dispersed internet hosts. Finally, we investigate the feasibility of designing and programming spanners as a solution to mitigate the effects of supernovae on computer systems by using the distance between file access patterns and spreading the load across multiple disks. The approach remains theoretical due to a lack of empirical evidence on file access patterns and disk utilization. Interestingly, the resulting design possesses an interesting property where nearby files tend to be placed closer together. Lastly, we propose the concept of 'virtual spanners' – embeddings of Euclidean space (as a geometric structure) into a metric space with the property that maintaining a (t, α)-spanner in the original space also forms a (t, α)-spanner in the embedded space. The metric space itself serves as an efficient spanner, providing a possible solution to designing and programming this structure. Additionally, the technique allows for the development of novel algorithms to approximate nearest neighbor searches and other queries in the original space by leveraging the efficiency of the metric space. Finally, we provide a framework called'spanner-based filtering' for reducing the complexity of point set distance computation by utilizing the efficiency of the metric space to discard unlikely neighbor candidates based on their proximity in the embedded space. The approach remains theoretical due to a lack of empirical evidence on the spread of geometric point sets and file access patterns. Moreover, the resulting design possesses an interesting property where nearby files tend to be placed closer together. A vast number of IoT devices are being deployed every day, generating a flood of data that is frequently utilized for identifying the devices involved. This process is crucial for recognizing the devices connected to a network or the individuals to whom devices are assigned. Due to the vast amount of data and computational constraints, robust feature extraction methods are in high demand to support efficient IoT device identification. This study specifically focuses on using principal component analysis for feature extraction and investigates the impact of the number of principal components on accuracy and computational costs. Remarkably, it is observed that the method's efficiency can be forecasted with reasonable precision and that optimal performance often requires only a minimal number of principal components. Consequently, a novel, cost-aware approach to feature extraction is proposed, enabling the seamless transition between expensive and affordable computational environments and the efficient utilization of principal component analysis for feature extraction. Furthermore, the final model's functionality is also examined using a multi-layer perceptron neural network. Interesting observations were made about the interplay between computational costs and accuracy, which are not commonly known about principal component analysis. This knowledge can be utilized to create a more efficient feature extraction method by selecting the optimal number of principal components based on specific requirements and the available resources. Additionally, a decision support system is developed to determine the most suitable feature extraction method for a specific use case, enabling a more adaptable and efficient technique for identifying IoT devices. The code for this study is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/JUEMiller/IoT-Feature-Extractor. Utilizing Raspberry Pi 4 for data collection and feature extraction, the project provides a comprehensive feature extraction method that can be utilized by other researchers and developers. Due to space constraints, the complete dataset is not included with the code; however, it can be accessed upon request via a public link. This study is the first in a series, with a forthcoming publication expanding on the associated techniques and data, which were initially presented at LOUVEAC 2020. Our results demonstrate that previous experimental and computational studies on the free expansion process contain an inherent error, revealing a crucial aspect of phase space volume dynamics. We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the dynamical transition point (DTTP) in a three-state quantum walk model. The study reveals distinct scaling behavior in different directions from the DTTP. In one direction, we find global dynamical scaling similar to a known two-state quantum walk model. In another direction, we observe an additional pre-dynamical critical point and a scaling plateau before the actual dynamical transition point occurs. Our results indicate that pre-dynamical critical phenomena can be witnessed during the finite-time evolution of the three-state quantum walk model. Furthermore, we develop a scaling scheme incorporating both time and system size to analyze a generic quantum walk model exhibiting a dynamical transition. Our proposed scaling scheme successfully describes the complex dynamics near the DTTP in various quantum walk models. Additionally, we explore the many-body generalization of the three-state quantum walk model and identify a novel critical point characteristic of quantum criticality. In contrast to known scaling behaviors in quantum critical systems, we propose a different scaling scheme near the emergent dynamical transition point (EDTP) observed in the three-state quantum walk model. Our study provides an in-depth analysis of the scaling behavior near the EDTP and explores its implications for understanding the dynamics of closed quantum systems. Moreover, we leverage our developed scaling scheme to identify pre-dynamical critical phenomena in the many-body quantum walk model and the two-state quantum walk model under the influence of an imaginary imaginary imaginary unit. In this context, we explore the possibility of harnessing pre-dynamical critical phenomena for achieving faster speed and dynamic range in quantum information processing tasks. Lastly, we investigate the connection between scaling behavior near the EDTP and the critical behavior near the thermal critical point in three-state quantum walk model with imaginary imaginary unit and its many-body generalization. Our study reveals an intriguing correlation between scaling behavior near the EDTP and the thermal critical point. Moreover, we propose a scaling scheme near the thermal critical point and the EDTP, and our analysis sheds new insights into the pre-dynamical critical phenomena in closed quantum systems. Although vision transformers have surpassed convolutional networks in image recognition capabilities, they have yet to surpass them in feature extraction capabilities. A major reason for this is the absence of invariant properties in vision transformers, which are crucial for developing rich and semi-holistic features. In this paper, we introduce a novel architecture called Property Guided Vision Transformer (PG-VT) that uniquely combines the insertion of invariable properties into vision transformer computations with learning these properties alongside the patch embeddings. The insertion of these properties serves as explicit short-range connections, while their learning acts as implicit long-range connections. In contrast to prior multi-scale representations, our properties are capable of encapsulating full image information while still effectively capturing short-range connections. The computational efficiency of our proposed method is supported by theoretical analysis and is validated through superior performance on various tasks without the need for additional network complexity. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenLi8129/PG-ViT. Experimental results demonstrate our proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet, COCO, and Pascal VOC for multiple task types, often with a reduced number of parameters. The inserted properties can be interpreted as high-level semantic properties that are comparable to layer features. Additionally, the parameter-efficient design facilitates the development of dense feature maps. The insertion of invariable properties into vision transformer computations has heretofore been overlooked, yet our proposed method proves they to be pivotal components. Furthermore, the inserted properties can be learned from raw images without manual labelling, which is a valuable property in itself. The findings of our study may be applied to other areas such as computer vision, where the concept of invariable properties could be readily integrated. This project focuses on developing a mark elimination method, an essential concept in reversible concealment, utilizing Bayesian neural networks (BNNs). In concealment studies, an object's presence is allowed, and then its mark is eliminated without affecting its detection status. Most existing methods are non-reversible and fail to meet this requirement. Our novel approach leverages BNNs to analyze the mark elimination process from multiple perspectives. Firstly, we employ a predictive network to assess the reliability of eliminated marks. Secondly, we use a generation network within an optimization framework to create marks that can reverse the elimination process. Finally, we analyze the network's internal state to gain insights into its prediction or generation capabilities. Our BNNs-based method achieves state-of-the-art performance in object detection and mark preservation, and successfully enables the reversal of mark elimination. In this research, we investigate a specific aspect of the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis by focusing on a specific situation where four parties engage in a joint measurement of a shared outcome with maximal dimensionality. Importantly, our findings indicate that this local hidden state model remains constrained by a specific upper bound for the associated entropy, a relationship tied to the PPT set through the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis. In simpler terms, a two-dimensional set-valued mapping can be represented as a sum of one-dimensional projections onto its image. However, this approach poses challenges for mappings with low codimension (such as single-valued maps from a two-dimensional space to a three-dimensional space) as they cannot be represented by one-dimensional projections onto their images.

A flow box can be thought of as a three-dimensional flow on a five-dimensional manifold that is constrained in a specific way. It allows for the representation of a two-dimensional set-valued mapping as a flow box that is Lipschitz with respect to its domain. However, this technique is only feasible when the domain of the mapping can be embedded in a five-dimensional space.

Even with vast amounts of data, some NLP models struggle with certain languages. The issue isn't just a lack of data, but also the quality, as some languages have irrelevant or confusing terminology. A novel approach provides weak supervision by creating task representations that can be used across languages without direct labeling. Instead, task representations guide a model to focus on relevant features, and the model learns to associate them with correct outcomes on a task-specific basis. This approach allows for seamless cross-lingual transfer, demonstrated on a range of tasks including multi-labeled document categorization and single-labeled sentence classification. Compared to strong supervision, task representations yield comparable results, but with reduced data requirements and complexity. Ultimately, this method facilitates independent cross-lingual knowledge transfer and reduces the complexity and data needs in multilingual NLP. A comprehensive evaluation shows that high-performance models can be created with minimal adjustments for languages with scarce resources, but also improves performance in languages with abundant data, revealing potential for optimization. The proposed task representations offer a unified framework for weak supervision and cross-lingual transfer, paving the way for generalizable NLP models across many languages. A new, model-independent toolkit named \mernis provides access to task representations through a user-friendly interface, featuring a task browser, data modules, and example models. This toolkit enables NLP developers to create weak supervision modules for their favorite tasks and models, and efficiently compares their performance with strong supervision, as demonstrated in an online demo. A prominent Video Super-Resolution (VSR) method, Video Enhancement Network (VEN), has limitations such as inaccurate future frame prediction and alignment. To overcome these shortcomings, we have developed a new VSR network called BasicVSR++, which builds upon VEN's backbone network and makes concurrent use of two alternative propagation methods, BiPhasesp and Syphasesp. This unique combination leverages the strengths of the two methods while mitigating their weaknesses, resulting in more accurate future frame prediction and improved propagation. Additionally, we have introduced a simple yet effective frame alignment scheme called Average Alignment (AvA), which provides robust frame registration and outperforms VEN's phase alignment. By integrating the BiPhasesp+Syphasesp propagation duo with AvA alignment, our BasicVSR++ method achieves state-of-the-art performance and surpasses VEN in VSR tasks. The source code of BasicVSR++ can be found at https://github.com/HyUKim/BasicVSR++. Experimental evaluation has demonstrated the superiority of BasicVSR++ over VEN and several other prominent VSR methods on NTREND and VIDEOSR benchmarks in terms of accuracy and speed. Specifically, BasicVSR++ has attained a 0.38 ABSORRE in video super-resolution under 4 times intra-coded frames (VSR-4IC) and demonstrated faster processing times than VEN and other methods while producing similar or higher quality output videos. The study provides support for the findings by analyzing the effects of propagation methods and frame alignment schemes on VSR performance. Also, an alternative VSR network called VEN+ has been proposed which is nearly identical to VEN but lacks phase misalignment, and has served as a baseline for comparing the performance of BiPhasesp+Syphasesp and AvA alignment in VEN. Furthermore, the study validated the hypothesis that BiPhasesp+Syphasesp can function effectively in place of VEN's phase misalignment and proved the superiority of BasicVSR++ over VEN+ and several other prominent VSR methods in VSR tasks. The research provides a new framework called Time-Biased VSR (TBSVR) for evaluating the performance of VSR networks and demonstrated the superiority of BasicVSR++ over VEN+ and several other prominent VSR methods in the framework. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can be beneficial, allowing tasks to be solved more efficiently by exploiting learned patterns across tasks. However, when tasks are solved through trial-and-error using reinforcement learning, common representations can sometimes lead to destructive interference, where learning from one task hinders learning from another. We examined how to prevent such interference in a model-based multi-task setting, where each task involves navigating a different maze. A shared neural network model is trained to predict task rewards and trajectories throughout. Despite initial benefits, simultaneous training on all tasks consistently led to poor performance, as each task's model repeatedly destroyed the others. We investigated several methods for overcoming this interference and found that a simple approach of regularly "freezing" the shared model by resetting its weights was highly effective, allowing all tasks to be learned successfully. This method performed better than alternatives, including periodically synthesizing task representations by combining the best models from individual training sessions, and demonstrated robustness to a variety of challenging conditions. Additionally, the weighted model averaging technique was found to be effective but only after the shared model had fully recovered and performed well on all tasks. We believe these findings could be extended to other multi-task settings beyond our study. Importantly, our work highlights the potential dangers of destructive interference in multi-task training and suggests a straightforward solution to preventing it. Additionally, it reveals that model-based reinforcement learning can be highly susceptible to interference and as such, may not be an ideal choice for certain multi-task applications. On the other hand, it was found that learning to solve multiple tasks through trial-and-error using deep reinforcement learning can be resilient to interference. A key decision in multi-task reinforcement learning is the policy by which tasks are selected and processed, and a novel method was introduced which incorporates this 'policy' as a key component of the credit assignment problem. It was found that a maximally diverse policy, seeking to balance learning on all tasks, prevented destructive interference and yielded better results than simpler policies that prioritize speed or completion times. We provide theoretical justifications for these findings and offer a simple rule for creating such diverse policies that surpasses random selection. Moreover, a maximally diverse policy was found to be compatible with any choice of task frequencies and can be easily scaled to learn patterns across an unlimited number of tasks. We demonstrate the superiority of our findings over the prior state-of-the-art multi-task reinforcement learning results through a series of rigorous experimental evaluations. It was found that learning to solve multiple tasks through trial-and-error using deep reinforcement learning can be resilient to interference and yield better results

Recent studies have leveraged quantum optimal control to enhance the performance of heat engines. However, this approach often necessitates extensive numerical simulations. In contrast, our analysis provides a simplified framework for these systems. We consider a quantum system coupled with heat baths at distinct temperatures, capable of performing work within a limited spatial area. Our approach introduces new, continuous variables that describe the system's state, leading to a simplified picture of its evolution. Specifically, we examine a two-level system, demonstrating that its optimal work output corresponds to a truncated geometric series, whereas restricted control leads to damped exponential motion. Our framework also enables the derivation of analytical expressions for work distributions and heat flows. Moreover, we identify the maximum efficiency of these quantum systems within a limited spatial area and its relationship with fundamental boundaries. Our findings indicate that restricting control in either time or space results in a reduced maximum efficiency compared to unrestricted cases, as predicted by a renowned result due to Scoville and Schr\"odinger-Fermi. Furthermore, we verify that our simplified picture maintains a high level of accuracy with regard to work output and system-state characteristics. Our analysis provides a new level of understanding of these quantum systems and offers an effective method for applying quantum optimal control without relying on numerical simulations. We anticipate that our framework will be beneficial in analyzing and optimizing a wide array of quantum systems. Additionally, we have verified its applicability to diverse scenarios such as coherent population transfer and also to a system exhibiting spontaneous emission. Our work is expected to be a valuable addition to the field of quantum thermodynamics. It is possible that future research will build upon our results and extend them to other areas of this field. To facilitate this, we have made our code available for public use. In the future, it would be desirable to explore the applicability of our approach to more complex systems such as those involving multiple levels or interactions with bounded environments. It is also an area for potential future research to analyze the applicability of our approach to the optimal control of systems undergoing rapid changes in their state. In such scenarios, it is likely that restricted control would lead to significant decreases in work output relative to unrestricted cases. Our simplified framework is expected to provide valuable insights in these complex scenarios. Extreme weather events like hurricanes and storm surges have a severe impact on the energy infrastructure in the Gulf Coast of the US, resulting in considerable damage to power lines, towers, and distribution equipment. To effectively mitigate the effects of such storms, it is crucial to identify areas of high energy infrastructure density that are most vulnerable to storm surges. This research aims to analyze the spatial and temporal influence of hurricanes and storm surges on the energy infrastructure in the Gulf Coast, enabling informed decision-making for infrastructure planning and emergency preparedness. By combining hurricane forecast data with storm surge heights and energy infrastructure location details, we created a predictive model to assess the probability of infrastructure damage based on storm surge intensity and the distance from the coast. The results allow utility companies and emergency managers to prioritize repair efforts, allocate resources, and ensure public safety and communication strategies before and after a storm. The findings indicate a significant correlation between storm surge height and infrastructure damage, with relative probabilities of failure increasing by 10% for every 1 meter surge height increase. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that locations with a surge height of 6 meters or more experience near-total power outages, whereas sites with lower surge heights face partial outages or no outages at all. The utility of this framework was demonstrated in the 2021 hurricane season, with regular storm updates and notifications, and we anticipate continued success in supporting decision-making for both utility and emergency management operations. The full process involved in generating these results is an approachable method for assessing energy infrastructure vulnerability to storm surges, and the associated code can be accessed on a public repository for validation and extension with other regions and infrastructure types. Future developments will encompass more detailed energy infrastructure models and additional storm conditions, such as fire behavior and wind impacts. Ultimately, this research seeks to apply its techniques to various infrastructure types and storm-related effects beyond just power outages. By leveraging geospatial analysis and statistical modeling, we strive to provide actionable insights for energy and emergency management officials, utility companies, and the broader public. The integration of our storm surge assessment framework and the ISSF tool hold immense potential for infrastructure planning, emergency management and preparedness, and decision-making processes across various sectors. The issuance of hurricane forecasts by national and local weather services can be complemented with our detailed storm surge analysis to aid decision-making for emergency responders, utility companies, and the general public. The incorporation of our research findings into risk assessments and decision-support tools can ultimately translate to cost savings and lives saved. The entropy approach is a widely utilized tool in the analysis of 2D piecewise 1-dimensional maps. Its success in many instances has led to a broader exploration of its applicability to other scenarios. However, this paper demonstrates that two maps from the Heterochaos baker family do not admit any approachable sequence of 2-tuple natural invariant measures, which are essential for the entropy approach. Consequently, we identify the natural invariant measures that are robustly occurring under arbitrary natural dynamics in the interior of the space of all 2-tuple natural invariant measures. Notably, these measures do not convey any information about the space's topology. Additionally, we show that the measures from the entropy approach are not uniquely maximal entropy measures. Lastly, we formalize the relationship between the natural measures and the entropy approach measures, which includes a new addition, and observe that this relationship is one-to-one for the entropy approach measures, as well as for the measures from another method called the additivity approach. Interestingly, the one-to-one relationship between the entropy approach measures and the additivity approach measures holds for a distinct set of 2-tuple natural invariant measures that include those associated with the entropy approach, as well as some other measures, whose natural codes exhibit a specific combinatorial structure. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm for identifying all approachable sequences of 2-tuple natural measures, and provide a method for computing the natural codes of the entropy approach measures. Additionally, we introduce an entropy rate evaluation test and provide an analysis of its outcomes for the entropy approach measures. The natural codes of the entropy approach measures are found to be those with weakly adding natural codes of a certain maximum length. The entropy approach measures are found to be robustly occurring under arbitrary natural dynamics in two other spaces as well. Lastly, we observe that one of the maps from the Heterochaos baker family is topologically equivalent to a combination of two 1D maps, including the Dyck system, for which we establish some new results including the topological entropy and the entropy capacity. Moreover, we show that the natural codes of the entropy approach measures are those with a specific combinatorial structure and that these codes exhibit a specific pattern of periodicity. The study of the Heterochaos baker diagrams provides new insights into the analysis of the Dyck system. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic graph. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN hinder its ability to learn a pitch representation. To overcome this, QPNet incorporates a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution layer in the network architecture. Experimental results in low-bitrate and medium-bitrate scenarios demonstrate a 50% improvement in the generation of speech and musical instrument recordings using quasiperiodic WaveNet. Additionally, the researchers found that incorporating auxiliary tasks, including a pitch classification objective and an error-minimization method for the Riemannian gradient of WaveNet, led to a 5-6 dB improvement in the fidelity of generated speech. However, these auxiliary tasks did not significantly impact the generation of musical instruments, likely due to the incorporation of the quasiperiodic convolution. Furthermore, the analysis shows that the generated spectrograms using quasiperiodic WaveNet exhibit lower errors and are closer to the true spectrograms across various frequencies. The waveforms generated by the model also exhibit lower L1 and L2 error rates when compared to WaveNet. To our knowledge, quasiperiodic WaveNet presents a novel application of dilated convolution neural networks in autoregressive generative models and achieves high-fidelity audio generation using this approach. The results have been validated through both subjective and objective evaluations and the code is available for download on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/zhengyuyes/qwaveNet.git. Recommender systems are now widely used and benefit society by addressing the information overload issue. However, many existing recommenders have not fully taken advantage of their potential. This research aims to leverage the characteristics of interactions (density) and user preferences (subjectivity) to develop a more precise prediction. To achieve this, a novel approach called BPR-BiClust is proposed. The proposed method involves dividing users and items into two-dimensional matrices, segregating users with similar preferences and matching them with shared interests. Subsequently, two machine learning techniques and the BPR-BiClust method are utilized to compare their ability to anticipate user interests on two publicly accessible datasets. The proposed method outperforms the control groups by at least 15.52% and significantly reduces data redundancy by up to 87.79%. Moreover, the experiment indicates that BPR-BiClust is robust against sparse preferences and indicative of users' subjective biases. Ultimately, the method offers a groundbreaking and efficient technique for processing preference data that considers both objectivity and locality. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/jjyang363/BiClust_BPR. In addition, the corresponding dataset can be found under the name User_Specific_BiClust.zip. Further information about this research is documented in the file README.txt. Results are also displayed on two public websites: https://jjyang363.github.io/BiClust_BPR and https://github.com/jjyang363/BiClust_BPR. Visual representations of the findings are presented in two figures, Figure S1 and Figure S2, located in the supplementary material. The relationship between magnetic activity and spectral features in stars is significant because it allows astronomers to estimate stellar parameters and correct the light curves of exoplanet candidates for the effects of stellar activity.  Despite extensive research on this topic, the dependence of spectral features in solar data from the HARPS-N project on magnetic activity remains unclear.  Researchers used linear regression models to analyze the variation in spectral features in solar data from the HARPS-N project, taking into account several activity markers, including line broadness, line depth, and line shifts.  They found a significant correlation between these features and the spectroscopic index, S(420), and proposed new empirical relationships to characterize the variation in spectral features in solar data from the HARPS-N project, and suggested these relationships for general use in stellar research.  Additionally, the researchers evaluated several activity indicators, and suggested modifications to improve their performance.  Based on the observed variations in spectral features, the researchers estimated that the HARPS-N solar runs contain between 80-90 percent stellar activity signals.  The researchers also explored the potential for spectroscopic bias in solar data from the HARPS-N project, and proposed future observations to distinguish between stellar and solar activity signals.  The researchers concluded that solar activity signals are strong enough to obscure the planetary signals that were previously observed in the HARPS-N solar runs, and predicted that similar complications may arise in stellar and planetary research.  The researchers suggested several strategies for future observers to mitigate the effects of solar activity signals in their data, and proposed observational experiments to confirm or refute the observed variation in spectral features.  The researchers used solar data from the A2V star HD189567 to verify the proposed relationships, and found a good match between the observed variation in spectral features and the predicted variation based on magnetic activity.  The researchers noted that further observations are needed to confirm the proposed relationships, and proposed future work to characterize the variation in spectral features in stellar data from the ESPRESSO project. Key concepts from the theory of shaded bicategories are then adapted to define the theory of $\mathfrak{Sh}$-equivalences between shaded bicategories, along with the associated universal property.  It is then demonstrated that the theory of shaded bicategories is equivalent to the theory of bicategories with tracking data, a concept first introduced by Harris.  Ultimately, it is shown that the theory of shaded Sieved bicategories is equivalent to the theory of Sieved 2-categories. We propose an innovative approach to applying pre-trained neural networks in a universal image enhancement task. By training a single model to distinguish between different picture pairs, we're able to develop multiple transformations - one to brighten images and another to dim them. This model can then be used to create various brightness levels from a single input image by finding a balance between the two opposing transformations. Furthermore, since the style of the original image remains consistent across different exposure levels, we set up a loss function that compares the features of the generated images to that of the original image, effectively extracting its style. This method allows for a single model to perform both forward (brightening) and reverse (dimming) tone mapping tasks while maintaining a consistent image style. We demonstrate high-quality results on the dataset created by Chen et al., also achieving the best objective and perceptual metrics compared to previous studies, and even outperforming a custom-trained model that was specifically designed for this task. Our method is also the first to apply domain disentanglement in the context of neural image enhancement. As a by-product, we've developed an interactive tool that allows users to adjust the exposure level of an image simply by combining the forward and reverse transformations in a desired proportion. We introduce a new approach to autonomous robot navigation that outperforms existing methods. This approach, based on a detailed model of the world, uses predictive methods to identify the most relevant sensory data and interprets observations as evidence to guide the robot's decision-making. Unlike traditional methods that simply analyze data, our approach focuses on simulating the robot's actions to create realistic predictions and compares these to actual observations to determine the most likely outcome. This is achieved through a dynamic network that incorporates the uncertainty associated with sensory data, allowing the robot to optimize its course based on evolving predictions and observations. This method, which requires no pre-training, demonstrates superior performance in challenging scenarios involving uncertain and changing environments. Additionally, our approach facilitates the discovery of hidden structures in the environment, as evidenced by a simulation example. This has numerous benefits, including improved trajectory planning and enhanced decision-making. In radiation damage detection for Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments, we employ a 3D sparse Time-Projection Chamber (TPC). Introducing noise due to damaged particles, it generates substantial fake hits that obstruct track reconstruction. To mitigate this issue, we utilize machine learning-based image compression by training a Dual Convolutional Autoencoder (DCAE) on simulated TPC images. By extracting key features from these images, we facilitate efficient data compression while utilizing a sparse coding technique to sparsify the data. Utilizing the DCAE, we compress and decompress mock detector images, with intermediate decompressed data serving as input for a classifier to identify damaged regions. This approach demonstrates promising results in reducing compressed data storage requirements while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy for classifier inputs. Notably, our method surpasses the performance of individual Convolutional Autoencoders and alternative methods like Sparse Network of Convolutional Autoencoders in feature extraction. With a trained DCAE, we achieve a 5:1 compression ratio for our test data, and as an added advantage, the decompressed data exhibits intuitively meaningful region-wise reconstruction. This contributes to easier physics analysis and understanding of underlying phenomena in LHC experiments. Additionally, our method is adaptable to various detector configurations with minimal modifications, making it universally applicable to similar contexts. We anticipate extending our research to other radiation damage detection cases and exploring the potential of our method to tackle the looming radiation challenges in the LHC's duration expansion. Moreover, we intend to delve into more sophisticated data compression and decomposition strategies with higher levels of sparse data utilization. Lastly, we aim to evolve our research into a fully sparse, multi-layered architecture for more complex cases and make our code available for public use on GitHub and ZenHub. It will include the reconstruction of I and II regions in region III and IV, respectively, as well as exploring other loss functions like Contrastive Loss for a more robust and efficient compression mechanism. This will enable us to efficiently decompress mock detector images and extract meaningful features for downstream analysis with a higher degree of sparsity (e.g., 10:1). We aim to delve into these enhancements in a future work. By generating radial data through Bayesian inference, our findings reveal similarities with observations, including a cool-core peak and a broad temperature distribution. Notably, our results align with NuSTAR and Chandra observations for the cool-core clusters and observe a cool-core peak in line with XMM-Newton's findings for the warm-core clusters. However, some discrepancies with respect to length scales and levels of relaxation remain. With the incorporation of massive dark matter particles, we've also fitted relaxed clusters from sample MCXC to obtain mass profiles and compared with observations. Our results demonstrate that Finzi's gravity model can effectively reproduce the diversity of galaxy clusters we observe. It's worth noting that using Finzi's gravity theory, we've obtained cooler temperatures and shorter length scales than $\Lambda$CDM. Additionally, our model exhibits less tension with respect to NuSTAR's data than to $\Lambda$CDM, despite both models displaying some level of tension. Furthermore, Finzi's gravity theory has prompted us to re-examine the relationship between length scales and relaxation levels, which has significant implications for understanding galaxy cluster evolution and its potential to be tested further using future surveys. Ultimately, our research suggests that Finzi's gravity theory can provide a compelling explanation for the diversity of galaxy clusters we observe, and it's worthy of additional scrutiny from disparate fields of observation in space as well as from future surveys on the ground. On the other hand, our model also shows that by incorporating long-range modifications to the gravity at a cluster scale, it's possible to alleviate some discrepancies between $\Lambda$CDM and observational data with respect to length scales and levels of relaxation. Wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication holds the potential to revolutionize the way we access the internet on the go. By enabling direct device-to-device interactions within the same frequency band, D2D technology has the potential to significantly boost network capacity, cut power consumption, and enhance user experience. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of D2D connections is heavily influenced by environmental factors like temperature, rain, and signal blockage which can make optimal link establishment and resource allocation a complex task. In this study, we break down the link establishment process into a step-by-step scheduling process and utilize a deep learning approach to develop a real-time scheduling system that can predict and maintain the quality of D2D links and maximize network data transfer. The move marks a significant shift from traditional scheduling methods. The proposed system, dubbed ViolaNet, features an autoencoder-based neural network capable of accurately modeling and simulating environmental factors and predicting channel loss to prioritize high-quality links and maximize data transfer efficiency. The findings from our simulations reveal that ViolaNet achieves an impressive 80% higher data transfer rate and maintains 90% better link quality compared to existing scheduling methods. Moreover, ViolaNet allows for real-time and adaptive optimization, enabling its efficient deployment on wireless D2D networks. The empirical results validate ViolaNet's superiority over other scheduling methods, demonstrating its potential for real-world implementation. The research brings wireless D2D scheduling into a new era of machine learning-based approaches. The experimentally-derived models and the ViolaNet framework are now accessible online, enabling the reproduction of the findings and future exploration of this novel scheduling paradigm. The move paves the way for further research in this area. The code for ViolaNet can be found at https://github.com/Abdelhakim-Moussa/ViolaNet. Additionally, the models used in this study are available at https://a-moussa.wixsite.com/scheduling-frames-workspace. The dataset for the project can be accessed via this link as well. The work will likely lead to an optimized solution for wireless D2D networks that balances link quality, data transfer efficiency, and power consumption for a more comprehensive analysis. A new concept for generating intense, coherent X-rays has been introduced using a technique called "gain enhancement." This technique utilizes an undulator-based free-electron laser oscillator to produce high-intensity, coherent X-ray pulses via amplification in a discharge-based, relativistic plasma. The feasibility of "gain enhancement" was evaluated using advanced simulation software and compared to a traditional free-electron laser scheme called "gain switching." Our study found that "gain enhancement" offers several advantages over "gain switching," including increased pulse energies, higher average flux levels, and a broader spectral range. Furthermore, the "gain enhancement" plasma can serve as a natural undulator, enabling the optimization of X-ray pulse characteristics through a second phase of free-electron laser oscillation, referred to as "fine tuning." This allows for independent control over the pulse duration and spectral range of the X-ray output, resulting in improved coherence properties and a higher peak intensity. The demonstration of a high-average-power, low-pulse-duration-narrowly-spectrally-distributed X-ray source represents a major breakthrough for the development and application of free-electron laser lasers. Identifying suspicious incidents on a network is a critical task. Traditional methods, such as those used in transportation and computer networks, can be ineffective when detecting malicious activities among individuals, as human behavior is often multi-dimensional and induced by various incidents. A novel approach is presented that recognizes incidents based on temporal graph networks and temporal network learning. This method utilizes deep learning with temporal graph networks, focusing on preserving the temporal and structural details of networks to analyze anomalies. Improved accuracy is achieved by incorporating the transmission of incident information, enabling the recognition of various incident types. Notably, this method can identify incidents without prior knowledge, including those occurring for the first time. Experimental evaluations with two real-world datasets confirm the outstanding performance of the approach, as it consistently detects more incident types with better precision than existing methods. Furthermore, a comparative study demonstrates that our approach outperforms traditional methods in transporting incident information across the network, as well as meta-learning and one-shot learning techniques that require significant labeled data to train. Ultimately, the proposed method generates actionable insights for incident prevention and mitigation by identifying nodes at risk of future incidents and the key factors contributing to their anomalies. This research enables the utilization of network structures and incident information to detect suspicious activities, facilitating loss reduction and performance enhancement in dynamic networks. In a recent study by Mundy et al., it was observed that a relativistic shock wave propagates through a uniform gas and then collides with a planar interface separating two gases with different densities. The research assumed that the energy released per unit area per unit time is constant, leading to a predictable outcome only if the density of the gas it's moving through remains the same. However, real-world conditions involve density variations, which cause the energy released to vary, making the model's predictions unreliable. To take advantage of this information, many researchers utilize Bayesian optimization techniques.  This work introduces an innovative strategy that treats the circuit coefficient search as a maximization problem, substituting traditional Bayesian optimization. Furthermore, BAMO allows the application of the no-overhead variational Bayesian optimization, thereby yielding substantial performance gains. Lastly, BAMO proves to be highly adaptable and yields satisfactory results even when applied to problems with unfamiliar problems with unfamiliar parameters. Additionally, we find that the total cohomology space of the milnor fiber consists of directly indecomposable components, which can be calculated through a simplified method when the fiber is smooth and the critical level set exhibits quasi-varietal coherence. Furthermore, for nonsingular milnor fibers, we refine the quasi-varietal coherence condition, removing the requirement for the coherence of its boundary and showing that the total cohomology space is composed of directly indecomposable components, which can also be calculated through a simplified method. Finally, we provide an explicit statement of algorithmically decomposing the milnor fiber into coherent components, along with a preliminary computational test case. The study offers novel insights and results, along with their accompanying computational implementation. The generated code is available at https://github.com/DZETC/MilnorFiberDecomposition. L. J. Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers. We invite developers to contribute to Daany's further development. Further information on Daany can be found at https://daany.netcore.io/. The library is freely accessible on NuGet at https://www.nuget.org/packages/Daany/. You can explore Daany's source code at https://github.com/serish/Daany. Instead, I believe that mathematics served a secondary function to the primary role played by philosophical debates in facilitating the revolution's occurrence. Historically, significant breakthroughs were not achieved through mathematics but rather motivated by and in response to contentious philosophical issues. This depiction is supported by an examination of the Scientific Revolution's earliest phase, focusing on the debates between Galileo and the Aristotelians. Galileo's early writings, though frequently characterized as mathematical, actually relied on conceptual metaphors that were rooted in his geometrically enhanced understanding of the physical world. Conversely, his influential works against the Aristotelians were grounded in philosophical disagreements rather than mathematical contributions. Moreover, Ignorantius is not merely seen as a response but also as a comprehensive summation of the philosophical disputes between Galileo and the Aristotelians, mirroring the general debates of the time. Ultimately, Galileo's success can be attributed to his proficiency in philosophical debate, and his failure to produce original mathematical innovations, and this alternative view of the Scientific Revolution offers a fresh and insightful perspective on the period. copybooks, thereby streamlining the copying process of active records or
database tables into JSON documents. This functionality is pivotal in creating
compatible data backups, facilitating data integration, and enabling seamless
interaction with JSON-based APIs. Within an Elixir application, Scribe enables
the generation of copybooks via a straightforward command or as an automatically
running task, thereby allowing developers to efficiently produce compatible
data backups. Additional details and usage guidelines for Scribe can be found
on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/district0/scribe. (This article was
